en: *The Collected Texts of the Perfect Teaching*, Scroll Fourteen:
Various Texts on the Categories of Practice and Stages, Part One;
*The Record of Investigating the Profundity*, Fascicle One.
To explain this sutra, I shall briefly open ten gates: (1) clarifying the reasons for the arising of the teaching (*yathā-pravṛtti*), and so forth, up to (10) the word-by-word commentary.
First, regarding the reasons for the arising of the teaching: first, a general discussion; second, a specific elucidation. As for the general discussion:

"Now, the causes and conditions for the emergence of the Great Teaching are immeasurable," and so forth. Next, as for the specific elucidation: I shall briefly present ten meanings to demonstrate their inexhaustibility. Why is this?

There are ten reasons: namely, by way of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), by the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), by the resonance of the capacity of beings (*sattvārtha*), by being the fundamental basis, by manifesting qualities, by manifesting stages, by bringing forth development, by seeing and hearing, by accomplishing practice, and by attaining the fruit (and so forth). Regarding the sixth, "by manifesting the stages":
this is to manifest that the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the single path to Buddhahood reaches its fruition through the possession of five stages; thus, this also has two parts.

First, the gate of sequential progression and distribution refers to the stages of the ten faiths, ten understandings, ten practices, ten transferences, and the ten grounds, after which one finally reaches the Buddha-ground;
this is the gradual succession of stages from the subtle to the manifest.

Second, the gate of perfect interpenetration and mutual inclusion means that within a single stage, all preceding and succeeding stages are subsumed; therefore, the fulfillment of each individual stage leads directly to Buddhahood.
Regarding these two [realms], their unimpeded vastness is as explained in the various assemblies of the text below (and so forth).

As for "because they bring about the fulfillment of practice," this means that in order to demonstrate this universal Dharma, it causes all Bodhisattvas to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra—wherein a single practice is all practices—and to attain perfect enlightenment at the very moment of the first resolve, being endowed with the body of wisdom and awakening not through another. Furthermore, it says: "Bodhisattva..."
To uphold this Dharma and, with little effort, swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and so forth—this also has two types:
first, achieving many practices all at once; second, achieving universal practices everywhere. Both are explained below.
Chapter on the Delimitation of Doctrinal Tenets, Middle Volume, Section Three:
The Differentiation of Stages and Positions. Within the various teachings, all briefly demonstrate this through three meanings: first, clarifying the characteristics of the stages;

second, distinguishing non-retrogression; and third, clarifying the aspects of practice. Regarding the first, according to the Hīnayāna, there are four stages, namely: the stage of skillful means (upāya).

Regarding the stages of seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*): it is further stated that the twelve abodes (*dvādaśāvasthā*) of the Hīnayāna constitute the ultimate, as well as the nine grounds (*navabhūmi*) and eleven grounds (*ekādaśabhūmi*) of the three realms (*traidhātuka*), as explained in detail in the *Hīnayāna-śāstra*.

As for those who are "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*), this is because they attain non-retrogression upon reaching the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) through their practice therein. Their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also as described in those various treatises. Question: For what reason [is this] in the Hīnayāna?

Question: Are the characteristics of the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and so forth not extensively revealed? Answer: The intention here is that the teachings differ according to the distinctions in their meanings;

since there is no doubt that the principles of the Hīnayāna differ from those of the Mahāyāna, it is unnecessary to explain them further. Furthermore, even according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), the characteristics of the initial stage are revealed through three meanings.
Within this, there are three: first, to lead those of the Two Vehicles who follow the Dharma of the Ignorant (*bāla-dharman*); second... [text continues]... third... [text continues].

Because they have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], the teaching for those who have turned their minds is established; it likewise consists merely of the four stages of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as well as the names of the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), which are the same as in the Hīnayāna.

Alternatively, five stages are established: within the seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*) prior to the path of seeing, the first three are designated as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) because they are distant preparations, while the latter four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are designated as the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) because they are proximate.

By way of skillful means, the names of the remaining stages are the same as before; furthermore, they are also described as the ten stages beginning with "Dry Wisdom" (*śuklavidarśana*), where the ninth is named the "Bodhisattva Stage" (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) and the tenth is named the "Buddha Stage" (*buddhabhūmi*).
This is because, in order to lead those of the Two Vehicles, these are insufficient when compared to the higher [stages], and thus one must practice gradually until reaching the fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, that fruit of Buddhahood does not exist outside of the ten stages but is included within them, because it leads [the practitioner] [to the ultimate].

For that reason, the skillful means are the same as theirs; furthermore, because those of the two vehicles attain the fruits of sainthood within their present bodies, they do not belong to a subsequent stage.
Moreover, the characteristics of this stage and the characteristics of its practice are explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śrāvaka-viniścaya* and the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
Question: Why do the characteristics of the stages and practices of the śrāvakas elucidated in the *Yogācāra-bhūmi* and other texts differ?
Regarding the fact that the answers in the *Abhidharma* and other treatises differ from those here, there are two intended meanings:
first, to reveal that the followers of the Hīnayāna are deluded regarding all phenomena and fail to understand them; second, as a skillful means (*upāya*), to gradually lead them toward the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the teachings on the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and so forth explained herein are all skillful means taught in accordance with the Mahāyāna; this is why they differ. This...
Since it is neither the Dharma of the ignorant Hīnayāna nor that of the Bodhisattvas, one knows it to be the Śrāvaka-yāna among those teachings of the three vehicles.

Second, regarding the manifestation of the stages for those who advance directly: it explains the distinctions of the ten bodhisattva stages (*daśabhūmi*), further characterizing these ten stages as the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the stage common to those prior to the stages;
this constitutes the meaning of the twelve abodes (*dvādaśavihāra*) of the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because it resembles the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Furthermore, those [stages] prior to the grounds consist of forty minds;

since the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) also constitute distinct positions, these [stages] likewise resemble the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) preceding the path of the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore, the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:

"Just as there are four stages prior to the path of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), namely: Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*)."

The four stages prior to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi in the Dharma [Vehicle] are likewise: namely, the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Furthermore, because this is also a teaching for those who have "turned their minds" [from the Śrāvaka path], these four stages of faith and so forth constitute the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra-avasthā*).

Following the ten dedications, the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśala-mūlāni*) are separately established as the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). The stages of seeing (*darśana*) and so forth are the same as previously described. Question: For what reason is it that in this teaching...
Question: Why are the established names and numerical categories for the most part similar to those of the Śrāvaka-vehicle and others? Answer: It is because they conform to skillful means (*upāya*).

They appear similar in order to attract those [of other vehicles], as there exist superior skillful means; for if they were entirely different from them, it would be difficult for them to believe and accept, and if they were entirely the same as them, they could not be said to be "attracting" [them].

Question: If one is attracting those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), it may be necessary to resemble them; but for those who proceed directly [to the Mahāyāna], why rely on such a semblance of the Lesser Vehicle?
The answer is that there are two intentions, and thus it also somewhat resembles the Hīnayāna.

First, because the faculties of those who progress directly within the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna) are coarse and shallow, they cannot fully receive the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna; therefore, the dharmalakṣaṇas such as the stages shown to them resemble those of the Hīnayāna, yet their underlying principles remain distinct.
Second, all instances where the Mahāyāna is taught through terminology resembling the Hīnayāna apply to both [the Initial and Final Teachings].
The first meaning is to lead [beings] forward; the second is for those of shallow capacity. Therefore, this is called the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).
Regarding the meaning of "how" and so forth, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "What is the characteristic of a person (*pudgala*) who has already achieved accomplishment?
It refers to those śrāvakas who, having previously familiarized themselves with various wholesome dharmas, at whatever time they abide in a state of inferior accomplishment, at that time..."
If one possesses inferior aspiration and inferior application, one still goes to the evil destinies;

one does not realize the fruits of śrāmaṇya in the present life, nor does one attain parinirvāṇa in the present life. When one dwells in middling accomplishment, at that time one possesses middling aspiration and middling application;
one does not go to the evil destinies and realizes the fruits of śrāmaṇya in the present life.

If one does not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, yet at the time one abides in the highest degree of accomplishment, then there will be superior aspiration, superior application, and no rebirth in the evil destinies;
one realizes the fruit of śrāmaṇya in the present life and attains parinirvāṇa in this very life. As it is said for the śrāvaka, so it is for the pratyekabuddha as well. Why is that?

Because the path is identical to that of the śrāvaka lineage, and so forth, it is explained at length that even within the stage of a bodhisattva, three kinds of accomplishment are established as being similar to those of the two vehicles.
That treatise states: "If bodhisattvas dwell in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), it is called inferior accomplishment;

if they dwell in the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), it is called middling accomplishment; if they dwell in the stage of certainty (*niyata-patita-bhūmi*)," [it is called superior accomplishment].

The stage of the ultimate culmination of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "superior accomplishment. If a bodhisattva abides in even "inferior accomplishment," they may still go to the evil destinies;
this lasts for the entirety of the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and so forth, as explained at length. The remaining two great eons are assigned to the other two accomplishments.
There are numerous such textual variations, all of which should be understood by applying the aforementioned intent.

Regarding the second point, the stage of non-retrogression: according to the *Buddhatva-śāstra*, Śrāvakas reach non-retrogression at the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, Pratyekabuddhas at the stage of *laukikāgra-dharma*, and Bodhisattvas at the tenth stage of *pariṇāmanā*.

One should know that herein, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not "foolish dharmas"; therefore, they are all practitioners of the Three Vehicles within this Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*). Furthermore, it may also be [understood as] Bodhisattvas...

Prior to the *bodhisattva* stages (*bhūmi*), they are collectively described as subject to regression because they still fall into the various evil destinies (*durgati*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"If bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) still go to the evil destinies, this continues until the end of the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)," and so forth.
Regarding the distinctions in the characteristics of practice within these three stages, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The stage of practice through resolute belief..."
When dwelling in the stage of a Bodhisattva’s transformation, what is their practice and what are their characteristics?
At times they are fully endowed with wisdom, capable of receiving and upholding all dharmas, and able to penetrate their underlying principles; at other times they are not thus;
at times they are fully endowed with mindfulness, while at other times they fall into a state of delusion regarding sentient beings.
Although they are able to understand the skillful means for disciplining others, they have not yet realized the skillful means for correctly eliciting [realization] within their own Buddha-dharma;
thus, when they teach, instruct, admonish, and urge others to practice, because they do so through mere exertion rather than through realization, they cannot know things as they truly are.
At times, they waste their efforts in vain, like shooting in the dark, where whether they hit the mark or miss it depends merely on whether their desires are fulfilled.
At one time, having already generated the mind for great enlightenment, they subsequently abandon it;
out of intentionality, they desire their own happiness, and out of discursive deliberation, they desire the happiness of others.

Or, at another time, upon hearing the teaching of the profound and vast Dharma, they give rise to alarm, fear, hesitation, and doubt. Such categories as these are called the "stage of practice through resolute conviction."
It is said that this is the second stage of the twelve stages (*dvādaśa-vihāra*), while the characteristics of the first stage of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*) are even more inferior;
furthermore, the characteristics of the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*) are all as described therein.

According to the Final Teaching (*paryanta-śāsana*), the distinctions among the ten bodhisattva grounds are also explained, yet they are not designated by such names as "seeing" (*darśana*) or "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). Moreover, prior to the grounds, there are only the three levels of the worthy ones (*tri-kalyāṇaka*).

Faith is merely a practice and not yet a stage (*bhūmi*), for one has not yet attained non-retrogression. The *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma) states that prior to ascending to the stages (*vihāra*), these ten minds exist, but it does not refer to them as "stages.

It further states: "From the ground of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) onward, when encountering the Buddha or Bodhisattvas within the correct teaching, if one gives rise to a single thought of faith and awakens the bodhicitta, at that time this person is said to be 'prior to the stages' (*vihāra-pūrva*)."
The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa is also called the Bodhisattva of Provisional Names or the Bodhisattva of Names.
Such a person briefly cultivates ten mental states, namely faith, diligence, and so forth, as explained at length in that same text. Furthermore, the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states:

"Prior to the stage of 'Cultivating Patience' (*śikṣā-kṣānti*), the bodhisattva practicing the ten wholesome paths may advance or retreat, like a light feather drifting east and west with the wind; it is here that such cultivation occurs."

Because one enters the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) after ten thousand *kalpas* before attaining non-retrogression, it follows that from the very beginning of the Ten Abodes one does not retrogress into the lower stages of the Two Vehicles,

let alone into the realms of evil destinies or the stage of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). As for the statement in the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma) that there is retrogression at the sixth mind of the Ten Abodes,
the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on Awakening Faith) explains that passage as being intended to demonstrate retrogression for the purpose of [correcting] pride.
Those who are lax should rouse their minds; thus, when a Bodhisattva enters the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*), they immediately attain non-retrogression.

As for its characteristics, the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states that within the initial stage of the Three Sages (*trividha-śaikṣa*), one attains a partial vision of the Dharmakāya and is able to manifest the eightfold path of enlightenment (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa-abhisambodhi*) throughout the worlds of the ten directions to benefit sentient beings, further assuming bodies through the power of vows.
Mastery is also not bound by karma; furthermore, by relying on samādhi, one may also obtain a partial vision of the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*.

All that they practice accords with true nature (*dharmatā*); that is to say, knowing that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, they practice in accordance with the *dānapāramitā* and so forth, as explained at length therein.
Moreover, in the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the ten stages of faith are called "ordinary person bodhisattvas."
"Explanation" refers to the sages, bodhisattvas, and others; their stages of practice on the grounds are understood to be double those of the preceding [teachings].

Therefore, one should know that the distinctions between the shallow and deep characteristics of the stages of practice herein and those of the previous Initial Teaching (Śākyadeśanā) are now clearly revealed.

Question: Does this teaching not also universally cite the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha)? Why then do its stages of practice not resemble those described for the Lesser Vehicle? Answer: All subsequent teachings... [are likewise].

All [stages] are induced by the profound and supreme; even the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are purely established for those of superior capacity, and thus do not require a semblance of them.
If one relies on the Sudden Teaching (dun jiao), all practices and stages are ineffable because they are free from marks (lakṣaṇa);

for when not a single thought arises, one immediately attains Buddhahood. To perceive distinctions such as the differences between practices and stages is itself a perversion (viparyāsa). If one speaks by way of metaphorical reliance...
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The first stage is itself the eighth stage," and so on, up to: "What sequence of stages could there be?

Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* says: "If a person hears this true nature of all phenomena and exerts themselves with diligence, practicing according to the teaching, they do not go from one stage to another;
if they do not go from one stage to another, such a person..."
Regarding such matters as abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there are two meanings:
first, it subsumes the stages and practices elucidated in the preceding teachings, as these serve as its skillful means; second, based on the Separate Teaching (Biejiao), there are three meanings:
first, manifesting by way of provisional stations, meaning that from the ten faiths up to the stage of Buddhahood, the six stages are distinct, and one may attain any of them accordingly.

One attains all stages because they are subsumed by the six aspects: the aspect of the principal and its retinue, the aspect of mutual inclusion, the aspect of mutual identity, and the aspect of perfect interfusion.
As the Sūtra says: "Abiding in a single stage, one universally encompasses the merits of all stages.
Therefore, within the Sūtra, at the stage of the final advancement of the ten faiths, one attains all stages as well as the Buddha-stage.

This is the meaning of that matter. Furthermore, because the various stages and the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) are mutually identical and so forth, cause and effect are non-dual and the beginning and end are unimpeded;
thus, within each and every stage, one is simultaneously a bodhisattva and a buddha—this is the principle.
Second, regarding the clarification of the characteristics of the stages by way of retribution (*vipāka*), there are only three births (as explained in the "Three Births" section).

Third, regarding the clarification of the stages (*bhūmi*) by way of practice, there are only two: namely, the stage of self-maintenance (*svabhāva-bhāga*) and the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).

This gate encompasses the preceding stages, being explained in terms of the limits of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) and the stage of attaining the Dharma (*dharmaprāpti*), such as that of the youth Samantavyūha and others.

As for his body, it abides in a world-system equal to [the number of] atoms; he should be understood as residing in the rank of the White Pure Jewel-Net Universal Monarch (*śvetapariśuddharatnajāla-cakravartin*).

One attains the "universal-seeing" fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which perceives world-oceans as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields; this is not the case for the fleshly eyes of the Three Vehicles.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The fleshly eye sees only that which is within the three-thousandfold world system" (and so forth).
Question: Since all stages are contained within a single stage, and one attains Buddhahood upon the fulfillment of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa-citta*), why is it necessary to...?
Question: Does the teaching regarding the subsequent stages mean that what is first and last is identical to everything?

As it is with the beginning, so it is with the end. Question: If the beginning already possesses the end, and by attaining the beginning one attains the end, then since the end also possesses the beginning, if one does not attain the end, should one likewise not attain the beginning?
Answer: It is indeed so; however, at the time of attaining the beginning, there is no [attainment of the end].
Because one cannot obtain the later [attainment] first, there is no case where one has not obtained the later yet obtains the initial. Question:

If this is so, why is it said that one attains the various stages in a descending order? Answer: This is because within this scripture, the establishment of the various stages possesses two types of skillful means (*kauśalya*):
first, regarding their characteristics and access points, the sequence of the stages is provisionally aligned with the three vehicles (*triyāna*) as a skillful means to guide those practitioners.
This is the "Teaching of Commonality" (tóngjiào). Second, regarding the essence (*tǐ*) in terms of phenomena (*fǎ*), their mutual entry before and after is perfectly interfused and sovereign;

this is distinct from the Three Vehicles and is thus the "Distinct Teaching" (biéjiào). However, because they are constantly identical through the gate of non-displacement (*bùyí mén*), yet remain constantly sequential despite that identity, these two meanings are harmoniously integrated and do not contradict one another. Question: If this is so, then is the first gate itself all things?
Question: Why do you not say that one attains [realization] at the initial stage of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), but instead speak of the final stage and so forth?

Answer: If one were following the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), one would not rely on the stages for accomplishment; however, here we are speaking by way of the final teaching of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). (As seen in the "Three Kinds of Birth and Species.")
*Tanxuan ji*, Fascicle 1 (The Essential Purpose): 7.

Specifically opening up the inclusion of the *dharmadhātu* to establish cause and effect. This means that the *dharmadhātu* of Samantabhadra is the cause, and the *dharmadhātu* of Vairocana is the fruit.
Therefore, the essential purpose consists solely of the cause and fruit of the *dharmadhātu*. Within this, there is further differentiation.

Regarding the ten matters in five pairs: first, the cause and effect of what is to be believed, as explained in the "Lotus Treasury World" chapter within the first assembly, where the fruit of the Lotus Treasury World is clarified first, followed by the revelation of the cause of universal adornment;

second, the differentiated cause and effect, as taught from the second assembly through the "Minor Characteristics" chapter, wherein the first twenty-five chapters explain the differentiated causes of the five stages, and the final three...
The chapter explains the differentiation of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) as the fruit, while the three equalities refer to cause and effect:

the nature of the universal cause is explained in the "Universal Good" (*Samantabhadra*) chapter, and the fulfillment of the equal fruit is explained in the "Arising of Nature" (*Tathāgatotpatti-nirdeśa*) chapter. These two preceding sections concern the cause and effect for generating understanding.

As for the cause and effect for accomplishing practice, they are as described in the "Transcending the World" (*Lokottara*) chapter, where among the two thousand dharma-practices, the causal practices are first clarified and the resultant fruit is subsequently revealed.

The practice of the five modes of realization (*pañca-praveśa*) regarding cause and effect is as follows: first, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśaparivarta*), the fruit of mastery is manifested within the Jeta Grove;

subsequently, Sudhana elucidates the causes for realizing these modes of entry. Thus, the five cycles of cause and effect throughout this entire section are completed (etc., see the section on "Doctrinal Purport").

Regarding the second part of the *Tanyuan ji* (Exploring the Profundities), the "Exegesis Following the Text" for the tenth section: This scripture of thirty-six thousand verses consists of seven locations and eight assemblies.

Specifically, there are three locations among humans and four locations in the heavens, making seven assemblies in total; the Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsa*) constitutes the eighth assembly. Within these:

There are thirty-four chapters. The first chapter is the introductory section (*nidāna*). From the "Vairocana Chapter" onwards, the main body (*saddharma*) and the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*) are clarified.

Whether the dissemination section exists or not is explained through four meanings: First, from the verse beginning with "The mind of sentient beings and a mote of dust," two verses constitute the dissemination section, as they serve to conclude the praise and encourage faith.
Second, because the transmission of the sutra was incomplete, the dissemination section is missing. Third, for the sake of this sutra... [text ends]
Because this is taught as the Dharma-gate of the Dharmadhātu, there is no general circulation [of the text]. Question: If that is so, how can there be an introductory section (nidāna)? Answer:

Because there is seeing and hearing through which one universally enters, there is a beginning, which serves as the introduction; because that which is entered is infinite, there is no end, which constitutes the circulation.
It is like the cultivation of the Buddha-fruit, which has a beginning but no end. If it were not so, why would there be the eight [sections]?
In each of the sixteen assemblies of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there is no separate circulation text at the conclusion of those assemblies;
whereas in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, such circulation texts exist at the end of every assembly.

Since this [present] sūtra is not like that, we know that its distinct structure indicates a specific underlying intention. Fourth, it employs the dharmas of the other three vehicles and so forth to accord with the differences among sentient beings' capacities.
Benefiting sentient beings constitutes the aspect of the benefit of circulation. Furthermore, the Great Dharma Master Fayuan divided this sutra into four sections:
first, the "Section on the Expedient Origin for Purifying the Faculties"; second, the "Vairocana Section," titled "Section on Proclaiming the Thesis and Encouraging Resolve";

third, from the "Section on Names and Titles" down to the eighth assembly, titled "Section on Manifesting the Path and Encouraging Cultivation"; and fourth, the final section concerning Samantabhadra.
The recitation of the verses is called the Section on Entrustment and Circulation. Now, examining the subsequent text as a whole, it is divided into five parts:

First, the first chapter is the Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching; second, within the Śamantabhadra Chapter, one cycle of question and answer is called the Section on Exalting the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith;
third, from the second assembly through the sixth assembly, one cycle of question and answer is called the Section on Cultivating the Causes.

The section on "The Realization of Fruition Arising from Understanding" is divided into four parts; the first cycle of questions and answers within the seventh assembly is titled "Entrusting the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct.

The section on "Relying on Persons to Enter Realization and Accomplish Virtue" is divided into five parts; the second cycle of questions and answers within the eighth assembly is titled [the aforementioned].

Regarding the circulation of these sections, they have already been distinguished above. These five parts all rely upon what precedes to give rise to what follows, such that the sequence of the texts gives rise to their meanings.
Because the principle is complete and sufficient, there is neither addition nor subtraction.

In the third volume of the *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities), in the second chapter on Vairocana Buddha, from this point downward, the main body of the teaching (*zhengzong*) is elucidated; to explain this text, it is analyzed according to four gates.

First, the explanation of the title; second, the purpose of the coming [of the teaching]; third, the essential tenets; fourth, the commentary on the text (and so forth). Within the fourth section, the commentary on the text, there are two parts:

first, a general discussion of the boundaries of the explanations in the sūtras and śāstras as a skillful means for generating understanding; second, the specific commentary on the main body of the text (and so forth).

From this, one can know [the answer].
Moreover, the *Benye jing* (Sutra of Primary Karma) mentions only forty-two sages and saints and does not speak of fifty-two; thus, one may inquire [about the discrepancy].

If that is so, why does the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) state that the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), yet still establishes only the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-piṭaka-ārya*)?
Answer: This is because they mutually encompass one another. How so? According to the underlying meaning, there are four propositions:

first, because the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is subsumed within the fundamental stage, there are only the three stages of the worthy ones; thus, the name "faith" is omitted, and only the actual abiding stages (*vihāra*) are discussed. The supporting textual evidence for this can be found [in the sūtras].

Second, because the provisional means (*upāya*) subsume the fundamental stages, the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) are termed the "ten faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*); thus, the name "ten abidings" is subsumed within the "ten faiths.
Therefore, the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "The ten faiths, the ten cessations, and the ten upright minds do not discuss the ten abidings, but are simply called the ten faiths.
Third, because the provisional means are opened up as distinct from the fundamental stages, there are these ten minds prior to the abidings that serve as the provisional means.

These four [stages] are provisionally designated as the "correct position" (*samyaktva*) within the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), as previously explained in the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*). If categorized according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are two meanings:

first, if based on the self-dharma of Samantabhadra, all are without position; second, if categorized by way of metaphorical attribution (*prajñapti*), they are identical to the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*).
However, at the juncture of entering the position through the fulfillment of faith, all subsequent positions are subsumed therein; there is nothing that does not reside within this.

To be fully endowed with this is because it subsumes the stages according to practice. Question: Since faith is actually devoid of a formal stage (*bhūmi*), why does the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*) describe it as a stage?

Answer: Because the faculties of those for whom the Initial Teaching is intended are coarse and their wisdom shallow; since their stages of practice are not clearly distinguished and merely resemble those of the Hīnayāna, four stages are taught. However, because the faculties of those for whom the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) are subtle and their wisdom deep, they are distinguished according to actual reality.

The Five Aspects of Practice: 1. The aspect of the object of focus (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*). 2. The aspect of mental application (*manasikāra-lakṣaṇa*). 3. The aspect of the mode of activity (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*). 4. The aspect of the attainment of fruit (*phala-prāpti-lakṣaṇa*). 5. The aspect of the distinction between the superior and the inferior (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding these, in the Initial Teaching (śākyadeśanā), it refers to the practice of the ten mental states, such as faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth.

In the Final Teaching (niṣṭhādeśanā), it refers to the four kinds of faith and the five gates of cultivation as set forth in the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*), and so forth. In the Perfect Teaching (pariniṣpannadeśanā), it refers to what is explained in these three grades [of practitioners], and so forth.

Sixth, regarding the removal of hindrances: in the Initial Teaching, as previously mentioned, it removes the hindrance of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) in those who are icchantikas; in the Final Teaching, it is as follows...

Regarding the discussion on the profound subduing of afflictions, etc. (as detailed), and the fact that in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), as the text states, the hundred obstacles are entirely extinguished, etc.

(as detailed)—these all refer to the time when the mind is fulfilled. As for the seven types of "advancing and retreating," those who have cultivated faith but have not yet completed ten thousand kalpas will all regress because they belong to the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi).
This is according to the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma), which likens them to light feathers following the wind, etc.
[Question: It is said that even if one possesses the sixth stage of non-retrogression, this is merely the cultivation of such a mind of non-retrogression;

because it is not yet the actual stage, one has not attained non-retrogression. Furthermore, some interpret this as "non-retrogression through faith" (*śraddhā-avivartika*), but this interpretation seems untenable.
For the sutras state that [such a person] is like light feathers and lacks a fixed station, and the treatises state that they have cultivated faith for less than ten thousand kalpas.
Because every *kalpa* involves regression, if faith were already perfected by the tenth thousandth *kalpa*, it would not constitute the sixth stage;

therefore, according to the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*), faith is described as a stage in accordance with coarse characteristics. Consequently, the subsequent three stages of the *pṛthagjana* (the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences) are also described in accordance with coarse characteristics.
Thus, it is only upon reaching the ten transferences that one attains non-regression, as stated in the first fascicle of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
Question: Since that treatise records the assertions of the Sarvāstivāda masters, how can it be considered Mahāyāna? Answer:

Although these are indeed the assertions of the Sarvāstivādins, they do not belong to their own school because [the treatise] speaks of ten stages of the *pariṇāmanā* (dedication of merit), whereas such stages do not exist in the Hīnayāna.

If, according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*), one enters the stage of "abiding in the fulfillment of faith," this constitutes non-retrogression; as stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, when faith is perfected, one enters [the path].
This is because of the non-retrogression of the resolve (*cittotpāda*), as well as the subsequent passage stating that the profound mind and pure faith are indestructible, and so forth.
Because they are identical in their ultimate fulfillment, it is only after entering the stages (*bhūmi*) that they are designated as "non-retrogressive faith.

This is because the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, just as in the case of the eightfold virtues such as "faith-patience" (*kṣānti*). Furthermore, regarding the "attainment of pure virtue" within the Initial Teaching (*śrāvaka-yāna*), it is the cause for attaining the iron-like [stage].
The retribution of a Wheel-Turning King can also enter the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) and other levels of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*).

Once the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) has been accomplished, one is then able to see, even in part, the Dharmakāya Buddha manifesting the eight signs of attaining enlightenment and so forth (and so on). In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the subsequent stages are thoroughly accomplished:

if considered from the perspective of the cause, the three karmas of Samantabhadra pervade the entire Dharma-realm; if considered from the perspective of the fruit, they pervade all worlds within the dust motes.
Regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment, as stated by Bhadrapāla in the *Dvayāloka-parivarta*, the central theme (*artha*) consists of ten profound meanings;

its purpose is to establish faith, and its objective is the practice of understanding. Fifth, concerning the explanation of the text: herein, the three chapters constitute three stages—the first chapter clarifies faith and understanding;
the second chapter, based on that understanding, gives rise to practice; and the final chapter represents the perfection of virtue through the completion of understanding and practice.
Furthermore, [the commentary] explains the virtues of the initial practices and subsequent vows (and so forth).
In the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), this chapter is explained by means of four gates: first, the explanation of the title (and so forth);

second, the purpose for its inclusion, which is that it is included in order to consolidate the preceding practices and vows into the vast and great virtuous functions of Samantabhadra; third, the essential doctrine...

Regarding "the destination" (*gati*): this clarifies that the essence, characteristics, and functions of the stage of Samantabhadra’s practice are vast and boundless, encompassing both beginning and end.

It should be understood as belonging to the gate of faith (*śraddhā-mukha*), which subsumes all stages and leads to the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood; this is what is elucidated here. Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text:

herein there are two parts—first the question, then the answer. Within the question, there are also two parts: first, the sequence established by the sūtra compiler, and second, the reason for the text [being thus arranged].

Regarding the response of the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha) to the special inquiry: it is through faith that the myriad practices are gathered; without the virtue of the Sublime (Maitreya), there would be no way to initiate this faith. It encompasses the six stages;
without the virtue of the Worthy (Mañjuśrī), there would be no way to proclaim it (and so forth). Within the response of the Worthy Leader, there are three hundred and sixty-three verses in total:
the first fifteen are five-character lines, and the subsequent three hundred and fifty-seven are seven-character lines; among these, the total length is as follows.

There are eight sections: first, the section praising the profundity and difficulty of explanation; second, the section briefly indicating the modes of practice; third, the section briefly distinguishing superior capabilities;
fourth, the section subsuming all stages of practice; fifth, the section on boundless great functions; sixth, the section using metaphors to illustrate the profound intent;
seventh, the section on comparative evaluation and exhortation to resolve; and eighth, the section revealing the realization of reality. Within the first section, there are seven verses, among which:
This is divided into three parts; the first two clarify the virtue of the extensive and the concise explanation (as detailed in the section on "Generating the Bodhicitta").
Question: For what reason can a bodhisattva at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) possess such vast and great merit? Answer: This is the merit of Samantabhadra’s practice within the *dharmadhātu*.
It is merely manifested here through the gateway of faith; therefore, it cannot be fully described. If one were to analyze it exhaustively, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, if one distinguishes [the stages] solely by way of the gate of faith according to their respective levels of progression, then this faith pertains only to the stage of the wholesome realms (*sugati*), like light feathers and so forth;
as is taught in the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-alaṃkāra-sūtra* (Yingluo benye jing) and the *Ratnaketu-rāja-sūtra* (Renwang jing).

Second, if one distinguishes them solely by way of the essential virtues of Samantabhadra, it is as taught in the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" (*Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*). Third, both are meant: that is, by way of...
That "gate of faith" reveals these virtues of Samantabhadra as explained in this chapter;

this is spoken in terms of the causal stage (*hetu-bhāga*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which may be categorized as four, both, or neither, as it cannot be definitively stated. This is spoken in terms of the resultant stage (*phala-bhāga*).

Therefore, the "stage of faith" (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) clearly taught in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) differs in its meaning from the "ten stages of faith" (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*) within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). Second.
From "Because it is not without cause" onwards, six verses clarify the section on the brief indication of the mode of practice;
herein, first, one verse provides a general heading, while the subsequent verses explain the reasons why the arousal of the mind is so vast (and so forth).
Third, from "The profound mind and pure faith are indestructible" onwards, nine verses clarify the section on the brief discernment of superior capabilities; herein, the first two clarify faith.

The ability to accomplish the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is due to this being the root of practice; the subsequent seven [perfections] clarify that faith can accomplish the remaining virtues because it is the basis of practice (and so forth).

Furthermore, regarding "faith that cannot be destroyed" within these [seven], it means that through the attainment of the perfection of faith, one reaches the stage of non-retrogression; thus, it is called "indestructible.

Since the arousal of the mind is based upon this faith, we know that this mind has already entered and abided [in the stages]. However, this is stated in terms of the skillful means (*upāya*) by which one enters.
Therefore, following the section on Faith, this concludes the explanation of the perfection of virtue (*guṇa*).

It not only establishes the preceding stage of the initial resolve at the beginning of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), but also extends to establish all the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) within the subsequent stages.
For this reason, the twenty merits to be accomplished herein are briefly set forth: first, the ability to generate merit and wisdom—namely, the source of awakening and the mother of blessings.
(As stated above) Nineteen: The Gate of Long-Cultivated Wisdom; Twenty: Manifesting the Fruit of Sublime Enlightenment.
Of these, the first eighteen pertain to the qualities of one’s own level (*svabhūmi*), while the latter twelve constitute the virtues of further advancement (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).
These merits are all virtues accomplished in subsequent stages up to the stage of Buddhahood, yet they are all achieved within the state of faith. (As stated above). Fourth.

If one has faith and respects the teachings, there are fifty verses below that clarify the section on "the extensive inclusion of the stages of practice. Within this, there are two parts: first, the inclusion of practice;
second, from "if one generates the unsurpassed bodhicitta" onwards, the inclusion of the stages (as explained at length).

Regarding the second part, the inclusion of the stages, the inclusion of the final four stages constitutes four sections. The first consists of two and a half verses clarifying the inclusion of the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), namely: Bodhi... [text continues].

Focusing the mind is the practice of entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). Diligently cultivating the virtues of a Buddha is the practice of the second stage, the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*).
Being born into the family of the Buddhas is the Stage of Noble Birth (*janma-vaṃśa*), meaning one is born into the Buddha-family with a noble lineage.
Non-attachment is the practice of the fifth and sixth stages. Profound mind and wondrous purity are the practices of the seventh and eighth stages. These are distinct.
The "supreme unsurpassed mind" refers to the ninety-two stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), all of which may be understood according to the preceding explanations.

Second, regarding the attainment of the "absence of above and below," the three verses clarify the inclusion of the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*). Within these, the *pāramitās* collectively enumerate the ten practices.

The Mahāyāna is distinct from the practice methods of the Hīnayāna. "Offerings to the Dharma" refers to practice in accordance with principle, namely the first four practices. "Recollection of the Buddha" [refers to the remaining six].
Samādhi is the practice of departing from delusion and confusion, seeing that the Buddha is eternally abiding; these latter five practices are subsumed under Prajñā.
Third, from "If one knows the Tathāgata" onwards, two and a half verses clarify the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Within this, because the practice is accomplished in accordance with principle, the Dharma is said to exist forever—meaning it is the Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Dharmadhātu—and thus the saving of sentient beings is explained.

This "rescuing sentient beings" refers to the meaning of dedicating [merit] toward sentient beings through various gateways, as seen in the preceding seven dedications which involve the relinquishing of the characteristics of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*).

"Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) refers to the great compassionate practice accomplished within this stage, which serves as the antidote for abandoning the obstacle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) who lack great compassion.
4. From "If one attains great compassion" onwards, there are thirty-three verses that clarify the inclusion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The first half-verse of the middle section summarizes the first bhūmi; that is to say, "rejoicing in the profound dharma" refers to the pervasive *tathatā* (suchness) realized in the first stage, the Stage of Great Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
(And so forth. Twenty-one and a half verses clarify the tenth bhūmi, which is divided into three parts:
first, thirteen and a half verses clarify the excellence of the three types of action (body, speech, and mind). (And so forth. Second, if...
The four verses beginning with "The seeds of the ten stages" clarify the section on receiving the position at the final moment of the ten stages;

the phrase "this consecration with the water of ambrosia" clarifies that one receives the office within the fulfillment of this faith. Third, the four verses beginning with "If the body... clarify the conclusion, praise, and manifestation of its excellence.
The first [verse] clarifies that entering the principle is profound and vast, such that neither devas nor humans can know it; it states that this *dharmakāya* fills the ten directions of space.
Because this movement is such, within this peerless realm (*asamasama-dhātu*), neither the devas nor the people of the world can know it.

Next, regarding the accomplishment of the fruit through practice: the benefit derived from seeing and hearing is vast; there is nothing among one's original practices that does not bear fruit, for since all that was sought has been completed, there is nothing that does not reach its fulfillment.
Furthermore, as explained in the "Chapter on the Dharma" below: those who see, hear, or make offerings shall all abide in non-retrogression.

Because it does not regress from the stage [of realization], it is said to be "not empty. The next one and a half verses concern the power that protects the Dharma and constantly benefits others without interruption;

as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "That this sūtra remains in the world is due entirely to the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya. Furthermore, the first [half-verse] concerns the essence, the next the qualities, and the last the function.

The latter half of the verse concludes the preceding lines: the first phrase concludes wisdom (*prajñā*) and the second phrase concludes merit (*puṇya*), both of which are inexhaustible like the ocean.
Regarding the statement that within this gateway of faith, the successive links of the chain encompass these ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth:
it is because faith is the primordial source of the Path and the mother of all merit; since the characteristics of all stages and practices are accomplished through faith, it is as stated above:

"Faith can transform and excel, bringing all practices to completion and leading one to the abode of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is said: "Abiding in the first stage, [one pervades] universally..."

The subsumption of all the merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*) is the teaching of the perfect dharma of this Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*); within the Three Vehicles, it is not possible in such a manner.
Fifth, from the passage "In some lands... downwards, there are two hundred and fifty verses clarifying the section on the boundlessly great activity;
because one attains this stage of the Worthy One (*śaikṣa-mūrdhan*) through the fulfillment of faith, it is identical to the vast threefold activity (*trikarma*) of Samantabhadra and others.
This cause and its fruit function as the great activity of the infinite *dharmadhātu* at all places and throughout all times;
this is their constant mode. When discussed according to their essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*), they do not depend on various stages (*avasthā*).

However, when manifested within the gate of faith (*śraddhāmukha*), they are subsumed under faith. Yet, because that great activity is boundless and difficult to describe in full, it is here analyzed by way of ten examples to manifest it.
Inexhaustibility is the functional activity of thirteen samādhi-gates: (1) the Samādhi-Gate of the Perfectly Luminous Sea-Seal;
(2) the Samādhi-Gate of the Wondrous Practice of the Flower Adornment; (3) the Samādhi-Gate of the Indra’s Net; (4) the Samādhi-Gate of Producing Vast Offerings from the Hand;
(5) the Samādhi-Gate of Manifesting All Dharmas; (6) the Samādhi-Gate of Gathering Beings through the Four Means of Integration.
7. The Samādhi Door of the Body Being Identical with the World; 8. The Samādhi Door of the Radiant Awareness of the Light from the Hairs;
9. The Samādhi Door of the Majestic Adornment of Principal and Retinue; 10. The Samādhi Door of the Boundless Quiescence and Functionality (and so forth).

Regarding the first section, there are five and a half verses, which are divided into two parts: first, clarifying the karmic function; second, revealing the basis. Within the first part, there are five [sections]; the first verse clarifies the manifestation.
In the Buddha’s teaching, the second of the two verses following the preceding section clarifies the accomplishment of deeds through effortlessness (*anābhoga*);

because no effort is exerted, it is said that "expectations are severed. Furthermore, it is explained that because the causal stage is fulfilled, there is nothing further to be sought, hence the term "severed.

Next, one verse among the three clarifies the manifestation of the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*). Next, one verse among the four clarifies the manifestation of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Finally, one verse manifests...
The final two lines of the miscellaneous section conclude by identifying the basis for this function as the "Ocean-Seal" (*sāgaramudrā*). This is named after a metaphor:
just as the four armies of the *asuras* arrayed in the sky have their images reflected within the great ocean, so too does the meditative mind of the Bodhisattva resemble the great ocean;

it manifests various forms in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, just like those reflected military images. As the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, fascicle 14, states: "It is, for example, like [the reflection in] Yama..."
Within this ocean of forms—including the bodies of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and all other external forms—there are reflected images.
For this reason, it is called the "Great Ocean Seal. The Bodhisattva is likewise;
having attained the Great Ocean Seal Samādhi, he is able to discern and perceive the mental activities of all sentient beings, attaining the light of wisdom regarding all dharma-gates.
This refers to a Bodhisattva who, having attained the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), perceives the inclinations and mental activities of all sentient beings.

The commentary explains that the character "perceives" (*jian*) here is also synonymous with "manifests" (*xian*); that is, it is through perception that they manifest. One should understand that this applies to both [the provisional and the ultimate]. Question:
Since these are Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) who manifest as Buddhas, is this a temporary transformation-manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), or is it a real accomplishment?
Yeda (as follows) [referring to the three types of beings].
*Tanyuan ji*, fascicle five (Third Assembly), Chapter Nine:
"The Buddha Ascends to the Summit of Mount Sumeru. Regarding the explanation of this text, there are four gates as above. First, the explanation of the name. There is...
Second (and so forth). Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: within this assembly there are six chapters, which are divided into two parts.

The first two chapters clarify the initiation of the skillful means, namely the introductory section (*nidāna*). The remaining four chapters constitute the main body (*samyak-artha*) of this assembly.

Within the former [two], the first chapter is the "Introductory Section on the Response of the Tathāgata," clarifying the perfection of the fruit-virtues; the subsequent chapter is the "Introductory Section on the Gathering of the Assembly and Radiant Praise," clarifying the cause.
"Virtue being perfected" means that within the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), both cause and fruit are fully and perfectly established (and so forth).
Regarding the eleventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Ten Abidings," first is the explanation of the title (and so forth). Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text:

within the main body of the teaching, there are four chapters divided into two parts; the first three chapters concern the practices and virtues of this specific stage, while the final chapter concerns the superior progress toward the next.

The three categories—initial, middle, and final—are divided into three sections: the first section clarifies the stages (*bhūmi*), the second clarifies the practices (*caryā*), and the third praises the virtues (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, the first corresponds to understanding (*adhimukti*), the second to practice (*pratipatti*), and the third reveals the virtues, as explained above regarding the three categories beginning with "difficult" (*duṣkara*) and so forth.

Within this specific category, there are seven parts: (1) the Section on Samādhi, (2) the Section on Bestowal (*adhikāra*), (3) the Section on Arising (*utthāna*), and (4) the Section on the Fundamental (*mūla*).

The fivefold exposition consists of: (1) the section on the sixfold manifestation of reality; (2) the section on the establishment of realization; and (3) the section on the verses (and so forth). Within the fourth part, the "Fundamental Section," there are two divisions:
first, the proof of the fundamental nature, and second, the teaching of the fundamental nature. This also follows the sequence of essence followed by characteristics.

Regarding the first of these, as for the preliminary selection and analysis of the preceding and succeeding stages: why is this meaning not present within the stage of faith? Because that is not yet an established stage; this [stage], however, is a stage.
Why is this called "lineage" (*gotra*) up to the tenth stage being called "well-determined"? Because this stage is the most inferior, it is named after the lineage itself;
the ten stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) are named after the activities that arise based on the lineage as they progressively increase;
the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are named after the great vows that follow those practices, because they turn all prior practices toward the realization of the correct [enlightenment].
Because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have already attained true realization and are necessarily so, they are termed "well-determined" (*suviniścita*).

All of these [preceding stages] are, within their respective positions, the pervasive essence that gradually increases according to the position; thus, there is this gradation of levels. For this reason, the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) and the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) lack "great well-determination," as they are inferior.

Furthermore, because they belong to the lower and middle ranks among the three levels of the stage of worthies (*trayaḥ śaikṣāḥ*), and because they are the most inferior, they have not yet discerned this great function.
Furthermore, because self-benefit increases and because the seeds have not yet manifested, the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) is briefly explained through three gates:
1. **Explanation of the Name:** "Seed" (*bīja*) has the meaning of cause; "nature" (*prakṛti*) has the meaning of essence. Furthermore, "nature" has the meaning of clan, referring to a "seed-clan.
Moreover, "nature" has the meaning of category, referring to a "category of kind. 2. **Delineation of the Essence:** There are two types: first, the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*). (End of excerpt)
Second, regarding the nature of the lineage of cultivation (*abhyāsa-gotra*), there are two gates: First, the gate of conditioned impermanence, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

"The six sense bases are preeminent, beginningless, and transmitted through succession; they are obtained by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-pratilabdha*)," and so forth. Second, the gate of unconditioned permanence, as stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra*:
"As for the nature of true suchness (*tathatā-gotra*), it is as explained in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-samudgata-sūtra*," and so forth. This refers to the lineage of cultivation.

Regarding the existence or non-existence of the nature (*prakṛti*): first, according to Ratnamati, it refers exclusively to the innate nature (*prakṛti-gotra*); second, according to Sthiramati, it refers exclusively to the acquired nature (*samudānīta-gotra*);

third, according to Dharmapāla, it includes both; fourth, according to the *Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyā*, it excludes all three; and fifth, the various classifications are presented in five sections: first, the distinction between innate and acquired natures regarding anteriority and posteriority;

second, regarding the five lineages (*pañca-gotra*); third, regarding the six lineages (*ṣaḍ-gotra*); fourth, regarding the stages of practice (*avasthā*); and fifth, regarding the various teachings, as explained in detail elsewhere.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" states: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that within his own body there are all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because that Bodhisattva’s mind is never separate from all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
Just as it is within his own mind, so it is within the minds of all sentient beings; thus, they exist immeasurably, boundlessly, and nowhere are they absent."

Regarding the six phrases within the "Inconceivable and Indestructible" section, the first phrase is general, meaning that among the five types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*), other positions are excluded;
thus it says, "the Bodhisattva lineage. The following five phrases specifically reveal the meaning of the lineage:

1. **"Profound" (*gambhīra*)**: This has the sense of being deep and remote. - First, regarding the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it penetrates to the ultimate limit of the future. - Second, regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)... [text fragment ends]

First, because its nature is *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), it is free from characteristics and free from self-nature; second, because its function gives rise to supreme virtues that are inexhaustible; third, because it penetrates to the same level as the fruit of Buddhahood;

Accomplishing tasks without effort, as if with a sense of urgency; hearing sounds as if they were fixed; the arousal [of activity] through the power of vows; and so forth—these ten [aspects of] the inconceivable, whether in accordance with or contrary to [the world], are called the "Great Vows.

They universally respond to the capacities of various beings to bring about benefit, manifesting in manifold ways of accord and opposition that cannot be fathomed by those of inferior status. Nevertheless, these great vows are inexhaustible in their actual merit;
based upon them, ten [specific vows] are distinguished, all of which are revealed in detail within the subsequent sections on the "Universal Salvation" and others.

It should be understood that "clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to the vastness of benefiting others, while "extensive" (*vipula*) refers to the vastness of self-benefit; these manifest throughout the three times and so forth, each possessing the ten preceding meanings.
Furthermore, within this context, the first is the aspect of contemplation (*lakṣaṇa*), the next is greatness (*mahattva*), and the subsequent is non-weakness (*anavalīnatā*);

among the six certainties (*niyata*), there are three [of these]. The remaining meanings are the same as explained previously. Second, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pradarśana*), there are two parts: first, citing the number to manifest its excellence, namely, the three.
The World-Honored One, in common with all [Buddhas], speaks to reveal the excellence of the essential Dharma. This consists of two parts: first, listing the names to reveal their excellence;

second, citing what has been spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods to further demonstrate that excellence. Regarding the listing of names, the meaning of the ten dedications is briefly presented through five sections:

(1) explaining the names, (2) the characteristics of their meanings, (3) their essential nature, (4) their stages and positions, and (5) the distinctions among their practices. First, regarding the explanation of the names, we begin with the general name.

Regarding the enumeration of the ten *pariṇāmanās* (dedications) based on their number, this is explained as an *adhikaraṇa-saṃkhyā-vyākhyāna* (an explanation where the number is an attribute of the subject).
Furthermore, there are three types of dedication: first, regarding principle (*tattva*), "giving up signs" is called *pariṇāmanā*, and "entering into principle" is called *pariṇāmanā*;

second, regarding benefiting sentient beings, "attaining principle without realizing [nirvāṇa]" is called *pariṇāmanā*, and "following existence with great compassion to save living beings" is called *pariṇāmanā*; third, regarding *bodhi*, it refers to the wholesome roots that are cultivated.

The roots [of virtue] do not aspire to the three realms of existence or the two vehicles; this is called "turning toward" (pranidhāna) the correct path toward unsurpassed bodhi (as explained at length).

Second, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of the meaning, there are two parts: first, the specific, and second, the general. Within the specific [section] (as explained at length), the general discussion of each [aspect] contains three kinds of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*):
namely, dedicating roots of goodness toward sentient beings, dedicating them toward bodhi, and [dedicating them toward the welfare of all].

Regarding dedication to the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), there are two distinct meanings for each, which constitute the act of dedication. Furthermore, regarding sentient beings, there are two reasons:

first, because a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness necessarily depend upon sentient beings to become a portion of those beings, it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that they must be dedicated back toward sentient beings.

Second, generally speaking, since a bodhisattva must necessarily act for the sake of liberating sentient beings, and because these [roots of goodness] are the instruments for saving them, it is logically necessary to dedicate them to them; otherwise, it would not be so.
This is because [the former] is identical to the Two Vehicles’ self-deliverance and is not that of a Bodhisattva;

regarding the two types of bodhi, first, the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva depend upon Great Bodhi, as they flow from it and are its constituent parts, and thus by the nature of things (*dharmatā*) they return to it.
Second, generally speaking, the intention of a Bodhisattva must be to seek unsurpassed bodhi, for this is their innate disposition (*gotra*). Third, they are directed toward Great Bodhi.

Regarding the two aspects of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*): first, the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are accomplished through conditions and lack intrinsic nature; second, they are established based on the truth and flow forth from it.

Therefore, these are the true dharmas. By their very nature, they incline toward those two [aspects]. Generally speaking, because a bodhisattva must realize the truth and turn away from ignorance, they illuminate the two kinds of emptiness.
Question: For what reason are these three types of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) required? Answer: These three have many [purposes].

The meaning is briefly discussed in ten points: first, regarding the bodhicitta, because there are three types of mind (the meaning of these three minds is found in the section on "Generating the Mind");

second, regarding the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*): namely, the restraint (*saṃvara*) which avoids transgressions and is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);

the gathering of virtue (*kuśaladharma-saṃgraha*) which involves extensive cultivation and is directed toward enlightenment (*bodhi*); and the gathering of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*) through great compassion and is directed toward all living beings. Therefore, the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra* says: "If..."
The Bodhisattva abandons the mind of dedication regarding the three aggregates (*tri-rāśi*). The Bodhisattva should not dwell together with these three; they are condensed into two types of practice:
dedicating toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and protecting against the practice of afflictions (*kleśa*). The remaining two are condensed into two types of beneficial practice:

dedicating toward self-benefit for oneself and dedicating toward benefiting others for sentient beings. Regarding enlightenment (*bodhi*), it encompasses both types of benefit; furthermore, enlightenment is explained as self-benefit.

The benefit of sentient beings, the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the non-duality [of these] constitute the three virtues; through the practice of the causal stage, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are accomplished.

From the fruit stage, one accomplishes the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) by tending toward ultimate reality, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) by tending toward enlightenment, and the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*) by tending toward sentient beings—the three bodies may be understood in this sequence.
Sixth, regarding the accomplishment of compassion and wisdom: within wisdom, there is the illumination of principle and the manifestation of phenomena.

Second, there are three [reasons] because of the seventh [point], which refers exclusively to compassion (*karuṇā*): Why does one head toward enlightenment? It is for the sake of sentient beings. Why for the sake of sentient beings?

Because they do not know that those very beings are the Reality (*tattva*). Eighth, it refers exclusively to wisdom (*jñāna*): This means seeing that the deep characteristics of sentient beings are exhausted;
this is precisely the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Since their defiled characteristics are not destroyed, one bestows upon them the Buddha-wisdom for the sake of their birth [into Buddhahood].
Regarding the nine aspects of "heading toward Bodhi" in terms of non-obstruction: it means that the wisdom of Bodhi realizes the identity with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);

thus, the defiled appearances of sentient beings are immediately the True [Dharma] without distinction. Therefore, heading toward one is precisely heading toward three. Regarding the tenth aspect, "perfect clarity":

it means that the three dharmas are perfectly interfused, each encompassing the *dharmadhātu*, endowed with sovereign virtue, such that all dharma-gates are mutually identical and mutually inclusive without obstruction—contemplate this.

Mahāmati and other Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, by virtue of having received the empowerment of the Buddha’s hand and its supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), are able to preach the Dharma with mastery;

First, regarding the fulfillment of faith and practice, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*);

third, regarding the stage of practice, as explained in the context of the fulfillment of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the entry into the subtle *Indra-dharmadhātu*; fourth, regarding the stage of skillfulness, as follows.

within these five successive layers, the attainment of any single stage necessarily entails the presence of all principles and practices, for they are internally interrelated. Furthermore, among these five, the fulfillment of even a single stage constitutes the ultimate perfection of the cause, requiring nothing further.
Moreover, the attainment of one stage simultaneously entails the attainment of all other stages; in essence, they are all the functioning of a single dharmadhātu.
Although the five stages differ according to the distinctions of their respective gates, the essence of the Dharma is harmoniously integrated and inclusively subsumed without obstruction;
this is explained according to the school of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). In other teachings, this matter does not apply—this should be inferred accordingly (and so forth).

this is precisely that point. How could it be that what was profound and vast prior to the stages becomes inferior upon reaching the stages?
It is merely because they are different modes of provisional manifestation. Question: Should one not rather realize the stages [at this point]?

Question: Since the profound [stages] accord with the stage of Universal Virtue (*Samantabhadra-bhūmi*) and the shallow [stages] prior to that ground should accord with the three vehicles (*triyāna*), why is it not so?

Answer: The meaning of the text here is to demonstrate that the characteristics of the teachings differ; therefore, it is so. That is to say, if one attains the virtues of Samantabhadra upon the grounds (*bhūmi*), then there is no distinction from the teachings of the three vehicles.
Now, it is clarified that if these are the practices and stages of the three vehicles, they truly pertain to the stage prior to the grounds (*pūrvabhūmi*).
If one were to manifest this One Vehicle without mastery, it would not be so; therefore, prior to that stage, one attains mastery and the virtues of Samantabhadra.

Thus, if one were to take the stages above the ground based on this [description of] the stage of Samantabhadra prior to the ground, the characteristics of the practices on those higher grounds are exceedingly profound and far exceed what is stated here. This refers precisely to the following "Chapter on the Practice of Samantabhadra. If...

Based on these characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) and practices realized by the three vehicles, one takes the stage prior to the grounds (*pṛthagbhūmi*). The practice prior to this ground is extremely coarse and shallow, differing from what was previously described;
it refers precisely to the first two of the twelve dwellings (*vihāra*) within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śrāvakabhūmi* (the Bodhisattvabhūmi).

Question: Why are they not uniform? That is to say, while there are the virtues of Samantabhadra prior to the grounds of the One Vehicle, there are also [such virtues] upon the grounds of the One Vehicle.

Question: Why does the text not explain the virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*) of the three vehicles prior to the practices of these stages, as is taught in the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" where the virtues of the stages of the three vehicles are described in detail?

Answer: Because the primary tenet (*śāstra-mukha*) of this sutra clarifies the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it therefore discusses the practices of the One Vehicle extensively while briefly identifying the stages of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, another explanation is that because the ten stages of the One Vehicle are profoundly deep, they are treated comprehensively [therein].

The three vehicles and so forth are subsumed collectively as the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which are further manifested as inexhaustible through the sixfold characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) and the *dhāraṇī* gateway, thereby establishing the meaning of the sovereign mastery of Samantabhadra’s ten stages.
Prior to these stages, one is unable to do so; rather, it directly manifests Samantabhadra alone, and thus differs from the stages themselves (and so forth).

third, the former is not shared [with other bodhisattvas], being said to be the virtue of Samantabhadra alone, whereas this is shared, as it concerns these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Because it is commonly practiced by those of the three vehicles, as well as by humans and devas alike, the *Dilun* states:

"It can also produce and bring forth the practices of the human and deva paths; this should be known. (4) Previously, only causal practice was discussed; here, the fruition is integrated. (5) Previously, the stage of comparison (*upamāna*) was addressed;

The Dharma is non-dual and cannot be indicated by means of phenomenal characteristics; for this reason, what precedes is coarse while what follows is subtle.
Thus, the two [vehicles] are subsumed under the stage prior to the ground (*bhūmi*), whereas the One Vehicle’s distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*) is the Dharma of Samantabhadra.

Therefore, there is the ascent to heaven and the gathering of the assembly to signify its superiority, yet it is taught that the stages from the first ground onward are merely provisional stations shared with the three vehicles. Consequently, its sovereign characteristics are concealed, as is the case with other sutras.

This is stated because the former is subtle and the latter is coarse. This text is divided into two parts: first, nine chapters clarify the causes and effects of conditioned cultivation (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*);

second, three chapters clarify the manifestation of virtues at the stage of fruition. Regarding the first of these, there are also two sections: first, one chapter on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the first oral addition, among the ten phrases, the first phrase is the general [statement] (and so forth). Within the nine subsequent phrases, there are two distinct parts, namely, the two powers of self and other (and so forth).
