The doubt is as follows: Why is it necessary to apply [power]? It is because there is the power of causes. If there is already power, why must one further apply causes?
If it were not produced by causes, then there would be no need for them; yet, it is precisely through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) that it is capable of benefiting sentient beings.

If one were to pursue [the Buddha] according to the capacities of sentient beings to benefit them, one would lose his own essence, because his body is pure and perfect. Furthermore, it is explained that the first two [aspects] concern self-benefit:

first, the practice of teaching; second, the practice of realization. Next, there is the single aspect of the essence. Following that, the next one concerns benefiting others, and the final two concern the perfection of both benefits.
Thus, within the three meanings of "accomplishing virtue," the first reveals the benefit manifested within its own stage, while the latter two are distinguished by way of contrast.

Because it excels the initial causal stage and reaches its ultimate consummation, it is called the "Bodhisattva's final stage. Because it brings benefit to completion, it is said that there are two benefits.
This means that the Dharma-body and the true principle are exclusively the object of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as its direct realization;

they are not what is grasped by the defiled mind, mentation, or the other [consciousnesses]. As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "Grasping at marks is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); not grasping at marks is called wisdom (*jñāna*). This is the underlying principle.

It is because it reveals the power of one’s own strength and distinguishes its excellence—this is why it is taught here (and so forth). Within the Five Main Sections, there are three gates. First, regarding the explanation of the title:

Citing the Commonality of the Three Times to Clarify the Essential Superiority of the Grounds Regarding the first [section], these six determinations (*niyama*) constitute the entire essential nature of the grounds. Now, they shall be explained through five gates: 1. Explanation of the Names 2.

In the first part of the commentary on the text, the explanation of the title has two sections. First, regarding the general title: "Six" is a numerical term; "decisive" (*niścaya*) is a term for meaning.

Since the meaning is manifested through the number, this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (appositional compound) with a numeral, meaning that noble wisdom realizes the truth, makes a decisive determination, and establishes it as the standard;

it accords with principle and is free from faults, and is thus further termed "virtuous. This refers to the "determination through realization" among the three determinations in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Generally speaking, there is... [text continues].

The six meanings are: first, regarding the essence of practice, it is determined, vertically firm, and non-retrogressive; second, in relation to that which is realized, one is determined to have already realized it;

third, regarding the afflictions, one is determined to be able to sever them; fourth, regarding that which is believed, one is determined to be free from doubt; fifth, regarding those to be transformed, one is determined to be able to deliver them;
sixth, in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood, one is determined to be able to achieve it. Second, as for listing the names: first, the goodness of observing characteristics.

"Certainty" (*niścaya*) refers to the illumination of principles by correct wisdom; it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because it accords with reality, and it is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it is named after its own essence.

This constitutes the second [type of] truth. "Excellent certainty" (*suniścaya*) is so named because true wisdom is free from the faults of inverted delusion and because its realization of principles is not false;

thus, the name is established in relation to its counterpart. "Superior excellence" (*viśeṣa*) is so named because it surpasses the inferior and possesses superior virtues; this likewise applies both to the characteristic and to the essence.
Regarding the four causes for establishing names based on their forms, "good" refers to being able to accomplish the fruit; thus, the name is established from its functional capacity.
Fifth, "greatly good" refers to universally benefiting all sentient beings with a mind free of limitation; it receives its name from its essence and function.

Sixth, "not timid or weak" refers to having no fear or apprehension in the mind as one enters from the cause into the fruition of virtue; this name is established from the perspective of the mental object. Second, this is a general discussion based on these [names].
The distinctions in the essential nature of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are briefly presented in ten sections.

First, [the essence] consists of these six determinations (*niyama*), and so forth (see *Daśabhūmi-śāstra-saṃgraha*). Third, regarding the inclusion of these within the six determinations of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-yogācāra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that there are six determinations:
first, being able to personally cultivate and give rise to the bodhicitta vow, thereby surpassing all other pure vows; second, ... [text continues].
1. Possessing an incomparable and unshared fruit that transcends all other worldly realms; 2.
Following through with the deliverance from the suffering of all sentient beings, which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; 3.

Generating a single thought-moment of aspiration whose nature is naturally joyful toward immeasurable pure dharmas and untiring practice; 4. Attaining inexhaustible vows that never regress; 5. Increasing [these qualities].
The ultimate great awakening (*mahābodhi*) is the fruit of the long-lasting victory; this is the true meaning of the vow.

The commentary explains that here, the third [stage] corresponds to the fifth in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), because according to the intent of the *Dichijing* (Stages of Yogic Practice), one must encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others before they can serve as the cause. The remaining characteristics may be understood through their respective correlations.

Regarding the aspects of the four practices: among these six, the first five are the aspects of natural practice (*svabhāva-pratipatti*), while the last one is the aspect of superior progress (*viśeṣa-pratipatti*).
Regarding the practice, there are four [points] in the first part concerning self-benefit and one in the latter concerning the benefit of others.

Within the former, the first three clarify the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and qualities (*guṇa*) of the practice, while the last one reveals the functional efficacy (*kāritra*) of the practice—meaning it possesses the merit of achieving results.

Within the former of these, the first two clarify the perfection of the essential nature of the practice, while the last one clarifies the completeness of its qualities. Within the former of these, the first clarifies the intrinsic body (*svabhāva-kāya*) of the practice, while the last reveals the practice’s state of transcendence (*viveka*).

Because it transcends these [faults], its intrinsic nature is free from defects and encompasses virtues; taking this as the cause, the two benefits are perfected and the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished—this is the characteristic of this practice.
Fifth, regarding the commentary on the text (*yìwén zhōng*): [as follows]. The first phrase is the general [heading]. "Bodhisattva vow" identifies the person and distinguishes the specific dharma;
establishing a vow to seek toward great enlightenment is called "generating the bodhicitta," and since this is also a vow, it is so named.

The commentary explains that this clarifies the commonality [of the vows] by distinguishing them from those made prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). It says "definitive" (*niyata*) because it is definitive;
that is, it is the true nature of realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*). Therefore, what is definitive is good, and what is good is definitive; thus, it is called "good and definitive.

This "good and definitive" is distinct from the six internal [factors], as it is the direct realization of truth through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), unlike the contemplative mind that still carries mental images (*nimitta*). This is because...

First, it is called the "aspect of single flavor" because it is free from the faults of manifold ignorance. Second, it is called "reality" because it transcends all worldly phenomena subject to destruction;
being reality, it is not perceived by mundane wisdom. Third, this wisdom is identical to the *dharmadhātu* realized therein, as it possesses all supreme virtues.
Regarding this, there are two explanations in the treatise: first, an explanation based on the literal text, which states that it is the "Great *Dharmadhātu*."
The term "Victorious" (*jina*) refers to the large characters within this commentary on the Sūtra; it is called "Victorious" because it is the root of all Buddhas.
The term "Dharmadhātu" refers to the broad characters within this commentary on the Sūtra. Following this, there is a separate explanation of the two meanings of "opening.

First, four names are established to show that the essence is non-different, yet these four meanings are explained as four distinct categories according to the characteristics of the phenomena. First, the explanation of "Great" (*mahā*) refers to all...

"Dharma" means dharma; "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) refers to the *dhātu* (element/realm), and since this *dhātu* is the true nature (*tathatā*), it is called "dharmatā. All subsequent instances should be understood according to these two explanations.

The first explanation, "superior," means that the wisdom of the pure *dharmadhātu* transcends that of ordinary beings and those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles. The second explanation, "vast," means that the Mahāyāna *dharmadhātu* extensively gathers great practices.

The third explanation, "lofty," means that the untainted white dharmas (*anāsrava-śukla-dharma*) rise high above the mundane world. Furthermore, there is an initial explanation [of the term *dharmadhātu*].
This clarifies the *dharmadhātu* as it truly is: what is called "supreme and excellent" (*viśeṣa*) in the treatises is called "vast" (*vipula*) in the sūtras;

"vast" (*viśāla*) and "lofty" (*unnata*) are all synonymous names with no distinct essence. These collectively clarify the nature and characteristics of the *dharma*, which explains the term *dharma*.
"All phenomena are thus by their very nature" (*dharmatā*) explains the term *dhātu*. The remaining three [aspects] explain the ground of wisdom that conforms to the *dharmadhātu*. (1) Correct.

There are three types of wisdom: first, the wisdom of the essence; second, the wisdom of application; and third, the subsequently attained wisdom. Furthermore, ancient masters have said there are three:

first, the path of realization; second, the non-abiding path; and third, the path of assistance. Another explanation states that the first is the wisdom of direct realization, while the latter two are subsequently attained wisdoms.

Within the subsequently attained wisdom, the first skillfully gathers great practices to accomplish the benefit of others, while the second turns back to contemplate the internal to accomplish one's own benefit.
Third, because all three are identical in their conformity with true nature (*dharmatā*), they are said to be "like the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). Fourth, regarding the meaning of being a cause:
first, it is the producing cause (*janakahetu*) that gives rise to the conditioned fruit of bodhi; second, it is the revealing cause (*jñāpakahetu*) that reveals the unconditioned fruit of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, it is explained that this single true wisdom possesses all powers: first, it serves as the supporting cause (*niśrayahetu*), for by depending upon it, the responsive and transformational functions arise in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Second, it is for the purpose of subsuming causes by returning function to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, the former [aspect] immediately responds to the capacities of beings to manifest deficiency and fullness, while the latter continues uninterruptedly until the end of time. Moreover, the former externally initiates transformative activity, while the latter internally realizes the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, the former is quiescent yet constantly active, while the latter is active yet constantly quiescent. In the sutra, the "constant fruit" is omitted for brevity.
Because the five great compassionate benefits for sentient beings pervade the entire realm of birth, it is said to be "all-encompassing" (*vyāpin*); it is also called "Great" (*mahat*).
The preceding "well-determined" (*suviniścita*) was the cause of the former "eternal fruit"; because this vow guides that great goodness, it is called "great goodness.

Because [the Bodhisattva] does not abide in *nirvāṇa*, it is the eternal cause; because [he] does not abide in the world, it is said that he does not dwell exclusively in either the world or *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, because one enters the realm of the Buddhas, it is said that "there is no timidity. This section has three parts: first, "protected by all Buddhas" is the heading;

second, "Why is this? is the inquiry; and third, the explanation, which states that because one enters the ground of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they provide such protection.
Within these six [stages], the six characteristics are perfectly inter-inclusive, as can be understood. The substance of the grounds is thus concluded.

In the fourteenth fascicle of the *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Investigating the Profundities), the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), is likewise treated through seven gates as before (etc.). Seventh, in the "Explanation of the Text," there is first the section on "Praise and Request" (etc.).
Second, within the section on the "Actual Exposition," there are eight parts; the first is the part on "The Means for Fulfilling the Stage."
1. "The section on gathering" refers to the fact that all practices cultivated in the preceding nine stages are collectively taken as the means (*upāya*) to fulfill this stage. 2.

"The section on attaining samādhi" refers to the fact that the practices and virtues of the first stage are immeasurable; since one must rely upon samādhi when assuming office in this stage, it is singled out for mention. 3.

"The section on receiving the position" refers to the practice of correctly abiding in the stage, meaning that by relying on superior concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to encompass [all qualities].
The name "Buddha-wisdom" refers to this. Regarding the fourth section, "Entering the Great Culmination": this is the practice of the perfection of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Since this stage, when compared to the preceding ones, is already the ultimate limit and the pinnacle among all culminations, it is called the "Great Culmination. (And so forth.

Second, regarding the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices thus," which clarifies the section on attaining samādhi: herein, first, the preceding is restated to introduce what follows; then, "immediately attains" and below constitutes the main exposition.
This clarifies what is attained therein: first, the four [sections] specifically clarify ten gates; second, they collectively conclude with the "one million" [verses];

third, "the bodhisattva’s dwelling" below explains the ability to enter and the ability to know; fourth, the final name is clarified by taking the first from within the internal treatise—since it cites the beginning and so forth at the end, it says "Free from Defilement" (*Vimalā*) and so on—and by citing the subsequent one million [verses], it says "Retinue Free from the Defilement of Afflictions," which serves as an explanation.
Regarding its characteristics: because this stage is the place where obstructions are exhausted, those who do not exert further effort achieve the corresponding realization;
thus, the remaining nine are distinct. This is because the sixth and seventh concentrations together abandon one type of defilement, whereas [this stage] abandons eight types of defilements.
First, regarding "entering the distinctions of the *dharmadhātu*": entering the secret and stainless refers to the profound depth of the *dharmadhātu*, which is called the "secret place. Second...

1. Practicing in proximity to the fruit of Buddhahood is called the adornment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*. 2. The light and functional activity of the three bodies (*trikāya*). 3. Eloquence of the four types of speech and the power of dhāraṇī.

4. The manifestation of supernormal powers through mental activity. 5. Vastness. 6. Profundity. 7. The simultaneous manifestation of the Pure Land and its immeasurable qualities. 8. Extensive explanation of the correct contemplation; explaining the aforementioned virtues of self-benefit. 9.

"In accordance with all [beings]" and so forth refers to the stainless virtue of benefiting others by transforming sentient beings. The above two [points] constitute the section on the virtues of benefiting others.
Regarding "knowing the nine aspects of one's own stage as they truly are" and so forth, this refers to the superior progress of higher awakening, termed "immaculate perfect awakening.

This means that when one is about to achieve perfect awakening, all Buddhas appear before one and collectively witness and certify it. This is as explained in the section on "receiving the office" in the text below, which states:
"The wisdom of all-knowledge is non-conceptual," thereby explaining "all-knowledge"; the wisdom of all-knowledge is equanimity.

"Receiving the Mandate of Authority" explains the reception of the position through wisdom; "Fulfilling the Matter of Samādhi" explains entering its essence completely and knowing its functional activity.
Third, regarding "this samādhi appearing before one," the following clarifies the section on receiving the position, which contains six parts:
first, "regardless of what seat [one occupies]" means that when a prince of the world receives his office, he sits upon a throne of Jambu-river gold or white silver.
The Bodhisattva Gajaratna is likewise; when he receives the office of a Buddha, he is seated upon the Great Jewel Lotus King Throne (and so forth).

Sixth, at that time, the passage beginning with "All Buddhas" clarifies the attainment of the respective stages. Within this, there are four parts: namely, the Dharma, the Simile, the Synthesis, and the Conclusion.

Regarding the first, the Exposition of the Dharma, there are also four sections: first, the Emission of Light; second, the Entry into the Crown; third, the Attainment of Benefit; and fourth, the Conclusion.

Regarding the initial stage of the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) (and so forth): in the fourth summary of the stages, those who have entered the Buddha’s realm share the same realization; they equally possess the power and virtue of the ten practices; they are equally included among the ranks of Buddhas;
and they equally achieve the virtues of a Buddha and are thus counted among the Buddhas. This is like one who has newly left the household life:
although they have not yet received the precepts, they are nonetheless counted among the Saṃgha (and so forth).

In the tenth fascicle of the *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Investigating the Profundities), section twenty-three, "The Chapter on Manifestation," the first part explains the title: "Manifestation" (*ming*) refers to the sovereign and subtle function that illuminates exhaustively; "manifesting" (*ming*) refers to the limitless application of this illumination.

To distinguish these ten [aspects] by relying on the perfect [nature] is an explanation based on numerical designation (*daishu shi*). Second, regarding the intent of its inclusion: first, it is discussed generally...

The purport of these following five chapters is as follows: First, while the preceding section revealed the perfection of the realized state (*pramāṇa*), the present section clarifies its superior progressive activity (*prayoga*).

Second, while the preceding section concerned the essence of the state, this section distinguishes its active functioning. Third, while the preceding state involved internal practice, this state concerns subsequent practice.

Fourth, while the preceding section dealt with the fulfillment of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the present section distinguishes the great function of subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*). It is for these four reasons that they follow. — Ancient Commentary.

"Human beings also have their counterparts. Regarding the meanings of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha-bodhi*), since these are not distinguished within this sutra, how much less so in the preceding *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*, where the final mind already reveals the meaning of Equal Enlightenment?
This chapter is explained separately because it answers the ten questions on mastery (*vaśitā*) from the previous section.
Furthermore, in the alternative translation, the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-sūtra*, these are called the "Ten Clarities" (*daśa-vidyā*) within its questions. (Thus it is said.)

[End of quote]. Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha. First, regarding the explanation of the title: it is so named because the fruit-dharmas of the Tathāgata far transcend words and thought.
Second, there are three reasons for the intent behind this chapter: first, the "remote" [intent], whereby the following three chapters serve as a general introduction.

The answer is that because ten questions—beginning with "the ground of the Buddha Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabhā*) and so forth—were asked, he asks again; yet if the previous question was already answered at length, why is there this further request?
The explanation is that because they are separated by a great distance, it is further initiated. If that is so, why did the preceding chapters not do the same?

The explanation is that while the preceding chapters were all within the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), the present discussion concerns the dharmas of the fruit (*phala-dharma*), which is a distinct stage.
For this reason, it is further explained that this is a recitation (smṛti-vācana) requested out of a desire for the Dharma, rather than a separate formal invitation (adhyeṣaṇā).

If so, why is there no such precedent in the preceding chapters? The explanation is that because the resultant dharmas (phala-dharma) are profound and subtle, and in order to manifest the vessel of the Dharma (dharma-bhājana) with earnest devotion, a recitation was required;

since the causal dharmas (hetu-dharma) are the opposite of this, they do not serve as a precedent. Second, regarding the intent of the sequence: it is because the cultivation and arising [of the path] have already been analyzed previously.
Third, regarding the reason for its immediate succession: the preceding "Chapter on Dwelling" (*vihāra*) was the cultivation of the fulfillment of the cause;
this present chapter is the beginning of the accomplishment of the fruit. Therefore, it follows immediately after. Third, as for the essential purport (*abhiprāya*):
herein the virtues of the Buddha-fruit are clearly elucidated. Briefly stated, there are four sections, the first of which is a general exposition.

Regarding the Buddha’s virtues, there are three sections: first, the distinct manifestation of their meanings; second, the definitive determination of this text; and third, the revelation of the inconceivable. In the first section:
if one speaks of the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and so forth, it applies generally to the Hīnayāna and the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

If one distinguishes the pure *dharmadhātu* and the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) as virtues, it applies throughout the gradual teachings from beginning to end. However, if one considers them solely as the single-flavored reality of virtue, then [it pertains only to the ultimate].

The Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), as explained in such chapters as the "Chapter on Light-Awakening" (*Prabhāsa-bodhi*), states that if one is endowed with all inexhaustible virtues, as described in these passages, this constitutes the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Second, regarding the distinct manifestation of its characteristics: the merits of all Buddhas do not exceed two kinds—those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-ja*) and those inherent by nature (*prakṛti-stha*).
These two categories, when contrasted, comprise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). (See the section on "Types of Buddha-Bodies. Fourth, the explanation of the text.

Regarding the statement "the dharmas of the three grades of fruit below this also possess various virtues which are to be assigned to the three bodies"—namely, the first as the *dharmakāya*, the next as the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the last as the *nirmāṇakāya*—I fear the text may not be consistent with this.
For within this chapter, the functions such as the eight marks (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) are extensively revealed; how could it refer solely to the *dharmakāya*?

Furthermore, while it might be appropriate to assign these to the Buddha’s essence, attributes, and functions in the latter two chapters, there is an obstacle in the case of the first chapter for the following reason.
Within this chapter, there are also characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*). Now, it is said that this chapter generally reveals the excellence of the Buddha’s essence and function;

next, the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgara-parivarta*) specifically reveals the marks of his excellent qualities; and finally, the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-parivarta*) specifically distinguishes the beneficial functions of those excellent qualities (and so forth).

Regarding the twenty-ninth chapter, the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Ocean of Marks," first is the explanation of its title (and so forth). Third, as for the essential tenets (*abhiprāya*), they are correctly established as follows:
The boundless ocean of marks of the Buddha-fruit is taken as the primary theme; to explain this meaning in detail, eight sections are briefly composed.
First, regarding the explanation of the names (etc.). Third, regarding the types: according to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, there are three types:

first, the most abbreviated description, which speaks of thirty-two marks; second, the abbreviated description, which speaks of eighty-four thousand marks; third, the extensive description, which has...
Regarding the "Infinite Characteristics," as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* (Flower Ornament Sutra) for the sake of Samantabhadra, Bhadramukha, and others:

the term *saṃpuṣpita* is an alternative name for the *Avataṃsaka*. Within this chapter, the characteristics and names, which are as numerous as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds, are called "infinite.

Among these three [categories], the first is exclusively the Hīnayāna; the second includes the former and constitutes the Triyāna; and the last incorporates all preceding ones and constitutes the Ekayāna. Furthermore...
First, there is the vision exclusive to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); next, the vision exclusive to those on the stages; and finally, the vision that encompasses all five stages.

Furthermore, first there is the mark of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) alone; next, the mark of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) alone; and finally, the mark of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*). (And so forth. Regarding the seventh point, "Establishment," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 5, states:
Question: Why are the marks of a Bodhisattva exactly thirty-two, neither more nor less? Answer: Some say it is because they are beautiful... [and so forth].
Because they are correct and not disordered—if there were too few, they would not be upright; if there were too many, the bodily marks would be confused.
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhajanma-samādhi Sūtra*, because the Buddha was born into the world to manifest as a human being, he spoke of the thirty-two marks as superior to those of the devas;
he spoke of the eighty secondary characteristics for the sake of the bodhisattvas; and he spoke of eighty-four thousand marks because bodhisattvas cultivate eighty-four thousand [dharmas].
Because there are four thousand practices of the perfections (*pāramitā*), the preceding [section] was explained according to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

If, however, these ten [characteristics] are explained according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*)—as they are for Samantabhadra and others—as being as numerous as the atoms within a Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), it is because they cultivate the inexhaustible ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices. Eighth, regarding the clarification of functional activity (*karman*):

the functional activity of the One Vehicle is as explained in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Kṣudraka-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*); the characteristics and functions of the other vehicles are explained separately. (End of quote)
(Tanxuan ji, Fascicle 16; Chapter 30:
"The Merit of the Radiance of the Buddha’s Minor Marks"). First, explaining the title: "Buddha" (Fo) designates the person and signifies his virtue.

The "minor marks" refer to the physical forms; "greatly distinguishing the essence with radiance" refers to the arising of function based upon the essence; and "merit" refers to the benefits accomplished through that function.
Thus, these names are established by manifesting the virtues of the person in terms of essence and function. Second, regarding the purpose for their introduction:

in the preceding chapter, each of the major marks possessed its own radiance that illuminated the entire Dharma-realm, yet the specific characteristics of the benefits produced by that illumination had not been revealed; therefore, [this chapter now addresses them].

This chapter clearly elucidates the beneficial functions as the "Great Characteristics" (*mahālakṣaṇa*); because these are difficult to clarify, the "Minor Characteristics" (*kṣudralakṣaṇa*) are distinguished. Furthermore, although the Minor Characteristics are numerous, only one characteristic is discussed.

Within this single characteristic, there are benefits spanning many periods of time; however, for the sake of brevity, only those of a single period are explained. Since even the benefits of this single period are difficult to clarify, the Buddha himself has spoken of them.
Based on this analysis, the karmic functions of the aforementioned Great Characteristics are boundless, and such boundlessness is extremely difficult to fathom.
The knowledge of the ears follows next because it arises from the excellent secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) that flow forth from the aforementioned primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the three points of essential purport, the primary doctrine clarifies the utility of the Tathāgata’s marks and virtues; this is briefly presented through two gates. First, regarding the fixed boundaries:
since the thirty-two primary marks are adorned by eighty secondary marks, one should know that a single mark [is as vast as] the number of atoms in ten *padma-garbha* worlds.
First, each [of these] possesses secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) equal in number to the atoms of the universe;

furthermore, since these major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are each profound and vast, differing from the various marks among the thirty-two [major marks], one knows that the secondary marks are likewise extremely profound, vast, and immeasurable.
Second, regarding the analysis of their function: while the eighty secondary marks merely adorn the Buddha’s form to inspire pure faith, here it is explained as follows:
Regarding the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, the wheel-mark (*cakrāṅka*) served as the lowest rank among the secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This refers to emitting a single ray of light that illuminates lands as numerous as the atoms within ten worlds; the sentient beings in the hells therein all attain rebirth in heaven and achieve the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten faculties of sight, hearing, and so forth.
Furthermore, the fragrance from the pores of this celestial son universally perfumes sentient beings, enabling them likewise to attain the ten stages. White.
Furthermore, this Pure Wheel-Turning King emits light that causes immeasurable sentient beings to likewise attain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the ten eyes (*daśacakṣus*).
In this manner, continuing through the succession of ages until the end of the future and its infinite limits, there are none who cannot become Bodhisattvas.
Since this is so for even the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), the mastery and utility of the ocean of the Tathāgata’s major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are beyond description.

It is said that what is unspeakable is spoken. Regarding the fourfold explanation of the text, there are two parts: first, the brief exposition, and second, the extensive exposition. Within the former, there are also two sections:
first, clarifying the benefit conferred by the function of the fruit; second, from "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva... onwards, clarifying the benefit conferred by the function of the cause.

As for why the Buddha himself speaks [of this] in the first section, ancient commentators explain: the preceding "Chapter on the Perfection of the Cause" (Saṃgha-parivarta) clarifies the culmination of the cause, while this chapter clarifies the culmination of the fruit.
Because it has been concluded, only the Buddha spoke; furthermore, he explained that while the *nimitta* (mark) is extremely minute, its function is immensely vast.
Since this matter is difficult to clarify, the Buddha himself spoke, addressing Ratnapāṇi because he is capable of grasping [the meaning].

The "secondary marks" (*anuvyañjana*) of the Sea King refer to the minor marks located at the edges of the major marks, such as the *cakrāṅka* (wheel-mark) on the soles of the feet. This is because the functional application of the other major marks is difficult to explain.

Because it is difficult to clarify, the function of the wheel-mark (cakrāṅka) on the soles is explained; furthermore, because even the great marks (lakṣaṇa) are still difficult to clarify, the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are explained;
because there are many such secondary marks, one mark of the Ocean-King (Sāgararāja) is explained;

because this resultant function is still difficult to clarify, the benefit provided while he was a bodhisattva in Tuṣita is explained. Regarding this causal function, there are two parts, the first of which is to cause...

Leaving suffering behind, one is born into the heavens to accomplish the practice of peace and joy; having already been born in the heavens, one subsequently commands others not to become attached to celestial pleasures in order to accomplish the practice of universal benefit.
Furthermore, the former body benefits those who follow, while this empty voice benefits those who preceded it. Regarding the purification of the ten eyes and so forth within this interval:
because those sentient beings possessed the seeds of the Dharma of Samantabhadra from having previously seen and heard it, they further encountered the Dharma-realm of Vairocana.
"By the touch of light, one obtains the benefits of the ten eyes of Samantabhadra" (and so forth). In the second section, the extensive analysis, there are also two parts:

first, the extensive explanation of how the preceding light rescues those in the evil realms; second, the extensive explanation of how the preceding sound benefits those in the celestial realms. Within the first of these, there are also two parts: first, clarifying the emission of light; second, clarifying the benefit of its illumination.
Regarding the first of these, the "Light of the Universal Illumination King" is the light among the great marks of the *cakra* (wheel) on the crown.
Regarding that, within the marks of greatness (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), there is this minor mark (*anuvyañjana*) of the Sea-King named "Pure" (*viśuddha*);
having excluded many [other] lights, only one is mentioned here. As for "universally illuminating" below, it refers to the benefit of illumination;

therein, "according to the sphere of sentient beings" means according to their various states of abiding, which are likewise different according to what is observed. "According to their roots of goodness" means according to their respective past seeds. What?

Regarding the phrase "the roots of goodness that accord with the inclinations": the distinctions in their mental dispositions (*āśaya*) also involve differences in their aspirations (*praṇidhāna*), all of which are called "roots" because they bring about benefit;

they surpass the benefits described in other sūtras, hence it says "up to the Abhidharma," etc., because the following section speaks only of the single benefit of illuminating the hells and being reborn in Tuṣita, thereby excelling the others. Second, the extensive benefit in the heavens.

Within this section there are six parts: first, the initial cause consisting of exhortation and the resolution of doubts; second, "You all should now... and below, the formal exhortation to repay kindness;

third, from "At that time, the sons of the gods heard this sound" and below, the arising of offerings based on the exhortation; fourth, from "Therefore, O sons of the gods" and below, the instruction to resolve the mind [of awakening] and repent;
fifth, from "When this Dharma was being taught" and below, the benefits obtained upon hearing the teaching; sixth, at that time, the various devas...

Regarding each and every pore, the following clarifies the attainment of benefits, the transmission of realization, and the accomplishment of inexhaustible practices; this section has three parts: first, the exhortation; second, the obstacles;
and third, the explanation (as detailed below). At the end, the conclusion identifies Śākyamuni as the one who provides the general exhortation through this initial gateway.

Thus, the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*) has two aspects: first, in terms of causes and conditions, as exemplified by the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Because that which is attained is free from the subtle defilements of its own two hindrances, there are two points regarding the fruit, the first of which is as stated in this passage:
it indicates that one who is about to attain Buddhahood dwells here in the heavens; by abiding in this samādhi, they are able to benefit sentient beings and cause them to be free from defilement.
The phrase "that which the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot know" concludes [the discussion] because its function is profound and vast (etc.). The fifth major section explains this Dharma.

At that time, those below heard the Dharma and obtained benefit; therein are four points: first, other *Tuṣita* devaputras obtained the benefit of *kṣānti*, which may correspond to the first stage (*bhūmi*) or the eighth stage;

second, the devaputras of the six desire realms generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), obtaining the benefit of these two stages; third, the celestial maidens obtained the benefit prior to these two stages;
fourth, at that time, those below obtained the benefit according to their capacity—the devaputras who were the appropriate audience—thereby [attaining] the five stages of Samantabhadra.
Because this Dharma of great skillful means in mutual inclusion is such that, immediately upon first emerging from hell, one hears this universal Dharma and attains the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
this is distinct from the gradual teachings of the three vehicles. Within this, there are six benefits: (1) the benefit of initially attaining the stage;

(2) the benefit of accomplishing practice; (3) the benefit of superior retribution; (4) the benefit of extinguishing hindrances; (5) the benefit of seeing the Buddha; and (6) the benefit of concluding the demarcation. These are as follows:

Although they have attained the fulfillment of the causes of the ten stages, because this distinguishes them from those who have realized the fruit, it says, "they are still unable to see," and so forth.
The sixth major section, "At that time, the sons of the gods [emerge] from each and every pore," clarifies the successive attainment of inexhaustible practices;
herein there are two parts: first, the emergence of Dharma-realm offering implements from the pores to make offerings to the Buddha.
The benefits produced by these offering implements are revealed in three parts: first, the benefit of the flowers, which is that one extensively sees various Buddhas;

second, the benefit of the incense, which is that one extensively extinguishes the obstacles of afflictions; third, the benefit of the canopies, which is that one extensively accomplishes the great practices (*mahācaryā*). (And so forth. Within the third section, the benefits of seeing the canopies, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies that by seeing this canopy of the dharma-gate of the *dharmadhātu*, one obtains [the vision of] as many wheels as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The roots of goodness of this king are like the pure white jewel net and so forth;

within the nature of this world-system, he is one of the ten thousand sons who have surpassed the wheel-turning kings such as King Priyadarśana-Sudhīmat, and is not merely a golden-wheel-turning king with a thousand sons over the four continents.

That is to say, among the wheel-turning kings of the pure white jewel net numbering as many as the sands of one Ganges River, the roots of goodness of this king were suddenly and instantaneously perfected upon his brief vision of this canopy.
Following the section on the two Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, this passage clarifies the benefits derived from those transformed by this [Buddha-]king.

Within it, first, regarding the vast number of those transformed, there are both the Dharma and the analogy; second, following the emission of the *māndārava* flowers, it clarifies the excellence of the benefits received, which likewise includes both the Dharma and the analogy.
Regarding those who encounter the light and attain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are three layers of benefit herein; first, the Buddha’s light is clarified.
1. The Universal Illumination Son of Heaven causes [beings] to attain the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*); 2.

the fragrant flowers, canopies, and so forth emitted from the pores of this Son of Heaven further benefit sentient beings, causing them to attain the status of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), which is likewise the tenth stage; 3. the light emitted by the Wheel-Turning King illuminates other sentient beings, also causing them to attain the tenth stage.
These three positions are entirely equal, being simultaneously and instantaneously accomplished, each [attaining] together.
If one reasons back from these many types, as numerous as atoms, they are all but the power of a single light within a single minor mark of the Tathāgata.
If it is so for one light, it is likewise for all other lights; if it is so for one minor mark, it is likewise for all other minor marks;
and if it is so for the minor marks, then the oceans of the remaining major marks and so forth are unspeakably, unspeakably vast. Such is the meaning of the text.

The phrase "reflecting thus" means that these sentient beings have all previously cultivated goodness; this clarifies that they possessed, in former lives, the roots of goodness for practicing the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) through seeing and hearing the One Vehicle.

The analogy is as follows: it is like one who, while still in the desire realm, has already attained the first dhyāna; although their body has not yet been transformed, they experience the bliss of that heavenly realm.
In the same way, when these sentient beings encounter this light, they suddenly attain the body of the tenth bhūmi, even though their bodies have not yet been transformed.
That one perceives universally with the physical eye is due to the power of the Dharma; this also clarifies that "one encompasses all" within the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
That a single stage cannot be exhausted even in kalpas as numerous as motes of dust clarifies that "all encompasses one.
Such unimpeded mastery over both slowness and speed belongs to this Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and not to other schools. (3) Thus.

This concludes the explanation of the characteristics of the benefits attained through the accomplishment of purity. Since it was stated that one attains the ten eyes and so forth within this very body, the precise extent of these attainments was not yet known;
therefore, among the ten eyes, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is the coarsest, and its extent is now explained.
The other eyes are profound and subtle, and their characteristics may be understood by analogy. (And so forth.)
Chapter Thirty-one: The Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. First, regarding the explanation of the title, we first distinguish the name of the section.

Within the second part, "The Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding," there are two divisions. The preceding portion has completed the explanation of the causes and fruits produced through cultivation;

from here on, the next two chapters explain the causes and fruits manifested through cultivation. This also corresponds to the previous explanation of differentiated causes and fruits, while the following reveals the equal cause and fruit.
Regarding cause and effect, within the fivefold cycle of cause and effect, this is the third, which clarifies the cause and effect of the essential nature (and so forth).

Second, regarding the purpose of its arrival, there are also two parts. First, the sequential arrival: it means bringing the previously explained differentiated causes and effects back to their state of equality;
that is, it brings the differentiated causes—from the second assembly up to the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling"—back to this universal [equality].

Because the causes are perfected by the wise, the three chapters—the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature," the "Assembly Chapter," and the "Chapter on the Inconceivable"—distinguish the fruits as they ultimately return to the equality of nature;

therefore, they follow. Furthermore, it is explained that what preceded clarified the causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles, while what follows here clarifies the causes and fruits of the One Vehicle, serving as the basis for the aforementioned Three Vehicles. Moreover, this deduces from the preceding distinctions...

It is because one has arrived here at the fundamental station; furthermore, whereas the preceding section clarified the cultivation of birth (*śikṣā-utpatti*), this section clarifies the cultivation of manifestation (*śikṣā-vyakti*).

(And so forth. Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: within the latter two chapters, this present chapter first clarifies the perfect cause of Samantabhadra, while the subsequent chapter reveals the fulfillment of the fruit arising from nature.
Within this chapter, there are two parts: the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*). Regarding the prose: [End of segment]

There are also two aspects: the formal exposition and the auspicious signs. Within the formal exposition, there are likewise two: first, the introductory statement regarding the cause; second, the actual manifestation of what is to be taught.
Furthermore, this may also be explained as threefold: first, citing the concise to manifest the extensive, thereby explaining the meaning of universality;

second, from "When a Bodhisattva gives rise to even a single instance of anger" onwards, citing evil to manifest goodness, which is also to cite the rigid to manifest the supple, thereby explaining the meaning of being noble.
Regarding the meaning of the three [aspects] following the "Son of the Buddha," the subsequent section distinguishes the sixty gates of practice to explain the meaning of these practices;

therefore, they are called the "Practices of Samantabhadra. Within the first of these two [sections], there is first a general indication of the "small" [practices], followed by an explanation of the reasons for their being "small.
Regarding the former, the phrase "as previously explained" and so forth contains two interpretations: first, one based on proximity, as in the previous "Chapter on Minor Characteristics."
That which was taught to cause the sons of the gods to accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra is a minor discourse,

spoken for the purpose of manifesting the functions of minor signs to those deluded sentient beings who are to be transformed according to their needs, or those whose karmic obstructions are heavy and have fallen into the evil realms. However,

if one were to explain the functions of the major signs and deeds for sentient beings with light obstructions and wisdom, they would be vast, beyond description, even beyond the "unspeakable" (anabhilāpya).
Second, regarding the distant [teaching], within the five cycles of cause and effect, it is as in the second cycle mentioned previously:
the causes consist of the gradual progression through the five preceding stages, while the fruits consist of the differentiated qualities of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

Although within these various gates there is also the meaning of Samantabhadra’s perfect interfusion—differing from the Three Vehicles (Triyāna)—the structural gradations of these gates remain similar to those of the Three Vehicles, as they follow the capacities and address the ailments of sentient beings.
Not exhausting the source of the Dharma is called the "Subtle Minor Exposition. Below this, two chapters clarify the causes and effects of Samantabhadra;

they follow the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) rather than establishing hierarchical stages based on defiled capacities, and are thus termed the "Vast Exposition. The meaning of the text is as follows. Regarding the commentary, there is first an inquiry and then an explanation.
Within the explanation, there is first a general explanation: "All Tathāgatas" refers to those who act in accordance with the illnesses [of sentient beings] in this manner.
This is because, as explained in the *Jīshì xuǎn*, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are exactly the same. Second, regarding the detailed explanation:

although the afflictions and defilements of the sentient beings being followed are numerous, ten types are briefly manifested: first, ignorance; second, the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); third, the calculation of "mine" (*mamakāra*);

fourth, attachment to the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); fifth, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*); sixth, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); seventh, arbitrary conceptualization; eighth, the bond of desire (*kāmayoga*), which serves as the cause for the aforementioned suffering; ninth... [text fragment].
The ten factors that constitute the fruit of suffering and the three paths leading to liberation from them are thus summarized below.
Since sentient beings are thus bound by all fetters, how could the Tathāgata, upon appearing in the world to preach the Dharma, ever fully exhaust the nature of phenomena?

Second, within the light of the practices of Samantabhadra, the vastness of what is to be remedied consists of hundreds of thousands of obstacles; subsequently, the vastness of the remedies is revealed to consist of six.
Regarding the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the first three consist of the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion (as seen in the section on the categories of obstacles to be severed).
*Tànxuán jì*, fascicle 17 (Seventh Assembly), Chapter 33, "The Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*):

In preparing to explain this text, the four gates are the same as before; first, there is the explanation of the name. (Note: The phrase "as seen in the section on the categories of obstacles to be severed" refers to the structural analysis of the preceding sections.)
First, regarding the title of the section: this is called the "Section on Entrusting the Dharma for the Cultivation and Accomplishment of Practice.
It is given this name because one accomplishes correct practice by relying upon the dharma of entrusted cultivation. Second, regarding the title of the assembly:

it is named the "Second Assembly in Universal Radiance" (*Samantābhāsā*) based on its location. Why is there a second assembly held here? Because the previous Universal Radiance assembly was the initial stage for generating understanding.

Now, it is explained that because practice arises based on understanding (*adhimukti*), these are brought together again. [Objection: If that is so, why are they not also brought together again in the third and fourth [stages] and so forth? [Response:

The preceding [stages] are methods for generating understanding, which may be entrusted to many locations; however, here we only establish practice based on those preceding methods, and therefore they are not combined further (as stated at length).
Second, regarding the purpose of this section, there are also three parts. First, as for the purpose of this specific division: the above has clarified cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The section on "Realizing the Result through Accordance with the Cause" concerns the arising of understanding regarding the Dharma; the present section, "Cultivating Practice by Relying on the Dharma," clarifies the meaning of initiating practice based upon that understanding. This sequence is necessary for the following two reasons.

First, the previous sixth assembly clarified the completion of realizing the result through accordance with the cause and the arising of understanding; next, it revealed the locus of correct practice, which is untainted by the world. Therefore, these two assemblies must follow one another. As for their arrival [in this context]:

the preceding sixth assembly elucidated the perfection of cultivating the cause to accord with the result and the arising of understanding; subsequently, it manifested the site of correct practice, which remains unstained by the mundane world. Thus, the sequence follows.
Regarding the arrival [of this chapter]: the preceding "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (Xingqi-pin) clearly elucidated the excellence of the fruit of nature;

now, following that, the application of practice arising from it is clarified, which is why it follows in sequence. (And so forth). Fourth, as for the explanation of the text: within this assembly, it is broadly divided into eight parts: 1. the introductory section (xu-fen);
2. the samādhi section (sanmei-fen); 3. the arising section (qi-fen); 4. the request section (qing-fen); 5. the exposition section (shuo-fen); ... [and so on].
(As stated above) Second, at that time, Samantabhadra enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which clarifies the section on the divisions of samādhi; herein there are two parts:

first, entering the concentration, and second, explaining the benefits. Within the former, Samantabhadra enters because he is the presiding host of this assembly, signifying that these dharmas of practice are universally pervasive, and from this state he emerges into those infinite practices.
The *Avataṃsaka* concentration is briefly presented through four gates: 1. [The Gate of]... (etc.)

Regarding the "Explanation of Names": because it causes the causal practices of the *Avataṃsaka* to manifest the characteristics of the fruition, [the name is established]. Regarding the "Two Essential Natures":

the ocean of the mind within the practice-gates of the *dharmadhātu* constitutes the essence, for its meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is vast, great, and immeasurable. Regarding the "Clarification of Functional Activity," there are two aspects:
first, because this [text] is taught based upon this [ocean of mind] to reveal the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma; thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* praises the virtues of the Bodhisattvas.

The middle passage states that one attains the Buddha-flower Adornment Samādhi (*Buddhavatamsaka-samādhi*) and proclaims the scriptures of all Buddhas; this is based on two points to demonstrate the practice of the *Avataṃsaka*.

As stated above: "Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, skillful means, and wisdom—all these merits are sovereign and inconceivable, due to the power of the *Avataṃsaka-samādhi*. The commentary explains: because the dharmas of all practices are profound...
Because they are so vast and manifold that they cannot be explained individually, it says "all sovereign [powers] and so forth," which refers to the two thousand dharmas of practice mentioned below.

Regarding the stages and levels, there are four propositions: first, if one subsumes the beginning into the end, one attains [the realization] as described for the Dharma-Cloud Ground (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) only at the tenth stage;
second, if one subsumes the end into the beginning, one attains [the realization] as previously described upon reaching the full mind of the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi).
1. As stated in the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta*, there are three [aspects]:

first, being unimpeded from beginning to end and pervading all stages, because it is not separate from the two previously mentioned [aspects] and because those beginnings and ends encompass the middle;

second, transcending beginning and end such that it does not depend on stages at all, as this text explains, for it distinguishes its characteristics solely by means of the dharmas of practice (and so forth). Fourth, at that time...

In the "Section on the Request" at the end of the *Puhui* (Universal Wisdom), there are three parts: first, a general statement of the intent of the questions; second, the actual presentation of the questions;
and third, the conclusion requesting that [the Buddha] speak [upon them]. Second, regarding the dharmas asked about, there are two hundred phrases.

In the separately circulated *Dushi jing* (Sutra on Transcending the World), these are treated as six distinct rounds of questioning and answered with six corresponding rounds of replies. This has been the tradition handed down from antiquity.
Based on the textual usage of that work, this sutra is divided into six sections: first, twenty phrases asking about the practice of the ten levels of faith;
second, from "From what does one give rise to the mind of Samantabhadra? below, twenty phrases asking about the ten stages of abiding;
third, from "By what is it maintained? below, thirty phrases asking about the ten practices; fourth, from "What is the precious dwelling? below, twenty... [phrases].

1. Nine questions concerning the practice of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), from "What is bodily action? (*katamaḥ kāyakarma*) onwards, consisting of fifty questions regarding the practice of realization in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). 2.
Five questions concerning the ultimate stage of the perfection of cause and fruit (*hetu-phala-paripūri-niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), from "What is observation?

(*katamā vipaśyanā*) onwards, consisting of fifty-one questions. In this sūtra, these six stages are explained in total three times throughout the text; this [passage] corresponds to the second [explanation].
The six stages are explained in terms of practice because the conduct of Samantabhadra encompasses all six stages. Therefore, the *Duli shijie jing* (Sūtra on Delivering the World) states:
"I shall explain only the practices of the bodhisattvas from beginning to end, so that there may be no doubt.

Although the six sections of that sūtra are not explicitly correlated with the six stages of faith and so forth, since it speaks of "from beginning to end," it clarifies the attainment of Buddhahood at the very conclusion.

Since the fruit is the culmination, it is known that the initial practice of faith is the beginning; this need not be stated explicitly, for it is understood that [the teaching] definitely concerns these six stages.
In the fifth major section, from "At that time, Samantabhadra... onwards, the section on the Exposition is clarified.
First, there is the general announcement; second, the formal response. Since each of the two hundred previous questions is answered by means of ten gates, there are two thousand lines.
The Dharma-exegesis of these two thousand *Samantabhadra-caryā-dharmas* is briefly organized into five sections: (1) distinguishing cause and effect; (2) dividing stages and positions;
(3) manifesting the universal and the particular; (4) clarifying mutual inclusion; and (5) discerning the characteristics of the practices. Regarding the first [section], there are four propositions:

(1) by means of the great positions, the preceding five stages and so forth are collectively categorized as causal practice, while the subsequent attainment of Buddhahood and so forth are collectively categorized as the fruit.
The two types of practice are distinguished in detail through two hundred gates; each and every one of these practices penetrates all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Therefore, at the conclusion of each textual passage, it is invariably stated that "one immediately attains Buddhahood," and so forth. This indicates that [the practices] encompass both the causal and resultant stages.

Alternatively, they may be categorized entirely within the causal stage, as even within the stage of Samantabhadra, there is the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood and gathering in sentient beings.
Therefore, the four [categories] may collectively belong to the fruit; for the subsequent text frequently states that although one attains Buddhahood, one does not cease the bodhisattva practices.

Thus, these practices are all "fruit-practices" (phala-caryā). Regarding the two divisions of stages (*bhūmi*), it means that the two thousand [practices] constitute the practice (*caryā*) and the six divisions are called the stages (*bhūmi*).

By synthesizing the practice, the stage is established. There are also four meanings regarding the emptiness of practice and the reality of the stage: first, the synthesis of practice establishes the stage.
1. These two thousand divisions are bound together to form six categories; 2. They are collectively subsumed under the categories, because the practices are all contained within these categories; 3.
They are collectively subsumed under the practices, because the essence of Samantabhadra’s conduct does not depend upon fixed categories;

4. There is only the "self-division" and "superior progress," which constitute the ultimate; 5. One practice pervades the six categories, and one category encompasses the two thousand [divisions]; thus there is non-obstruction.
Because it does not disrupt the sequence of before and after, it is the practice of Samantabhadra. Third, to manifest the universal and the particular:

this means that a single aspect of practice necessarily pervades all things, yet it is always unmixed. Because it is unmixed, the meaning of "particular" is distinctly divided; because it necessarily pervades, the meaning of "universal" encompasses everything.
It is like a brocade pattern where the vermilion and purple motifs are distinct, thereby forming the pattern, while the vermilion and purple threads are woven throughout.

One should know that the modes of practice within this [Samantabhadra-caryā] are likewise: the universal is the particular, and the particular is the universal; all are without obstruction, which can be seen by reflecting upon them.
If this is so, since the universal and the particular are fully integrated here, why is it specifically called the "Practice of Samantabhadra"?

The explanation is: it does not mean that one maintains the universal while being unable to act particularly, nor does it mean that one performs particulars while losing the universal. In reality, [it is both].

This means that while being able to distinguish [the stages], one does not destroy their universality; this is the practice of Samantabhadra. Regarding the mutual inclusion [of these stages], there are four levels:
first, the inclusion of stages by way of stages. Within each of the six stages, every single stage includes all other stages.
Therefore, a single stage possesses two thousand practices, totaling twelve thousand practices. As stated above, "dwelling in one stage, universally encompassing [all]."
This refers to the merits of all the stages (*bhūmi*). Second, by means of the "gates" (*mukha*), each of the two hundred gates individually encompasses all gates;
thus, there are two hundred sets of two hundred, which constitute forty thousand practices (*caryā*).
Third, by means of the "practices," each of the two thousand practices individually subsumes all practices; thus, it is established as follows...

"Two thousand" means two thousand; it also encompasses billions, trillions, and so forth. Fourth, the brief is used to subsume the extensive, as in what has been explained regarding the "two thousand practices.
The concluding verse below states, "like the teaching of a single mote of dust upon the great earth.
Because this brief explanation of a single mote of dust does not depart from the vastness of the ten directions, the subsumption of the extensive is likewise exhaustive. This is...

The dharma-realm of equality is boundless, transcending the limits of empty space; as it says below, "empty space may be measured, but the virtue of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible"—this is precisely what that means.
Fifth, regarding the analysis of the characteristics of practice: one should understand that the explanation follows the text.
Within these two thousand practices, they are divided into six according to the six preceding stages, as should be understood from before (etc.).

From here below, the sixth great section, beginning from the "ten kinds of observation" and comprising five hundred and ten phrases, answers the sixth [section] above concerning the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results;

herein it is divided into two parts: first, three hundred and twenty phrases clarify the ultimate practice of perfected causes, which corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);
second, from the "ten kinds of dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven" onwards, one hundred [phrases].
The ninety phrases clarify the perfection of manifest fruition and its practice, which is also analogous to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (and so forth).
Second, regarding the ten matters of dwelling in Tuṣita, one hundred and ninety gates clarify the perfection of the activity of fruition.
These largely concern the manifestation of the eight phases of appearance to elucidate the Buddha’s function; however, this also extends to the functions of Samantabhadra and others.

This is explained from the perspective of the Pure Land’s place of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*). Furthermore, it is interpreted that because this refers exclusively to the activity of a Bodhisattva, it only demonstrates the manifestation of the eight phases of attaining Buddhahood (*aṣṭa-mahā-prātihārya*) and not an actual attainment by others.

Alternatively, it is interpreted that since the actual attainment of Buddhahood is such that it can neither be said to be "attained" nor "unattained," it is described in terms of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] (and so forth).
*Tanxuanji*, Fascicle 18 (Eighth Assembly), Chapter 34:
"Entering the Dharma Realm. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the four gates are the same as before. First, in explaining the title, there are three parts.

First, the title based on the person (*puruṣa-nāman*): it is called "Entering the Realization" because it relies extensively upon the profound realization of the Dharma Realm by the friend [Bandhumant].

This constitutes the section on the perfection of virtue. Second, regarding the names of the assemblies based on their locations, the assembly at the Gabled Hall of Jetavana is so named because it signifies that this Dharma saves sentient beings and gathers in all life;
furthermore, as it manifests the aspect of compassion arising from fundamental wisdom as a re-emergence, it is located at the Gabled Hall.
Regarding the names of the three categories: "entry" (*praveśa*) refers to that which enters, meaning awakening, understanding, and realization; "Dharmadhātu" is...
The dharmas that are entered possess three meanings: first, the meaning of maintaining its own nature; second, the meaning of a rule or standard;

and third, the meaning of being an object of correspondence. The *dhātu* (element/realm) likewise possesses three meanings: first, the meaning of cause, because it serves as the basis for the arising of the noble path.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The *dharmadhātu* refers to the cause of all pure dharmas. Furthermore, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "Its meaning is the cause of the noble dharmas. Therefore...

The teaching on the *dharmadhātu* as the noble dharma (*āryadharma*) states that its meaning as "element" (*dhātu*) in this context is threefold: first, the sense of cause, meaning that the noble dharmas arise based upon this object;

second, the sense of nature, meaning it is the supporting nature (*āśraya-svabhāva*) of all phenomena, as the preceding passage of this sutra states: "The *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmatā* are likewise";

and third, the sense of demarcation, meaning that the various dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*) do not intermingle. (And so forth. Third, the explanation of the [three] knowledges (*vidyā*).

Regarding the fundamental purport (*abhiprāya*), since the chapters on the "Convergence" (*samavasaraṇa*) have already clarified the entry into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this [entry] is taken as the primary tenet.

Within this, it is analyzed through three gates: first, by way of meaning; second, by way of category; and third, by way of stage. In the first [gate], concerning the meaning of the Dharma-realm to be entered, there are five sections:
first, the conditioned Dharma-realm (*saṃskṛta-dharmadhātu*); second, the unconditioned Dharma-realm (*asaṃskṛta-dharmadhātu*); third, that which is both conditioned and... [unconditioned].
The Unconditioned Dharma-realm (etcetera; fearing that the text would become too voluminous, I cannot cite it in full). Third, regarding the entry into the Dharma-realm by way of stages:

according to the passage below, there are two great categories of the Dharma-realm entered, namely cause and fruit. For those who have previously [attained realization], there is nothing among phenomena or persons that is not subsumed within the Buddha-fruit;
this is precisely the sovereign mastery over the Dharma-realm manifested through the Tathāgata’s Lion’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi.

Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned dharmas, there are none that are not subsumed within the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*); this refers to the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm manifested by Mañjuśrī’s universal manifestation.
Within this stage of the cause, it is further divided into five parts, namely the Dharma-realm of the five stages beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

This can be understood through the principle of inclusion. Second, the clarification of the "one who enters" (*praveśaka*) also has two parts according to the text; here, it is explained in contrast to the aforementioned stage of the fruit (*phala-bhūmi*).
All Bodhisattvas enter the Dharma-realm instantaneously; whereas for those in the preceding causal stage, it is presented as Sudhana’s gradual entry into the Dharma-realm.

Since cause and effect are thus unimpeded, the gradual and the instantaneous are likewise perfectly integrated. It is only for the purpose of establishing the teaching and forming a definitive exposition that these distinct stages are provisionally established.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: within this chapter, there are two major sections: first, the explanation of the primary assembly; second, [the explanation of the secondary assembly].

At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Abiding Pavilion. This clarifies that the preceding section explains the resultant Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), while the subsequent section explains the causal Dharma-realm;
furthermore, the preceding section explains the sudden entry into the Dharma-realm, while the subsequent section explains the gradual entry into the Dharma-realm.

Moreover, the preceding is general and the subsequent is specific, such that the root and the branches are perfectly integrated and unimpeded. Regarding this, if one considers it in relation to the previous primary assembly, it is extensive.

The divisions consist of eleven sections: (1) the Introductory Section; (2) the Section on the Request; (3) the Section on Samādhi; (4) the Section on Manifesting Purity; (5) the Section on Assembling this Multitude;
(6) the Section on Elevating the Inferior to Reveal the Superior; (7) the Section on Praising Virtues in Verse; (8) the Section on Samantabhadra’s Development;

(9) the Section on the Beneficial Effects Shown by the Light from the Ūrṇā-hair; (10) the Section on Mañjuśrī’s Description of Virtue (*etc.*). Within the second section, the Section on the Request: [Translation of the subsequent text follows]

There are three parts: first, the initial assembly’s mindfulness of the invitation; second, the mindfulness of that which is invited; and third, the mindfulness of the manifestation of the invitation (and so forth).

Within the section on "that which is invited," there are sixty phrases in total. An ancient master explained them as follows: the first thirty clarify the Buddha’s own entry into the *dharmadhātu*, while the latter thirty clarify the Buddha’s causing others to enter the *dharmadhātu*.
In this current explanation, regarding the first ten [phrases] of the sixty which are the mindfulness of the invitation to the fruit-dharma, why is this?
Having understood that what was requested concerns the fruit, one next clarifies that those at lower stages cannot fathom it;

since they do not even possess the capacity to know it, how could they now wish to request it? It is said that although some may know it through the power of the causes and conditions of the subsequent ten clarifications, it remains uncertain whether this assembly possesses the power of knowledge. Thus, the subsequent ten clarify the faculties and capacities of this assembly.

Although the powers are manifold and the equipment complete, if there were no power of the Buddha, there would likewise be no one able to know [this]. This refers to the subsequent ten [perfections] which clarify the cause for the Buddha’s benefiting of others.
Although the causes for benefiting others are fulfilled, if there were no manifest activity of the fruit that benefits others, it would likewise be impossible.

This is because it is by means of this that one is made to know. Next, the ten [perfections] distinguish the fruit-activity that encompasses sentient beings. Since these conditions are thus complete, the conclusion of the request says: "May you, O World-Honored One, manifest [Buddhahood] and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding this, the first thirty phrases constitute the invocation by mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), while the latter thirty phrases constitute the invocation by mindfulness of the virtues (*guṇānusmṛti*).
Within the former, the first ten clarify the fruit-dharmas being invoked; the next ten clarify that which is profound, mysterious, and difficult to fathom;

and the final ten clarify that which can be traversed through the convergence of conditions (and so forth). Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards, the final assembly is clarified; therein, the preceding section is as follows:
Because the end is not different from the root, although it is rolled up, it is always extended; this refers to the subsequent text.

Because the subsequent is not different from the root’s end, although it is extended, it is always rolled up; this refers to the preceding text. Therefore, the root and the end are unimpeded and constitute a single chapter; the intent lies herein.
Now, to provide a general explanation of this, the following text will briefly present ten sections. First, the introduction.
Regarding the ten points of the ancient expositions—first, the number of assemblies; second, the opening and closing of the assemblies; third, the number of primary figures;

fourth, the fixed names and meanings of the assemblies; fifth, the comprehensive inclusion within two positions; sixth, the division into five aspects; seventh, the perfect integration from beginning to end;

eighth, the clarification of the human types within the Dharma-realm; ninth, the matters and meanings of the Dharma-realm; and tenth, the word-by-word commentary—the various ancient theories are extremely numerous and difficult to record in full.

To provide a brief enumeration, one school of thought states that there are forty-five spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) herein; however, since Mañjuśrī is not established as a separate category in the subsequent text, there are only forty-four.
The first is the spiritual friend of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); the next forty are the spiritual friends of the forty positions beginning with the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*);
the next two are the spiritual friends of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); and the final one is the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata*).
Since the old commentary lacks supplementary texts, I have merely distinguished the forty-fourth and forty-fifth [sections].
Virtuous masters such as Guāngtǒng and others mostly agree with this view. Furthermore, according to our own school, we do not assign fixed positions nor establish overarching outlines;

rather, we provide a detailed exegesis following the text according to each assembly. This is exactly as in the Wǔtái Lùn (Five Terrace Treatise) and the works of Master Yìfǎshī and others, all of which follow this approach.

Regarding the explanation of these two, the former [interpretation] slightly contradicts the literal text, while the latter does not hinder the meaning; this can be understood through careful reflection.

Second, regarding the clarification of the number of assemblies and their opening and closing, there are six points therein: first, if categorized according to the capacities of those to be gathered, there are only three assemblies:
(1) the assembly gathering the bhikṣus, (2) the assembly gathering the nāga kings, and (3) the assembly gathering Sudhana’s merits.
The "Clouds Have Already Departed" chapter is collectively subsumed under the third assembly because the sentient beings being converted therein are indistinguishable from those of that assembly.
