As for the fifty-two assemblies categorized according to the principal teachers who perform the conversion: the first three and the final fifty-fourth, the "Universal Gate City" assembly, all have Mañjuśrī as their presiding teacher and no other;
the remaining fifty-one assemblies each have a different individual as their presiding teacher.

Therefore, if categorized according to the primary [protagonists], there are only fifty-two assemblies. Third, if categorized by comprehensively distinguishing between the subject and the object, there are fifty-five assemblies;
that is, there are fifty-three for Sudhana, and one each for the bhikṣus and the nāgas.

Fourth, if categorized by separately distinguishing between the primary and the accompanying [retinues], there are one hundred and ten assemblies, as analyzed in the following text. Fifth, if categorized according to the basis upon which they are diffusely explained...
There are assemblies numbering as many as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, as explained later in the section on Mañjuśrī;
this refers to the drawing in of those with the capacities of the three vehicles, as distinguished in the sixth [chapter].

If one considers them according to the virtues of Samantabhadra, there are assemblies numbering as many as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, as distinguished in the concluding passage on universal penetration. Third, regarding the number of assembly leaders, there are two levels: first, if considered solely...

It is said that there are fifty-four persons because, among the fifty-five assemblies, there is only one person in four of them—namely Mañjuśrī—and two persons in four other assemblies—namely Samantabhadra and Viśvakarman, along with the boy and the girl.
Thus, while there are fifty-five assemblies, there are fifty-four principal figures; if one counts the assemblies together to reveal the number of persons, there are fifty.
Regarding the "seven persons," this refers to adding one person to each of two locations within the fifty-five assemblies; these may be understood as Samantabhadra and others (and so forth).
As for the "five encompassing the two positions" which collectively subsume [the assemblies]: these fifty-five assemblies are unified by two primary figures.

From the initial Mañjuśrī to the final Mañjuśrī, these constitute the stage of Mañjuśrī, which belongs to the Prajñā (Wisdom) gate. The final single stage of Samantabhadra belongs to the Dharma [gate].
Without Prajñā, there is no way to enter the Dharma-realm; therefore, Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī.
Without entering the Dharma-realm, there is no way to manifest Prajñā; therefore, Sudhana subsequently beheld Samantabhadra.
Thus, these two persons are assigned to two stages to clarify the entry into the Dharma-realm. Furthermore, the preceding section on Mañjuśrī clarifies the profound meaning of the Dharma-realm.
Subsequently, Samantabhadra reveals the meaning of the vastness of the Dharma-realm; therefore, these two gates reflect one another and possess all virtues. Question:
Since there were previously other spiritual friends such as Guṇamegha and others, why is it said that they are all Mañjuśrī? Answer:
Because they are all the result of Mañjuśrī’s transformative influence and virtue, and because they have all been born from the great ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom. Thus it is.
Therefore, the subsequent text sometimes states that Mañjuśrī taught me the method of revulsion toward phenomena (*dharmānubhava*), and Maitreya also says:
"That you are now able to see these various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who have come to my place is entirely due to the empowerment (*parigraha*) of Mañjuśrī. (Examine the text).
For this reason, the formal Mañjuśrī acts as the initial condition for awakening, while the formless Sublime Virtue (*Guṇa*) serves as the sublime conclusion.
Regarding the transition into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are three phases: first, the initial manifestation at the prior limit;

second, the thorough cultivation during the middle limit, as shown from the passage "descending from the Cloud of Virtue" (*Guṇamegha*); and finally, Mañjuśrī clarifies the ultimate return at the posterior limit. This, too, constitutes a single cycle of practice.
Within the middle limit, the first forty individuals clarify the causal conditions for practice within their respective stages; thus, these forty are provisionally established.

The ten stages following the stage of mind (*citta*) and the practices following the stage of illumination (*āloka*) refer to the various cultivations external to the stage of abiding in conditions (*ālambana*).

Regarding the six divisions and five aspects: this text is broadly divided into five aspects as follows: first, the aspect of cultivation by relying on the stages, which comprises forty-one individuals;

second, from the section below Lady Māyā, the nine assemblies and eleven individuals clarify the entry into the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through the conditions of the assembly; third... [text continues].
First, Maitreya alone clarifies the aspect of the cause being accomplished through the gathering of virtues; second, Mañjuśrī alone clarifies the aspect of non-duality illuminated by wisdom;
third, Samantabhadra alone clarifies the aspect of the vastness of the manifest cause. Furthermore, these five aspects are also the five types of bodhisattva practices:
first, the sublime practice; second, the great practice; third, the superior practice; fourth, the profound practice; and fifth, the expansive practice.
Seventh, regarding the circular inclusion from beginning to end: this means that within each of the distinct stages of these assemblies, every single one individually encompasses all gates.
Therefore, a single stage contains fifty-five, as well as one hundred and ten, plus numbers equal to the atoms of lands, and so forth;

as it is for one, so it is for all, with each layer following the same principle. This is merely done to manifest their differences by relying on dharmas and to arrange them before and after for the sake of contemplation.
Question: If one [reality] already possesses all, why must Sudhana travel extensively through various stations?

Answer: All that he travels through are the "all" within the "one"; therefore, they do not transcend the one. Question: If these are the "all" within the "one," then by attaining the one, one would attain the many;
why then must he still travel further? Answer: Attaining the one is precisely [attaining the many].
Because of these many reasons, one can see upon reflection that there is no obstruction between them occurring simultaneously (and so forth). Regarding the tenth section, the "Exegesis of the Text":

Now, following Zhixiang’s topical outline for the exegesis of this passage, within the first part concerning the characteristics of practice by way of provisional stations, there are forty-one spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Among these, the first, Mañjuśrī alone, serves as the spiritual friend for the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), because the stage of faith is not yet established as a formal rank.
It is not distinguished [separately]; because the remaining four positions are established among ten people, it is said that there are ten [in total] (and so forth).
*Tanchuan ji*, fascicle 20, "Chapter on Maitreya":
Regarding the number one hundred and ten, the ancient masters have three interpretations: first, it is said that from the preceding section up to this point, there should be one hundred and ten.
However, because these were omitted from the text, they are not listed in full. First, it is said that those enumerated above are the primary spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);

yet, if one takes both the principal and the attendant figures into account—including those who provide skillful guidance and so forth—there are one hundred and ten. For this reason, there is no deficiency in the preceding text;
the mention of King Paripūrṇa, King Mahāprabha, and others was already indicated earlier by the phrase "gradually passing through the multitudes."
Because they include [the entry into] cities, towns, wildernesses, and so forth, it is known that there are one hundred and ten locations traversed in total. One interpretation states:
the five stages beginning with faith constitute fifty; subsequently, Māyā, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Buddha constitute five.
Since each of these fifty-five has both its own stage (*svabhūmi*) and its progressive advancement (*viśeṣagamana*), there are one hundred and ten. These...
Furthermore, because these various explanations were insufficient in the older translations, they are now fully provided here so that no further divergent interpretations are required.
This is a general summary: the preceding and succeeding stages of knowledge comprise fifty-four positions; when the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī are added, there are fifty-five persons.
Since each possesses both their own stage (*svabhūmi*) and the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*), there are one hundred and ten in total. (End of quote)
(Thus it is said).

*Souxuan ji* (Record of Searching the Profundities), Fascicle One, "The Chapter on Vairocana," Part Two. From this point onward, the main body of the teaching is correctly elucidated; the text is divided into four sections.
[The preceding section] is concluded.
Regarding the textual explanation of the fourth division, there are two parts: first, correlating [the sections], and second, following the chapters.

This "Vairocana Chapter" belongs to the category of resultant virtues because the result is extensive while the cause is concise; second, from the "Names and Epithets" [chapter] onwards, it is judged to belong to the category of causal virtues because the cause is extensive while the result is concise.
The practice has another distinct half, as explained at the beginning of the second assembly. Regarding the division by chapter, there are three parts:

first, from "Light-Awakening" onwards, is the section that cites the fruit to encourage joy and engender faith; second, from "Difficulties" onwards, is the section that clarifies the cultivation of causes to accord with the fruit and engender understanding;
third, from "Transcending the World" onwards, is the section that distinguishes the cultivation based on conditions to accomplish virtue. The reason it must be thus is as follows.

Because sentient beings have meager roots of goodness and it is difficult for faith to arise, within this chapter the Buddha adds the teaching of Samantabhadra regarding the *āśraya-phala* (the fruit of the supporting environment) of the Pure Land;
in the second assembly, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha, explains the three karmas of the Buddha to clarify its *vipāka-phala* (the fruit of the primary retribution).
Having established faith through these superior environments and primary retributions, one must next be taught the Dharma.
In order to cause them to give rise to understanding, the "Chapter on Difficulties" (Nan-pin) below provides a detailed analysis of the characteristics of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*).

Having first exhorted reliance upon the clearly perceived Dharma, one must next exhort reliance upon the arising of practice so as to attain that which is to be realized. Therefore, from "Leaving the World" (*Li-shijian*) onwards, the section "Virtues Accomplished through Reliance on Conditions" (*Yuan-cheng-de-fen*) is elucidated, and so forth.
Chapter Two: Summary of Contents (The Chapter on the Ten Abodes; The Chapter on the Ten Pāramitās; The Chapter on the Ten Dedications). Regarding the meaning of the "Ten Abodes" (*daśa-vihāra*):

"Ten" refers to the number, and "abode" (*vihāra*) refers to the stage of non-retrogression. It is also called the "Ten Understandings" (*daśa-adhimukti*). 1. The Abode of the Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*);

2. The Abode of Holding the Ground (*dharaṇī-vihāra*); 3. The Abode of Cultivation (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*); 4. The Abode of Noble Birth (*janma-udbhava-vihāra*); 5. The Abode of Skillful Means (*upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra*).

The Foot-abiding Stage (1), the Sixfold Right Mind-abiding Stage (2), the Non-retrogressive Stage (3), the Youthful Truth Stage (4), the Dharma Prince Stage (5), and the Consecration Stage (6)—these are called "stages" (*vihāra*) because they are immovable.
Their essence consists of immeasurable skillful means and samādhi.

This is explained according to the Final Teaching of the Three Vehicles; according to the Initial Teaching, this is essentially the One Vehicle. As for the ignorant followers of the Small Vehicle, there is no fixed [stage].
It should be understood accordingly that when first turning the mind [toward enlightenment], the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are not mentioned (and so forth).
Regarding the ten *pāramitās*, they are the dharmas of the ten practices: first, the *dāna-pāramitā* (and so forth);

these are the ten practices because giving alone brings joy to both oneself and others, thus it is called the "Practice of Joy" (*pramuditā-caryā*); and because ethical discipline (*śīla*) accomplishes the benefit of both oneself and others, it is [the second].

1. It is called the practice of beneficial conduct (*anugrahacaryā*), because it accomplishes freedom from anger and resentment toward oneself and others. 2. It is called the practice of non-ill will (*avyāpādacaryā*), because it accomplishes supreme virtues through diligence (*vīrya*). 3.
It is called the practice of inexhaustibility (*akṣayacaryā*), because of the tranquility of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). 4.

It is called the practice of freedom from delusion and confusion (*mohavikṣepavirahacaryā*), because the wisdom of realization (*prajñā*) manifests the presence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 5. It is called the practice of excellent manifestation (*susaṃdarśanacaryā*), because of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

1. It is called the practice of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others; 2. It is called the practice of non-attachment, because one possesses mastery over activities and can accomplish them according to one’s will;
3. It is called the practice of reverence, because one achieves mastery over superior power to bring sentient beings to maturity; 4.

It is called the practice of wholesome qualities, because the three types of action performed for the benefit of others are not in vain, such that one acts as one speaks and speaks as one acts; 5. It is called the practice of reality.

"Arising and acting" is the meaning of *saṃskāra* (formative forces). This meaning does not apply equally across the three vehicles. In the teachings of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the initial teaching is that all is empty; the final teaching is that all is as it is (*tathatā*).
In the teachings of the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*), what is indicated is that these are expedient means (*upāya*). Furthermore, the number ten is used to manifest the infinite;
thus, it is subsumed within the One Vehicle. Question: The three vehicles also have the number ten; how do they differ from the One Vehicle? Answer: The three vehicles... [text ends]

The ten stages of numbers (*daśasaṃkhyā*) involve the transformational rituals according to various directions, which have no distinct standard rules; however, based on the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there are distinct standard rules. Furthermore, these exist within the samādhi;
one should know that their boundaries are entirely distinct, and the remaining meanings may be understood from the separate chapter [as follows].
Regarding the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*): first, the dedication to rescue and protect all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings; second, the [dedication...]
1. The dedication that destroys [obstacles]; 2. The dedication equal to all Buddhas; 3. The dedication that reaches all places; 4.

The dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; 5. The dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality; 6. The dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings;
7. The dedication according to reality; 8. The dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment; 9. The tenth [dedication].
The Dharma-realm is immeasurable dedication. What is the meaning of "dedication"? Non-dedication is dedication.
There are three meanings of dedication: first, dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); second, dedication to unsurpassed enlightenment; and third, dedication to sentient beings.
Within these three meanings, because one recognizes the ancient Dharma, this dedication is not a new dedication, but is identical to the ancient dedication. Why?
Therefore, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) has three meanings: first, the dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas flow from True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the Dharma-as-such;
second, that which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas is for the purpose of manifesting their original nature, and thus it is the equipment of the original nature;

third, since suchness is primordially present, this equipment is not newly acquired. Furthermore, dedication toward enlightenment (*bodhipariṇāmanā*) is also of two kinds: first, the practice of Bodhisattvas proceeds from the fruit.
The merit and wisdom that flow forth constitute all human dharmas; from these two capacities for achieving the fruit of virtue, one enters the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Furthermore, from the third aspect of the fruit of virtue, there is the dedication to sentient beings, which also possesses two meanings:

first, the Bodhisattva accomplishes all human dharmas together with what is bestowed upon sentient beings. Why is this? Because if there were no sentient beings, [these dharmas] would not be accomplished; therefore, [it is so].

These sentient beings are endowed with the two bodhisattvas who accomplish the virtues of human and dharma practices; as they serve as the equipment for sentient beings, they belong to sentient beings.
Therefore, this is not a new dedication—dedication is wisdom. This meaning applies to the three vehicles:
in the initial teaching it is emptiness, in the final teaching it is suchness, and that which is designated by the One Vehicle is the skillful means toward the One Vehicle. Furthermore...

As for the number ten, it manifests the measure of the celestial realms; thus, one enters the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) which subsumes other meanings, as explained in detail in a separate chapter (*etc.*).
Chapter Three: *Kongmu* (The Essential Gate). [Contents: Ten Stages Chapter; Six Determinations Chapter; Receiving the Office Chapter.

Regarding the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*): first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); second, the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*); third, the Stage of Radiant Wisdom (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); fourth, the Stage of Blazing Fire (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*); fifth...

The Sixth Ground is the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), the Seventh is the Manifest (*Abhimukhī*), the Eighth is the Far-Reaching (*Dūraṅgamā*), the Ninth is the Immovable (*Acalā*), the Tenth is the Good Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), and the [Eleventh] is the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā*).
Because they generate and maintain the Buddha-wisdom, they are called "grounds" (*bhūmi*); "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to a stage or position.
Now, these Ten Grounds encompass the causal stages of the Buddha; the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, the Śrāvakas, humans, and devas are all included therein as the Five Vehicles.
What all people observe is the stage of realization of Samantabhadra, wherein the functions subsumed within the fruit of Buddhahood are unimpeded and sovereign, exhausting all things. Why is this?
Because the dharmas of the ten stages constitute the primary gateway for gathering sentient beings; these stage-dharmas are profoundly deep and most difficult to discern.
To briefly distinguish their respective limits according to the five vehicles: the first consists of the human and celestial [vehicles], namely—
The vehicles of humans and devas, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas are grouped together as one, namely the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

That which is for the sake of the gradual teaching is one, namely the vehicle of gradual enlightenment. That which is for the sake of the sudden teaching is one, namely the vehicle of sudden enlightenment. The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is one, namely the ultimate vehicle.
Regarding the first, the vehicle of humans and devas, there are three ways of attaining Buddhahood: first, a Buddha manifests his body to rescue those in the three evil realms.
First, outside of those three evil realms, one immediately attains the Buddha-body; for example, as when the Buddha manifested the feet of a black elephant.
Second, in order to lead beings toward the human realm, he manifests the attainment of the Buddha-body; for example, as when the Buddha manifested the body of a tree deity for the elder Trapusa.
Third, in order to lead beings toward the human and celestial realms, he manifests his noble body; for example, as when humans and devas recognize the Buddha as a noble being and offer him worship.
Regarding those who accomplish worldly merit, there are seven meanings within the context of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*):

first, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), it refers to the nine stages of the three realms, the tenth stage, and the eleventh stage, beyond which one becomes a Buddha; second, regarding the levels of practice (*avasthā*), it refers to the completion of the paths of seeing and cultivation, beyond which one becomes a Buddha;
third, regarding the conduct (*caryā*), it refers to the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) after departing from learning, wherein Buddhahood is manifested.

1. Regarding the Buddha’s four [aspects], outside of the thirty-three minds of bodhisattva practice, one immediately becomes that Buddha; 2. Regarding the five [aspects], outside of the sixty kalpas of the Hīnayāna and the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one immediately becomes that Buddha;
3. Regarding the six [aspects], based on the final stage of birth-and-death (*bhava*), within the body of the final segment of existence (*prāntakotika-bhava*), one immediately becomes that Buddha;
4. Regarding the seven [aspects], according to the Hīnayāna, in the twelfth of the twelve stages (*vihāra*), the ultimate [stage].
The dwelling of the supreme Arhat is identical to that of the Buddha. Regarding these three points, there are eight meanings based on the teaching gate of the initial turning of the mind:
First, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): it refers to the ten stages beginning with the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*). Within the tenth stage, one attains Buddhahood.

The reason for stating that one attains Buddhahood within the tenth stage is that the Buddha intentionally descends to the level of the causal stages; therefore, this teaching is established. Second, regarding... [text continues]

1. Regarding realms and stages: beyond the three realms, nine stages, and eleven stages, one immediately becomes a Buddha. 2. Regarding the stages of seeing and cultivation: beyond these, one immediately becomes a Buddha. 3. Regarding the stage of training (*śaikṣa*):
beyond this, one attains the same stage as an Arhat who has completed their training (*aśaikṣa*), and thus becomes a Buddha.

4. Regarding time: according to the Mahāyāna, beyond the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one becomes a Buddha. 5. Regarding Bodhisattvas: [beyond this... [Note: The fifth point regarding time is explicitly linked to the Mahāyāna framework of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. The final fragment regarding Bodhisattvas appears to be an incomplete heading for the subsequent discussion.]
1. One becomes a Buddha externally after thirty-three mental moments; 2. Regarding the principle of non-discriminative emptiness, one becomes a Buddha in a single thought-moment;
3. Regarding the final stage of the *bhavāgra* (segmented) body within the cycle of birth and death, one becomes a Buddha—this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*;

4. Regarding the stage after the *vipākaphala* (retributive) segmented body, one becomes a Buddha; furthermore, according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), there is the position of direct advancement.

Regarding these seven gates, the first concerns the stages: from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) starting from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one then becomes a Buddha beyond that.
This is because the *paricchinna-kāya* (segmented body) of the Buddha’s realm is not the same as the *paricchinna-kāya* of the bodhisattva stages.
Second, regarding the stages again: from the Stage of Joy through to the end of the ninth stage, at the tenth—

1. Regarding the stage (*bhūmi*): it refers to attaining Buddhahood from the stage of non-retrogression; this is stated because one attains Buddhahood within the lower body at the lower level of the Śrāvaka path. 2. Regarding principle (*tattva*):
it means that within the non-conceptual emptiness of *tathatā*, Buddhahood is attained in a single thought-moment. 3. Regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):
it refers to attaining Buddhahood by realizing the fruit in the final thought-moment after the tenth stage. 4. Regarding time: [this refers to] the Mahāyāna perspective.
Sixth, regarding the culmination of practice, one becomes a Buddha immediately upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Seventh, regarding the Mahāyāna, one becomes a Buddha immediately after the twelfth stage, the Supreme Bodhisattva Abode (*uttama-bodhisattvavihāra*).

Furthermore, according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhānaya*) of the Mahāyāna, there are ten gates; the first concerns the stages, ranging from the practice of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhācaryā*)...
Regarding the two [positions]: first, that one becomes a Buddha immediately after completing the ten stages beginning with the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
second, that from the initial Stage of Joy up through the ninth stage, one becomes a Buddha within the tenth stage—as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
This latter explanation was made because [the Buddha] manifested as an ordinary person before the śrāvakas and attained the realization of the fruit; therefore, he spoke in this way. This should...

Regarding the three types of accomplishment—transformative, non-transformative, and actual—their stages are as follows: from the first stage, the Joyful (Pramuditā), up to the third stage, these are mundane dharmas identical to those of the three realms;

from the fourth stage onward, up to the seventh stage, they are identical to the untainted (anāsrava), and because one attains the untainted virtues of the three vehicles within a mundane body, this is termed "supramundane. At the eighth stage, [it is exclusively supramundane].
Having already proceeded to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), it is called "transcending the world" (*lokottara-lokottara*), whereby one immediately attains Buddhahood:

at the eighth stage, the *dharmakāya* is perfected; at the ninth stage, the *saṃbhogakāya* is perfected; and at the tenth stage, the *nirmāṇakāya* is perfected. This is stated as such because these are the specific characteristics of each individual stage within the ten stages.
Fourth, "attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment" is spoken of in reference to non-conceptual *tathatā*.

5. Regarding the fifth [point], it is explained by way of realization that one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), because one realizes [the fruit] in a single thought-moment within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

6. Regarding the sixth, one is called "attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment" when one realizes the fruit in a single thought-moment after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). These aforementioned "single thought-moments" are what is meant by "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*). 7.
Regarding the seventh, in terms of time, it refers to becoming a Buddha at the end of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of the Mahāyāna. 8. Regarding the eighth, in terms of practice, it is gold.

9. After the firm mind, one attains the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), which is precisely the Buddha. 10. Regarding the extinction of birth and death, there are seven types of birth and death;
after these, one becomes that Buddha. Tenth, according to the *Mahāyānasamānaya-sūtra*, there are three kinds of ten stages:

the ten stages of the śrāvaka, the ten stages of the pratyekabuddha, and the ten stages of the Buddha. This is for the purpose of attracting those of the Small Vehicle to accord with the Mahāyāna of the Final Teaching.
For this reason, I have made this statement. The names and other details of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are fully explained as set forth in the Commentary (*ṭīkā*).

Furthermore, the distinctions among the characteristics of the ten stages are extensive, as explained in the "Chapter on Cultivation" of the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Fourth, regarding the explanation according to the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*), there is only one gate, namely, the signless (*animitta*).
Why is this? Because by accomplishing the Samādhi of One Practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*), one mounts upon that single [vehicle].
Because it is accomplished through the taste of true suchness (*tathatā*), it cannot be said that there are various distinct characteristics;

the attainment of Buddhahood is likewise in all these respects, for it is the complete departure from all [distinctions], which is what is called "Buddha. Fifth, regarding the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*):

from the final stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the stages of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the Buddha-ground—all are the attainment of Buddhahood. Furthermore, in the... [text continues].
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) also result in the distinct attainment of Buddhahood, as explained in the *Dharmaratnacūḍa-sūtra* regarding spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Why is this?

Because the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is intended to lead those of the three vehicles and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to attain Buddhahood while still in lower stations and lower bodies.
Furthermore, from the eighth stage upward, one immediately becomes a Buddha; it is at these stages that one achieves unimpededness (*asaṅga*).

The Buddha is the body of all; this statement is made according to the distinct teaching (*bhinna-naya*). If one speaks according to the common teaching (*sādhāraṇa-naya*), it encompasses the principles elucidated by the preceding four vehicles;
all are the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Although the words are the same, their meanings are entirely distinct.

Such various differentiated characteristics of these dharmas are manifested in manifold ways through the gates of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) for the sake of protecting the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

This teaching is intended to cause all sentient beings to abandon overweening pride regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, according to the meaning of the six characteristics—the general and the particular—it is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);
according to the meaning of the distribution of characteristics according to their differences, it is the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). This is explained by way of the classification of teachings;

in reality, the dharmas of the One Vehicle and the ten stages have already reached ultimate penetration throughout the three periods of time. This is explained by way of realization; as for other meanings, they are as follows.
As stated in another chapter (*etc.*). Sixth, regarding "definitive certainty":
first, it is the definitive certainty of the aspect of contemplation because the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) has the single flavor of its aspect, as the Sūtra says, "because it is unmixed.
Second, it is the definitive certainty of reality because it is not the domain of any worldly [realm], being supramundane. As the Sūtra says...

Because it cannot be seen, this is superior in three ways; it possesses six meanings: first, it is superior because it is the Great Dharma-realm; second, it is superior because it is the root of all Buddhas;
third, it is superior because the differentiation of dharma-characteristics is the nature of things (*dharmatā*);

fourth, it is superior because the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) surpasses the wisdom of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles; fifth, it is superior because it accords with the Great Teaching; sixth, it is superior because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).

Because it is supreme, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states that it is the great dharma-dhātu; because it is the root of all Buddhas; because it is the meaning of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);

because its contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*) is superior to the wisdom of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles; because it is the natural principle of the Mahāyāna teachings; and because it is the pure dharma-dhātu.
Regarding the four causes, there are two kinds of "well-determined causes" (*suniścita-hetu*): first, the cause that brings about the fruit of impermanent, cherished existence (*anitya-iṣṭaphala*).
This cause is like space; because all forms arise in dependence upon it and yet forms are never exhausted, it is the second [type of] constant fruit-cause.

Through the thorough determination of goodness, one attains the path to nirvāṇa, as the sūtra says: "until the end of the future. The fifth is the thorough determination of great goodness, which accords with and performs deeds that benefit others, as the sūtra says:
"to protect and shelter the entire realm of sentient beings. This follows immediately after the previous thorough determination of goodness.
The vow that one does not abide exclusively in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa constitutes the sixth [perfection], non-cowardice.

Because of this non-cowardice, one enters with firm determination into the ground of the wisdom of all Buddhas. As the sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, these bodhisattvas even enter the ground of the wisdom of present Buddhas.
These six determinations constitute the essence of the ten grounds, as they pervade all ten grounds.

Because this applies from the ten stages (*bhūmi*) onwards, the Sūtra states: "Within the ten stages there are five determinations; the same applies to the ten practices (*caryā*), with the exception of the great goodness (*mahākalyāṇa*);
in the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) there are three determinations, namely: observing characteristics, great goodness, and not being disheartened.

This pattern of inclusion and exclusion reveals the relative height or lowness, and the increase or decrease, of the stages; thus the general principle can be understood. This meaning extends to both those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-ja*) and...
This primordial existence (*mūlāstitva*) is not known by those of the three vehicles or the Lesser Vehicle; the nature-arising of Samantabhadra resides within this stage.
Why? Because it is equally realized [by all]. Other meanings are as explained in other chapters (and so forth).

Regarding the meaning of "assuming office" (*adhikāra*), there is a brief explanation of three types: first, assuming office through phenomena (*dharma*), such as a Wheel-Turning Sage King who fully assumes the methods of office;
second, assuming office through principle (*tattva*), such as those of the Three Vehicles who realize the true reality and thus name it "assuming office";

and third, assuming office through both phenomenon and principle, such as a Bodhisattva who has attained their rank and sits upon the great jewel lotus king-throne while the Buddhas of the ten directions emit light.

The internal dharmas corresponding to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) within the consecration (abhiṣeka) and other rites are termed "receiving office" (śrī-grahaṇa). This is as detailed in the dialogues and the scriptural texts;
further meanings are found in separate chapters.
[This concludes] the first fascicle of the *Zhixiang Wenda* (Dialogues on the Ultimate Characteristics).
Question: Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood and the reception of office (*adhikāra*) according to the various teachings, how is this explained? Answer:

If one attains office according to the Hīnayāna, it is established solely within the meaning of the human realm and involves no distinct principle of reality. If one attains office according to the Triyāna, it is established based on the principle of celestial realms, yet it does not discuss the distinctions between principle and phenomena, or teaching and meaning.

However, if one attains office according to the Ekayāna, it fully encompasses the distinctions of teaching, meaning, principle, phenomena, and stages, as is extensively detailed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
*Yuanzong Wenlei*, Fascicle 14;
*Yuanzong Wenlei*, Fascicle 22.
Praises and Miscellaneous Texts on the Three Jewels:
A Praise of the Buddha, Composed by Emperor Renzong of the Great Song Dynasty.

Above heaven and below heaven, the World-Honored One, the Golden Immortal; with the ten titles in one mind and the four wisdoms and three bodies, he delivers beings from the five aggregates and transcends the six sense objects.
All living beings turn toward him in reverence; he is the so-called Benevolent One who extols the Dharma.
All phenomena are but mind; the mind must be brought to ultimate purity. From that single thought-moment, all practices can be generated.
To turn away from awakening is delusion; to realize the truth is to be a sage. I prostrate to this Dharma-gate, which clearly reveals Buddha-nature and praises the Sangha.
Unflagging in the six perfections, The four debts of gratitude are not constant; As the eyes for all beings, You assist the Buddha as a bridge and raft.
Your body is moistened by the single rain, Your mind is perfumed by myriad fragrances; The Way is nowhere absent— In this land and in other realms.
*Praise According to the Chapters of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*
Composed by the Great Liao Emperor Tianyou,
prostrating before the ten directions: To all the Triple Gems, I now praise this sutra,
so that sentient beings may realize perfect penetration.
Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the World Lords.
Praise says: The Great Vaipulya, the Perfectly Round Doctrine; The Lord who accomplishes the Path through time; The four adornments distinctly manifest the locus, Wherein the ten bodies sit.
The multitudes, both similar and different, gather like clouds; Their praises are proclaimed without end.
The inner ocean-like assembly of Samudramati and others together praised the Buddha’s merit;
the six kinds of earth trembled, and auspicious signs filled heaven and earth. Throughout all the oceans of worlds, pervading the entirety of space, the Tathāgata manifested his marks.
Chapter Two: Praise. It says:
The Tathāgata is able to manifest signs; the manifested signs are perfectly uniform and complete. He thought: "The assembly has various questions regarding the Buddha-ground and so forth.

The light from his forty teeth shines brilliantly; like clouds rushing toward their destination, he manifests auspicious omens for those with the karmic affinity to indicate that he will preach the Dharma.
Within the assembly, the leader Samantabhadra suddenly emerges from a lotus flower.
Flowing as the source of all teachings, The power of its praise is boundless; It is inexhaustible throughout the four quarters.
Chapter Three: The Samādhi of Samantabhadra. In praise it is said:
The Samādhi of Samantabhadra is the Tathāgatagarbha, Which all Buddhas of the ten directions sustain with their empowerment.
All lands, as numerous as atoms, enter [the Buddha’s body] and likewise emerge; at this time, the Bodhisattvas bring ten benefits to all.
All subtle movements adorn the realm, and the wondrous voice proclaims the Dharma rain.
The light from the mani-jewel hairs praises both the new and old requests. Those who wish to contemplate the profound principle shall know it through the following chapter.
Chapter Four: The Accomplishment of the World. The Praise says:
The world arises from ten conditions; once established, it relies upon various supports.
Its external forms are each distinct, and its internal substance is likewise manifold. All manner of ornaments are sustained by the power of utterly pure conduct.

Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust manifest various forms; They abide for kalpas or for brief periods. Able to transform and encompass all that moves people's hearts, they fully reveal their knowledge.
The Fifth Chapter: The World of Flower Adornment. The Praise says:
The essence of the Flower Treasury World is the past cause of Vairocana;
The pure practices of the Bodhisattvas are all able to sustain it. Like a wind-circle, it is arranged and established as a land;
Within a single mote of dust, the net of lands is described as having wondrous flower-light, Layered one above another, with all the lands surrounding them.
The ten oceans each circulate to the right, Arranged in a sequence of one hundred and eleven; Their perfect fusion is difficult to describe in full.
Chapter Six: Vairocana Verse of Praise:
Vairocana, the two-fold universal illuminator, In the past spoke of this majestic radiance— The realm of Pure Light and Supreme Sound.

A mountain emerges from the center of the ocean; upon the mountain is a forest in an eastern city. Within the forest is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where he encountered four Buddhas in succession.
The Victorious Clouds (Jayamegha) illuminate the ten directions. After the kings and others had prostrated at his feet, each praised him with verses.
Having seen [the Buddhas], he attained two samādhis and succeeded to the throne as a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
Later, the Great Skillful Means is taught. The seventh chapter is titled "The Names of the Tathāgata Flower-Eye Banner. The hymn of praise says:
His essential virtues constitute his name; In the opening section, the directions are the same as before; The Bodhisattvas reflect upon and inquire about them.
The Buddha replied by manifesting supernatural powers; furthermore, Mañjuśrī spoke: "The fundamental principles of the forty Dharma-gates have long been perfected as the Lords of the Three Times.
Manifesting within the midst of present causes, throughout the ten billion worlds of Sahā, the names of the Buddhas are infinite.
How can there be any distinction between these various forms? It is simply because they have achieved success through past karma."
Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths. Praise says:
The Four Noble Truths of this Sahā world, Possessing immeasurable causes and fruits: Suffering is called oppression;
Origination can destroy goodness; Cessation is termed tranquility; And the Path is the gateway to the One Vehicle.
Each possesses boundless names, Taming all beings according to their minds. In their mystery, they are equal to the various realms;
Their names are established like motes of dust. Perfectly interfused as principal and attendant, Each one fully endowed—hard to describe.
The Ninth Chapter on the Quality of Radiant Enlightenment. The Praise says:
The body illuminates the dharma-realm of phenomena; Wisdom illuminates the source of the two schools.
Beneath the wheel-marks of the World-Honored One’s feet, A hundred billion rays of light are emitted.
These twenty-six sections, Briefly explained in ten layers, With the first layer manifesting the fundamental realm.
Even unto the ultimate heavens, the praises and descriptions transcend both reason and emotion; the profound verses on the causes and effects of bodhi extol the eight marks and so forth,
encompassing the entirety of essential nature, activity, and practice, with majestic power and the nature of phenomena,
wherein the subsequent causes and effects are all-pervasive and perfect.
Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination. The verse of praise says:
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination, there are ten profound points concerning the Dharma. Mañjuśrī poses nine questions, which together correspond to the ten stages of faith.
What is the distinction between the single nature? Phenomena abide within that nature.
How are sentient beings tamed? The Buddha’s transformation descends according to conditions.
Suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, delusion and the causes of karmic retribution—all these phenomena are taught as one Dharma.
Though many gates appear according to faculties, the field of merit is equal and without distinction; it is divided only by the differences in the vessels, yet all are never severed.
Diligence or indolence depends on the person; upholding the Dharma gives rise to various delusions. If one takes medicine and another does not, though both possess wisdom, what use is it?
Like a king’s ministers assisting the wind, the World-Honored One has but a single path;
according to the feelings of sentient beings, they perceive this merit. The Nine-Headed One asked about the realm of the Buddha; the measure of Prajñā is like empty space.
The supernormal powers are all clearly manifested; within the ten directions such as these, in the eleventh chapter, "Pure Conduct," the praise says:
"O Foremost of Pure Conduct, you have asked about the three types of action and more than a hundred [other matters]; you now bring benefit and happiness to the multitudes."
The Praiser is Mañjuśrī; how does one obtain the supreme and wondrous? It is said that through causes and vows there are [these verses], numbering one hundred and forty-one.
Having attained them, movement shall certainly cease. Chapter Twelve:
The Chapter on the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha), titled "Praise. It says:
Mañjuśrī asks about the virtues of faith; Bhadramukha briefly proclaims the teaching. I now speak according to my ability, like a single drop from the ocean:
To resolve the mind and seek perfect enlightenment— The Three Jewels are the primary conditions, The source of the Path, and the Mother of all merit.
From the very beginning, one should be virtuous, Observing the precepts and training in the points of discipline.
Thus one’s merit and wisdom shall be complete; The gateways of samādhi are tenfold.
The great provisions are fully integrated through the exposition of the twenty similes, such as that of the dragon; The myriad practices of the bodhisattva are perfected.
Those who recite and uphold this chapter will possess merit superior to the former; All the ten directions will tremble, And the evil realms will cease without limit.
Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. The Praise:
The Assembly in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The Dharma-Wisdom of the Ten Abodes is vast;
All original abodes appear simultaneously, Yet without leaving anything behind, they ascend. Śakra beholds the Buddha’s arrival; He places him upon the Universal Radiance Seat.

Having requested that those who have entered the wondrous and supreme state cease all sounds of music, one should immediately bring to mind the roots of goodness and praise them throughout the three periods of time.

Once seated within the vast and expansive palace, one should likewise offer verses of praise upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, reaching throughout the ten directions. Chapter Fourteen: Verses of Praise. Thus it was said: [The Buddha] has entered the wondrously supreme [state]; Please cause all sounds of pleasure to cease. One should immediately recollect the roots of goodness; Throughout the three times, they are praised and extolled. Having sat within the broad and expansive hall, They likewise respond throughout the ten directions.
[Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru, Number Fourteen. The praise says:
In the palace of Śakra atop Mount Sumeru, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions have come to this land.
The light from the World-Honored One’s two toes universally illumines all through his spiritual power.
Dharma Wisdom of the eastern quarter extols them collectively; the other nine separately praise the Buddha’s merits.
Expounding the ten stages of practice and their basis, The stage of non-retrogression is perfected;
the practice is infinite. Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes. Praise says:
Wisdom abides in profound stillness; Having attained this stage, there is no retrogression. The Bodhisattva receives the majestic spiritual power.
Entering the Samādhi of Skillful Means, the Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within the lands beyond the realms all bestow instruction through their three karmas.
Upon arising from concentration, one attains supreme power; one’s dwelling place is equal to empty space.

With ten thousand stages of faith and practice fulfilled, one contemplates the Buddha through ten causal principles. With a mind of purifying the ground, compassion, and wisdom, one accumulates right practice without end.
Born into the noble lineage of the Buddha-Dharma, Skilled and proficient in both principle and phenomena, Through right cultivation, how could mindfulness waver?
Non-retrogression is the fusion of śamatha and vipaśyanā; Because one dwells as a child in Bodhi, The Prince shall succeed and flourish;
Consecration is the most supreme, Accomplishing the fullness of the stages; Manifest realization displays auspicious omens.
The Verses on the Profound Meaning of the Chapter on the Holy Life (Brahmacarya), the Sixteenth, state:
"The essence of practice is threefold: Precepts, the Four Immeasurables, and the elucidation of wisdom; Right mindfulness belongs to the Bodhisattvas."
Answering the Ten Sources of Brahma-Conduct: Contemplating that the body and so forth are without marks;
all return to the profound stillness where no dualistic understanding arises. The Dharma of the Buddha swiftly manifests before one.
Chapter Seventeen: The Merit of First Resolving the Mind. Praise:
Regarding the merit of generating the mind of enlightenment: The wisdom of the Buddhas of the three times is opened by it. When the Heavenly King asked about the Dharma, Maitreya answered;
this is exceedingly difficult to encompass. Relying on [the Buddha’s] power, I shall explain it for you. The subsequent parable is superior to what came before:
having already been able to know the limit, It encompasses five perfect supreme virtues, And all six types of earth tremble.
The realization in other realms is likewise so; the verse further clarifies this meaning.
Regarding the eighteenth chapter, "The Most Profound and Luminous Dharma of the Bodhicitta," the praise says:
Dharmamati clearly illuminates that which is illuminated, as well as the means and objects of expression; with diligence and desire, he requests that it be taught.
Having finished the praise and received permission, he asked about the practice and so forth. The answer was that the very substance of practice is entirely the cause of the qualities of practice;
when the cause is perfected, the qualities of the fruit are complete.
Because the meaning of these ten verses was to be further elucidated later, they were proclaimed again. At that time, having spoken this intention, [the assembly] rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. Praise says:
In the assembly within the palace of Yāma, the forest of virtues of the ten practices is elucidated. Without departing from the Bodhi tree, they ascend together to that heaven.
Having seen the Buddha, the Heavenly King’s throne and palace are each fully adorned.
Their essence is fully endowed with the fourfold equality, And their meritorious qualities are boundless. Having finished their request, the Tathāgatas accepted it;
Recalling past causes and conditions, they spoke verses in praise of the ten Buddhas.
In all realms they proclaimed this together, entered the hall, and sat cross-legged; Then, in an instant, there was vast and sudden spaciousness.
Chapter Twenty: Verses of Praise in the Palace of Yāma Heaven.
The praise says: Dust-mote worlds gather at this assembly; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions come like ten forests.
From their feet and ankles, hundreds of billions of rays of light are emitted; All of them likewise extol [the Buddha] in this manner.
Chapter Twenty-One: The Ten Practices. The Praise says:
In accordance with principle, he undertakes practice; Through samādhi, he enters contemplation. Outside of worlds as numerous as motes of dust, All Buddhas bestow their empowerment.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Forest of Merit, He preaches the Dharma beyond conception.
The ten [stages] beginning with Joy are enumerated; their realization is identical in terminology. The verses in repetition convey the same meaning as before.
Regarding the Ten Stages, they are somewhat like a ladder.
The Twenty-second Chapter, the Storehouse of the Ten Inexhaustibles, is praised as follows:
The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries, as taught by the Buddhas of the three times, are identical: The enumeration of their names and their total number;
the benefit to oneself and others; The mind’s purity is termed faith; based on the fusion of the perfected, dependent, and imagined natures;
The accomplishment of the prohibitions and precepts; the inexhaustibility of benefiting others; And shame, which is able to honor and revere what is wholesome.
Far removed from the assault of the three poisons, Lightly rejecting violence, evil, and shamelessness;
Coming amidst the five desires, hearing the vast and extensive teachings, Clearly understanding that which is designated as empty;
Ceasing [self-interest] to bestow gifts upon others, distinguishing the internal divisions, Discerning the wisdom of all phenomena, Knowing form as it truly is.
Causing the mind to be clear through mindfulness, the Bodhisattva abandons delusion; Without forgetting the words or their meaning, they maintain what has been recorded;
Skillfully proclaiming and knowing the true nature of reality, they do not contradict the scriptures of the Buddhas.
To those who thus praise their supreme capabilities, I pray that they may turn toward the ultimate goal.
Chapter Twenty-Three: Ascending the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. The Verse of Praise says:
The Lord of Transformation, responding to the faculties and aspirations [of beings], ascends to the Tuṣita Heaven.
He appears simultaneously beneath every tree, yet remains inseparable from his former state. His palace and throne are formed of wondrous jewels, and various offerings arise therein.
Contemplating the Buddha’s sublime virtues, explained through the two meanings of the beginning and the end: having accepted the invitation, he dwells in the palace;
the King attains benefit, goodness, and perfection; songs and music are all flourishing and magnificent.
Having taken his seat by the power of the Tathāgata of Boundless Praise, all others do likewise.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace. The praise says:
Assemblies from as many worlds as there are atoms in the Tuṣita realm have gathered, coming from all directions to the land of wondrous jewels.
From the knees of the Buddhas, light is emitted that shines everywhere; first among them is Vajradhvaja, who utters verses of praise.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Ten Dedications. The verse of praise says:
Dedicating toward the three spheres, Entering and arising from meditative concentration are the same;
All Buddhas grant their empowerment, Fully expounding the ten types of principles, To rescue and protect sentient beings and others, In accordance with the detachment from signs and perfect fusion.
With unshakable faith in the Three Jewels, employing the ten objects infinitely;
equal to all Buddhas, knowing phenomena as being like space; reaching everywhere, this is called the Great Vow;
a treasury of merit whose roots of goodness pervade all places and are inexhaustible in time; by relying on that which is inexhaustible, one follows the steadfast.
All rely upon the mental dharmas, Equally conforming to all sentient beings.
Accumulating roots of goodness, they should be called "well-united" according to their characteristics; They remain far removed from all delusions.
Knowing the sixty-first gate of liberation through non-attachment and non-binding, Equal to the infinite Dharma-realm, The Teacher’s station gives rise to great compassion.
The earth shook and faith was born; the devas throughout the world, And the assemblies of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, bearing the same name, gathered before the assembly.
With verses they exhorted the practice of cultivation; The one named Samantabhadra, dwelling in goodness, measured these merits.
Their limit cannot be fathomed, for they are boundless; All living beings together could not know their number.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter: The Bodhisattva’s Practice Difficult to Proclaim; The Ten Stages. The Praise says:
Because the ordinary and the holy are separated, he dwells transcendentally in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; the introduction clearly sets forth four excellences.
Entering the dhyāna of wisdom, as if rising from a state of meditative concentration already maintained, he universally proclaims the three meanings that elucidate the ten stages;
having completed the designation of their names, Vajragarbha remains silent. The three families extend five requests for the profound and mysterious Dharma-gate;
through joy, they attain the nature of the noble ones, capable of fully benefiting the two types of emptiness.
Free from defilement, all are fully pure; Laziness and shame are the root source. Emitting light, they accomplish meditative concentration and the boundless dhāraṇī-dharmas;
With flaming wisdom, they abide in the most supreme. Having perfected the factors of enlightenment, they attain the invincible union;
Their modes of activity cause mutual opposition, While the wisdom of dependent origination manifests before them.
Difficult to perceive, it maintains equanimity; having traveled far, it reaches the signless. The supramundane path is compassion, immovable and non-conceptual;
its profound practice is difficult to know. With excellent wisdom and unimpeded analytical knowledge, it extensively explains meanings that are inconceivable.
This "Cloud of Dharma" is called great gnosis; it contains all obscurations, just as space does.
The reflections collectively clarify the metaphors: As the four rivers enter the sea and fill it, Their positions are counted among the Buddhas;
their benefits pervade the ten directions. There is no goodness that cannot be attained. This verse concludes the layered repetitions.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Ten Samādhis. Praise says:
Reassembling in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the nature of the objective realm is established as meditative concentration.
In the kingdom of Magadha, the Perfect Enlightenment was first attained. The Universal Eye rose from his seat, joined his palms before the Buddha, and requested to inquire about four meanings.
In response, the Buddha commanded Samantabhadra to expound the ten great samādhis.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Extolling the Ten Supernatural Powers of the Boundless Dharma Realm. The Verse of Praise says:
Samantabhadra addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, fully explaining the ten supernatural powers, such as the knowledge of others' minds.
Abiding thus in the inconceivable, one’s unimpeded wisdom regarding the three periods of time is identical [to that of the Buddhas].
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Ten Kinds of Patience. The Praise says:
Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "By means of these ten kinds of patience, one attains non-obstruction."

The Three Honored Ones of the Past, Present, and Future have already been explained; now I shall speak of the summarized meaning of the verses within the preceding "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (Asaṃkhyeya-varga), the thirtieth. It is praised as follows:
Regarding the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers," the ten great numbers are established to indicate their universal application. Thus, the Sovereign of Mind addressed the Buddha and asked:
Praising and approving the profound teachings of the Sage, they reverently received his command.

Clearly manifesting the manifold, layered virtues whose excellence is utterly inexhaustible, Samantabhadra, in his depth and breadth, extols the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," the thirty-first. Thus he praises:
The lifespan of the Tathāgata is seen differently by sentient beings; The Mind-King addresses the assembly, separately enumerating ten layers of lands.
First, he speaks of the Sahā world and others, Whose worlds cannot exhaustively reach the ultimate mystery.
At the final limit, Samantabhadra fills them all.
Chapter Thirty-two: The Abodes of the Bodhisattvas. The verse of praise says:
The Bodhisattvas, according to their faculties, possess both compassion and wisdom; They dwell in many places, each with a different name.
In the mountains and seas of the eight directions, among sages and others, And in cities and towns, they dwell together in twelve ways.
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Inconceivable Dharma. The Praise says:
The fruit-dharmas of the Tathāgata transcend words and thought; The assembly of bodhisattvas brings this to mind.
The Buddha-lands and other such things are inconceivable; The World-Honored One’s empowerment is complete throughout the three karmas.
The Blue Lotus Treasury, Virtuous and Fearless, Is able to penetrate the Dharma-realm and universally receive its power;
He addresses all and proclaims it forth, Correctly revealing the complete sequence of the ten gates.
From the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks and Phases of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," Chapter Thirty-Four, the Praise says:
The Tathāgata’s ten bodies manifest his sublime virtues; Samantabhadra exhorts all to listen as he proclaims them in full.
Each is inconceivable and mutually interfused, Like the lotus-receptacle and its subtle atomic marks.
Chapter Thirty-Five: The Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance. The Praise says:
The Buddha told Baoshou Xuan: "My voice, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, emits light from Tuṣita Heaven;
it constantly possesses forty qualities. Within it, purity is proclaimed, and how could it fail to illuminate even a world-system as small as a mote of dust?
To hear its benefit is to find its meaning difficult to fully explain."
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct. The praise says:
Within the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct, the causes of equality are explained.
Furthermore, it is told to all bodhisattvas that one should simply follow the faculties of sentient beings; thus the realm of the Tathāgata is briefly expounded for the sake of those who lack wisdom.
If one gives rise to a mind of anger, One will encounter a million obstacles;
But by diligently practicing the sixty dhāraṇīs, One’s efforts will be diminished and signs of realization will clearly manifest.
All Buddhas join with the assembly of Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions; In all worlds, They proclaim verses to admonish and grant permission to listen.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgata, in which Compassion and Wisdom are Mutually Integrated. The Praise says:
There is the Dharma-body, the three bodies, and the ten bodies; These are collectively termed the "fruition-function" and the "transformation-function."
The Great Radiance was emitted to empower the two Lords;
Xingqi Miaode questioned Puxian through prose and verse, making all these requests.
The Tathāgata inconceivably manifested the boundless ten gates, answering them all as the fruit of equality; Within, there are further many aspects that are difficult to proclaim.
Various metaphors are taught, yet there is nothing to which they can be compared;

The secret, perfect stage is revealed, upheld through names, Causing the sixfold earth to quake and receiving the offerings of all assemblies. The realization in the ten directions is likewise for the Bhikṣus, And so it is throughout all worlds;
The layered verses of this gāthā have their meaning directed toward what precedes.
Chapter Thirty-Eight: On Transcending the World. The Praise says:
Within the Hall of Dharma during the eighth assembly, He preached the transcendence of the world and the severance of worldly ties.

The stages of practice manifest unimpeded, With the preceding and succeeding aspects perfectly interfused. The Buddha was present in Magadha and other realms, Amidst the majestic adornments of the human realm.
All stirred and listened to the sound; the arising from samādhi was likewise. The Bodhisattva, knowing the assembly had gathered, posed questions on the six stages of the fundamental principle.
Samantabhadra answered from the perspective of faith; the two hundred gates were fully exhausted.
He concluded by exhorting them to proclaim [the teaching] together. Auspicious signs appeared, filling all things; both persons and dharmas were realized and perfected.
In the verse, the meaning is also that of re-entering the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm," the thirty-ninth. The praise says:
The discourse on entering the Dharma Realm, Realizing the mutual penetration of subject and object, Was delivered within the Jeta Grove.
Mindful of the assembly’s shared intent, the Buddha entered the *bimbara* concentration.
Having gathered them, he extensively praised their merits, highlighted their failings, and manifested his own virtues; this indicates it is the system of the Hīnayāna.

Then, through the Bodhisattva’s reception of the Buddha’s spiritual power, within the chanting of verses, Samantabhadra universally brought forth the ten kinds of Dharma-phrases to their ultimate conclusion.
The light from the white tuft of hair illuminates and benefits all throughout the entirety of space;
Mañjuśrī describes these divine transformations, which completely fill the ten directions. This boundless light is a great function that benefits all beings, who receive its grace.
The preceding and following sections distinguish the beginning and the end; this assembly marks the conclusion, wherein the gradual and the sudden teachings mutually reflect one another.
The person and the Dharma are each mutually integrated; Mañjuśrī represents the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Sudhana accumulates and perfects [the virtues];
Meghaśrī and others represent the dwelling [in the stage of understanding]. The ocean of wisdom within the Buddha-realm—Sudarśana and others represent the practice of conforming to liberation.
The incense-seller and others represent the direction; the methods for compounding incense are fully proclaimed.
Vasundharā and the others take refuge here; All delusive latent tendencies are utterly destroyed.
Māyā reaches the assembly of Maitreya through the gathering of diverse conditions; Samantabhadra and Samantagambhīra— For those who see this sūtra, cause and effect are both fully perfected.
The merit obtained is most profound and mysterious, Like perfuming the seed of the vajra.
The indestructible power is ever more firm; I praise the merits of his deeds. Dedicated toward the infinite and boundless.
*The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, Praise by Chao Sanlang, Shangshu Zhukewai Lang, Qingche.*
Composed by Yang Jie, Duwei, Recipient of the Purple-Golden Fish Sash.
In praise of Vairocana Tathāgata:
Adorning the Pavilion with Raised Banners and Pennants, The Lion-Stretching One sits upon the site of enlightenment.
The great śrāvakas have not yet awakened; From between his brows, he emits white light from the ūrṇā-kośa.
Mañjuśrī praises the elephant king turning within the śāla grove; The stūpas and temples of the Tathāgatas of antiquity are now opened.
Having already traveled throughout one hundred and ten cities, why do you go again into the dust?
Bhikṣu Meghadeva praised the four quarters and sought everywhere above and below: "In which superior land is there a great bhikṣu?"
For seven days on Mount Sumeru, I saw nothing at all; my walking meditation was entirely upon the peaks of other mountains.
Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha praises the great ocean as vast and boundless; the ocean of the Buddha’s merit is profoundly deep.
For twelve years he contemplated the realm; A precious lotus throne emerged from the waves.
The Bhikṣu Shan-zhu praised the hidden and the manifest;
As he walked to and fro without lingering, What more could one seek in the tracks of birds in the sky?
The Buddha-realm of sentient beings has always been thus; how could it be otherwise?

Not only did the bhikṣu of Laṅkā and the Mahāsattva Maitreya praise the Great Lion Throne and manifest its majestic power, but [the Tathāgata] also ascended and descended amidst the adornments of the marketplace.
Who can discern the Dharma-gate of the letter *Cakra*? Its vocal sounds are identical throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The Elder Vimukta praised the lands as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions, wherein each Tathāgata sits at the site of enlightenment.
That Buddha does not come and I do not go; Clearly manifest is the reflection in the center of the water.
The Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja praises the gate of giving through renunciation, As Universal Eye Radiance reveals it to Sudhana.
The various transformations within every land and every atom do not come from outside a single dharma;
the laywoman Huisho praises the mind as being like the great ocean, which receives all things completely, and like Mount Sumeru, which remains unshakable.
Seated upon a universally adorned throne of gold and jewels, you can dissolve the sickness and afflictions of all sentient beings when seen.
The seer Vimukta praises the Buddhas of the ten directions,
as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields, and their adornments of various lands.
When grasping hands and dividing forms to go everywhere, the youth never once leaves his original place;

the Brahmin Śūramgama praises the origins of the "contrary" and "conformable," for these are merely strong designations— let the mountain of blades and the mass of fire remain as towering as they are.
Good Wealth’s heart gave rise to doubt and regret; Fortunately, the various devas served as witnesses.
The Compassionate Conduct Maiden praised the golden bells and precious mirrors on the pillars and walls, Wherein the mani necklaces were mutually interwoven and fused.
"You should observe my various palaces; throughout the dharmadhātu, each and every one is identical to Sudarśana.
The bhikṣu praised the bhikṣu Sudarśana, who dwells in the Three Eyes, saying: "It is only now in this life that I have gone forth."
In a single thought-moment, I have offered worship; The Lord of Beings, as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers, praised me in the past:
"Having seen the Teacher, you have realized and entered into the wisdom of skillful supernatural powers."
When ten thousand youths surrounded me, playing at gathering sand on the riverbank, the laywoman Pūrṇaśrī praised me:
"Your garments are white and your hair hangs down; you wear no necklaces. All the possessions in my house are empty."
A single vessel placed before one—who would call it small? It can satisfy all the desires of the great trichiliocosm.
The wise and enlightened householder praises the infinite lands and their sentient beings, for the various necessities and diverse desires of each differ.
Since the One of Clear Wisdom beheld the void, all those with requests have had their needs fulfilled.
The Elder Dharmakaraṇḍa praised the food, robes, jewels, and maidens;
the Bodhisattvas appeared within the highest tier, where the World-Honored One resides.
When the elder Sudhana first grasped his hand, The gates of the eight directions were all opened wide.
The Elder Universal Eye praised the healing of sentient beings throughout the ten directions; In the land of Vīraṇamūla, he was a great king of physicians.
Expertly knowing the methods for blending all fragrances, within each single fragrance there are immeasurable scents;
King Insatiable praises King Insatiable’s great skillful means, which can cause sentient beings to sever their false views.
Sliced by knives, boiled in cauldrons, and scorched by fierce fires— one should know that all phenomena are like illusions.
The Great Radiance King praises the Dharma of the Samādhi of Accordance with the World; the banner of compassion is erected high, emitting brilliant light.
The beings of the human and celestial realms throughout the trichiliocosm, with their palaces, clouds, and thunder, all turn toward the Queen;
the Upāsikā Acalā praises the golden light that dwells peacefully in the royal capital, and upon encountering this light, body and mind become naturally cool and serene.
I seek this Dharma without weariness; the Tathāgatas of the past produced sublime fragrances,
and when the wandering ascetic Vyāsa praised the ninety-six different heterodox views, I subdued them all through skillful means.
May all universally abandon the mind of attachment; Like the sunlight upon a mountain peak at midnight,
may the Elder Gandhārī, who sells incense everywhere, praise the blue lotus (*utpala*),
harmonizing and discerning all fragrances, thereby accomplishing pure, peaceful, and blissful happiness.
The fragrance of heaven and the human world is not the same; who can be equanimous and free from all attachments?
The boatman Vasistha praises the Great Being, who is able to traverse the ocean of birth and death, bestowing the treasures of the jewel-island upon all living beings.
He clearly understands all that accords with safety and peril; he does not linger where he rests, but moves forward.
This supreme and most excellent Elder is praised, surrounded by hundreds of thousands, as the Ornamented Banner in the Forest of No-Sorrow, supreme and most excellent.
Possessing great supernormal powers that are without dependence or effort, she has accomplished all the practices of a bodhisattva.
At the time when the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā was seated upon a precious throne throughout the forest, she praised the bhikṣuṇīs of the country of Sūna.
For what reason does Sudhana’s mind circumambulate you to the right, following you for hundreds of thousands of circuits?
O Vasumitrā, you who are praised with frequent stretching and winking,
and whose wondrous voice can eliminate the mind of lust wherever it touches.
In this perilous land, the people do not recognize it; The adorned jeweled ground is spread with gold.
The householder Vṛṣṭihanta praises the Tathāgatas of the three ages as never entering nirvāṇa; Upon the sandalwood throne, at the tip of the white tuft of hair.
Sentient beings and the self are fundamentally non-dual; One should contemplate the opening of the stupa in successive stages.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara praises Guanyin, who ever dwells in the presence of the Tathāgata, Universally manifesting before all sentient beings.
Mount Potalaka is steep and precipitous, with jewel groves and fragrant herbs interspersed by flowing springs.
The Samantagāmin praises the Samantagāmin who comes from the wondrous treasury of the East; Swiftly he proceeds toward liberation, opening the universal gate.
Pervading all four intermediate directions, above, and below, At every step, his radiance reveals itself to Sudhana.
The Great Deity praises him as he extends his four hands to draw up the ocean, Washing his face while manifesting a majestic and awe-inspiring demeanor.
Whoever encounters the *Khadiraka* tree, scattering many branches of golden flowers,
The earth-dwelling goddesses praise its light as it simultaneously causes the earth to tremble; The adornments of the jewel-treasury follow everywhere.
Having constantly enjoyed [this] since ancient times, how is it that one comes to know the directions through spiritual power?
When the sun has set, the Night-Goddess Pāṇḍavāvatī praises the city;
as she enters the eastern gate, her body appears in the sky with the color of pure gold.
The light can shatter all the darkness of delusion, causing each being to give rise to a mind of liberation.
The Night-Spirit Sovereign of Universal Virtue and Pure Light praises the seclusion that stills evil sounds, manifesting through the transformations of playful supernatural powers.
She reveals the correct path to the gate of renunciation, Delighting in delivering sentient beings through the long night of birth and death;
The Night-Spirit Joyful Observation sits upon a precious lotus flower attending the World-Honored One, With clouds of manifested bodies from hundreds of thousands of pores.
With wondrous voice, she clearly explains according to what is appropriate; The Universal Joy Banner marks the gate of liberation.
The Night Goddess Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Beings praises the goddess Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Beings; Great light extends forth from between her two arms.
When Sudhana entered her crown, his body was filled;
the Night Goddess Sovereign of the Ocean of Silent Sounds praised him with the verse:
"The wheel of the pure lamp of samādhi-wisdom, The ocean of light of liberation adorned by the vast, great joy born in every thought."
The Gate of the Universal and Boundless Dharma Realm, Within a Lotus upon a Maṇi Banner Throne,
The Night Goddess Who Protects All Cities and Increases Power Praises those who awaken beings from the slumber of ignorance, And protects all the cities of the Tathāgata.
As a great Dharma Master free from obstruction, you have spontaneously perfected the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
The Night Goddess who dwells by the blossoming tree praises the Sahā world as the sun sets, And the lotuses in the pure ponds close their petals.
Whether by water, mountain, city, or wilderness, having finished sightseeing, they are able to return home.
By the power of their great vows and diligent perseverance,
the Night Goddess who Protects Sentient Beings praises the mani-jewel net that covers the void, wherein the reflections of the sun, moon, and stars appear.
Equally entering all dharma-gates, The atom-sized buddha-fields are fundamentally the same.
The Night-Spirit Wondrous Virtue Complete praises the Adorned Pavilion,
Receiving Sudhana as the celestial beings surround her and the gates of transformation open.
I have personally entered the ocean-treasury of Vairocana; I once saw the World-Honored One come from Tuṣita.
The Śākya maiden Gopā praised his wisdom-light, Perfectly illuminating Indra; Through boundless oceans of kalpas, it has unfolded and multiplied.
Birth and death are fundamentally free from faults; who could go again to question her?
To the Buddha-mother Māyā, I offer praise:
she dwells throughout all worlds yet abides nowhere; my own body is neither one nor many places.
The jeweled pavilion and lotus receive the ten directions; The Mother of Bodhisattvas of the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds,
the Daughter of the Lord of Heaven,
praises the Buddha as he emerges from the womb with a lion’s roar, Until he attains perfect enlightenment and subdues the armies of Māra.
