I clearly recall all that was previously forgotten: the pure and majestic gateways of liberation.
Having universally consulted with teachers and youths throughout the human and celestial realms, how should one cultivate and train as a Bodhisattva?
The true kalyāṇamitra within the city of Vīra, who does not fail to open the gate of liberation;
the youth Kālāmasuta, praised as one skilled in all arts,
who is well-versed in the knowledge of characters for the training of bodhisattvas.
When Chang held these syllables, the Bhadrāvarī upāsikā praised the inconceivable Prajñāpāramitā as the liberation of the refuge-less site of enlightenment,
proclaiming it to benefit people and engage with all beings.
The samādhi of the six sense faculties is inexhaustible; the waves of merit and the light of wisdom are firm.
This elder praises liberation and seeks the true Dharma with tireless diligence, serving all Tathāgatas with complete faith and sincerity.
The power of pure, adorned, and firm resolve arises entirely from thoughts free of attachment.
As the Elder Candracchattra praised Sudhana before he had yet left the city of Utpalavatī, Candracchattra joyfully heard the name of the elder.
The light of liberating wisdom can clearly be seen; within the house there is only great radiance.
The Elder Anabhibhū praises the emergence from the city; liberation fully understands the inexhaustible mark.
Just as all Bodhisattvas possess great eloquence, so too has the World-Honored One, the inexhaustible treasury,
been praised by the most tranquil Brahmin with words of sincere aspiration; he has never spoken falsely, but has shown the way to sentient beings.
With boundless and immeasurable virtues, whatever they perform according to their will is never without merit;
the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavati praise the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī, having realized that the world abides entirely as an illusion.
The Bodhisattva’s practice of giving is likewise fundamental; who could endure the sorrow, grief, and suffering of birth and death?
When Maitreya Bodhisattva praised him before the hall and snapped his fingers, the multitude of gates opened, and within each gate stood a Sudhana.
Having now returned from whence he came, he departs to nowhere, for originally there was no coming.
Once again he beheld Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and praised him;
at that time, the hand that touched his head extended far, spanning one hundred and ten yojanas, its fingers reaching out to touch the earth.
Once Sudhana has been established as he dwells, where can one see Mañjuśrī at the Universal Gate?
The Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and others praise the ocean-treasury of Vairocana; when even a speck of dust is extinguished, the fragrant elephant leaves no trace—who can approach him?
Failing to give rise to the Great Mind and open the Universal Eye, how could one know that the body dwells within the body of Samantabhadra?
In the *Huayan Chahai Bianxiang Zan* (Praise of the Manifested Forms of the Flower Garland Ocean of Realms),
Qingliang (Chengguan) describes those who cling to the image or lose the image, or who grasp at emptiness and seek it outside of emptiness— such people merely stir the waves of consciousness.
Through vast kalpas one searches in the darkness; Within form, one perceives the formless. The myriad phenomena return to the tip of a hair;
Beholding a single leaf, the universal pivot is seen. In the Dharma-realm, one knows spring and autumn.
*Praise for the Diagram of the Flower Treasury World of Vairocana Buddha*

Liu Yuxi: Regarding the Buddha’s teaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the true person of wondrous enlightenment does not proceed by means of the various vehicles; none but one possessing great perfect wisdom can believe and understand it.
During the reign of Emperor Dezong, there was the "Dragon and Elephant" Master Guan, who was able to realize the primary truth within this sūtra and dwelt at its summit.
The name of Doyun Flower Temple is renowned throughout the ten directions; Master Miaomen succeeded to Zhaoming as its superior.

He compiled the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from its nine assemblies to form the *Flower Treasury*, so that people might gaze upon it with reverence and generate respect for its manifested forms. Consequently, he requested me to compose a hymn of praise, which I now speak:
[Insert Hymn of Praise]
A lotus flower, pure and unstained, Bears a world-system of ten billion, leaping forth from a vast, boundless sea of fragrance.
The wind-wheel supports it, revolving through the night;
At the nine assemblies, the Great Hero transforms the devas; Śakra, Brahmā, and the eight classes of beings arrive in dense array.
From darkness to awakening, not relying on conditions; The primordial and ultimate nature is spontaneously perfect.
Written upon silk, the colors and forms are complete; This is neither form nor non-form, beyond speech and silence.
True eulogy for the Patriarch Xianshou, the Master of the Avataṃsaka.
Composed by the Emperor Zhongzong of the Great Tang:

Having cultivated bright causes in former lives, he sought exclusively the True and Right. At the Garden of the Hermitage, he repented his past traces; throughout the Lotus Realm, he manifested emanations to propagate the Śākya teachings.
He rescued those lost at the ford of delusion, causing the single rain to flow eternally and purifying the six sense-dusts forever.
Second:
As the garden of his eloquence has opened and the spring of his speech flows deep and vast, he upholds patience and diligently cultivates vigor.
He gathers celestial blossoms through exposition and assembly; as a sign of this, the earth quaked. By mobilizing this power of the Dharma, he utterly destroyed the array of Māras.
Third, herein are set forth the ten contemplations, employed to accord with the four dhyānas. They universally sever the afflictions and distance one from the entanglements of the mind.
The source of the mind is reflected with clarity; the mirror of Dharma hangs suspended and pure. The raft of wisdom moves everywhere, and the lamp of compassion is transmitted forever.
His fourth name is Jian Zichen; his voice flows through the Azure City. He is the guiding principle for the assembly of Brahmā and the standard for the ranks of monks.

He brings peace and harmony to the four classes of beings without ever ceasing, spreading his excellence throughout the three thousandfold world and transmitting his fragrance across ten billion lands.

Imperial Portrait Eulogy for the Great Monk, National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan, the Chief Seat who Discussed the Three Teachings in the Inner Palace and served as Professor for the Translation of the Sutras,
in Commemoration of the New and Old Editions of the Avatamsaka Sutra and their Commentaries Copied at the Great Xingtang Monastery in the Capital.
An Imperial Composition by Emperor Wenzong of the Great Tang:
I observe that the Dharma-realm is vast and silent, without limit; Events arise in accordance with conditions, truly relying upon the empty faculties.
National Teacher Qingliang embodies the mysteries of the Gate of Profundity; Having fully possessed the vessel of the Dharma, my ancestors revered him as supreme.
His teachings harmonize the seas and mountains; his grace expands across heaven and earth. Surpassing the two Shus of old, he elevates those who were obscure and ignorant.
This rare and vital spirit has now arrived to reverently receive the Buddha-sun; its light coalesces throughout the four seas, and its blessings overflow the nine provinces.
Having entered the gate of the Golden Immortal, he has usurped the seat of the ancient sages; as a great hand and renowned official, he spreads the sutras and seeks further instruction.
Still following the master Juxiu, he preserved his remaining years through distant travels. Thus, he exerted his solitary brush to extol these flourishing achievements.

The True Void is inexhaustible; when the occasion arises, he mounts his carriage. Like the white moon in the empty autumn, like the clear breeze suited for summer, the wondrous non-being does not shift, and as conditions cease, it is said to transform.
Lofty indeed is the legacy of Yu, and resplendent is the vihāra.
True Eulogy for Venerable Zhinan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan,
composed by Cui Zhiyuan, Attendant-Reader and Hanlin Academician, Acting Vice Minister of the Ministry of War,
concurrently Supervising Official of the Bureau of Imperial Writings, Purple-Ennobled and Gold Fish-Bag Recipient.
The qilin among those who run, the phoenix among those who fly—such is this human hero. He is the ridgepole and beam of the Dharma gate;
his single voice roars like thunder, arraying the fourfold assembly like rows of stones. He can expound the six characteristics and master the ten mysteries.
Later he sketches the true form, and his radiance manifests transformation bodies. The patterns of leaves shine upon his palms, and his spirit dwells within the lotus realm.
The mirror hangs beyond the dust of the world; the lamp is transmitted to the shores of the sea. At Donglin, the shadow of the Buddha forever accords with this auspicious affinity.
In praise of Venerable Busik, the Patriarch of the Hwaom School in the Land of the Rising Sun (with preface).
By the Acting Director of the Bureau of the Central Secretariat, the Court Counselor of State, Examiner of the Grand Minister of Works, and Acting Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Written by Park Yim-ryang, Imperial Secretary, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Acting Director of the Chizhao Office, and Compiler for the Historiography Bureau.
The public name of this gentleman was Uisang;
he was a native of Silla. His enduring fragrance and remaining beauty fill the annals and biographies of the Great Song Dynasty in their entirety.
In my spare time from public duties, I have leisurely perused various records and collections;

while there are eulogies for eminent monks of successive dynasties, it is a pity that no one has yet composed a praise for the holy man Bu-sok. Only the Sixteen-Verse "Eulogy on the Portrait of the Spirit-Wandering [Master]" by Mr.
Choe Chi-won, the Hanlin Academician of Silla, exists. However, this was written concerning the Buddha Mountain (Bulsan) at Seoktise Temple.
The monk was able to recount the events of his dream, yet he did not fully capture the remaining splendors of Fusō (Floating Stone).
Taking up my brush to compose this text, I immediately extolled his virtue, saying:
Seal of the Ocean Samādhi, Śākyamuni, the Sole Honored One, Proclaiming the nature of the Dharma-realm, Opening the gate of the One Vehicle.
A great cloud covers the world; ambrosia washes away affliction. Entrusted from patriarch to patriarch, every word is proclaimed.
Ji Gui upholds the Dharma with righteousness; his vast talent stands out preeminent. Possessing many abilities beyond the common, he was one of the nine sages.
Seeking the Unsurpassed Teacher, he entered the chamber of Zhongnan. Having mastered the teachings, his teacher passed away; he departed from the void to return to the reality.
The virtuous and wondrous being possessed of form, seeking joy with longing attachment, beheld that the mind was not like stone.

He reversed his vow to practice the giving of gold-scaled [beings], who carried ships upon their backs to cross the waves of the sea with ease. A massive rock floated through the air, providing shelter for the mountain temple.
Wandering and lecturing among the ten mountains, monks gathered shoulder-to-shoulder in competition; the multitude of rocks listened intently, nodding their heads as if in response.
Westward mustard seeds, eastward needles; the six heretical teachers share one leaf. The lamp before, the lamp behind;
the ten sages transmit the Dharma. Hand-copied texts and meanings; incantations cast into the fire’s smoke—over two hundred characters.
Among the remaining ashes, whole characters remain; characters cast into the water. Line after line, like strung shells; over thirty phrases, curved and winding, forming verses.
A General Exposition of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Formed as a Diagram of the Dharma-realm: Vividly marked as its target, it is as brilliant as pearls;
From a single inch of pattern one knows the brocade, From a single hair one knows the phoenix. Briefly gathering its pure fragrance, I have hastily composed this hymn of praise.
[This was written] during the Tianhou era, at the request of Master Fuli, who questioned the scholars of the realm with verses on the True and the False.
The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally pure; from what cause could deluded thoughts arise?
If you allow that delusion arises from the true, how can this delusion ever be ceased? Without a beginning, there is no end; if there were an end, there should be a beginning.
To have an end without a beginning—how long have I harbored ignorance regarding this principle! I pray that you will reveal its secret mystery.
Answer of Dharma Master Lishè of Anguo Monastery on the Prayer for Deliverance from Birth and Death (by a person of the Kaiyuan era during the reign of Empress Wu).
The True Dharma is fundamentally not true; How could delusion ever have arisen? Delusion does not arise from the True.
In non-delusion, where could one dwell? Since it is granted that there is neither beginning nor end, how can one permit the questioning of a finality or an origin?
There is no beginning and likewise no end; who would be so ignorant as to fail to grasp this principle?
Why not hasten toward the unborn, rather than praying for birth and death?
Dengguan (fl. Yuanhe era), Commentator on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of Xingtang Temple, replies:
Delusion arises from deluded thoughts; when one awakens to the truth, delusion ceases. That which is capable of deluding is not itself what is deluded.
If one attains complete conformity [with this], one will realize that one has never been awakened before; therefore, it is said that delusion is beginningless.
To know that delusion is fundamentally true is precisely the eternal principle; If the discriminating mind has not yet perished, by what means can one transcend birth and death?
Answered by the Venerable Huahui of Zhangjing Monastery (a person of the Yuanhe era).
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither defiled nor pure; Truth and falsehood are not as they appear.
If one discards falsehood to preserve truth, where then would that falsehood abide? Since all things are fundamentally non-existent, One forcibly asserts non-existence, yet even this does not exist.
Existence begins with a starting point; To see a beginning is not to see the beginningless. All phenomena are by nature devoid of self-nature.
Chan Master Hongtao of Anguo Temple answers (his fellow student at Zhangjing Monastery): Without nature, there is no birth-and-death;
The true and the false are fundamentally provisional names. Awakening to the false, the false does not arise; The source of the mind-nature is eternally constant.
The constant nature has neither beginning nor end; The intent of the sages and the common folk is inherently profound. This profound nature is profoundly inexhaustible;

it is the Dharmadhātu, the perfectly pure body. From the very beginning, there is no fixed intent; In the Buddha-land there is not a single thing— who would be deluded regarding the principle of birth and death?
Dharma Master Hai of Yunhua Temple answers:
The essence of truth and falsehood is eternally as it is; There is neither cessation nor arising. Upon contact with the eyes, all natures are empty;
Ultimately, there is nothing that can be stilled. Suchness is fundamentally non-returning; How could one speak further of beginning or end?

If one maintains a view of beginning and end, one will always be muddled regarding the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Since birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, what need is there to pray for transcendence from birth-and-death?
—Written by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngnán Shàotáng Sī, clarifying the intent of Dharma Master Lǐ.

Now, one who wishes to answer the questions of others must be well-versed in the tenets of both their own and other schools; this has been the established rule for the masters of debate in the Western Regions.
Master Fali was a preeminent master of the sūtras and śāstras, serving as the chief among those in the translation hall during the reign of Empress Wu.
Since he posed these questions, they have circulated throughout the world. Does the purport of his inquiry not, by its very nature, fail to investigate the various schools thoroughly?

How much more so when speaking of those among the scholars of the world who, having already established themselves as pillars, yet have not studied under a master and are unacquainted with the principles of the teachings?

Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtra teachings, they are generally comprised of only three schools: first, the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school; second, the Refutation-of-Characteristics (Poxiang) school; and third, the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school.
Even those who have received the refined transmission of the Chan gate do not exceed these three categories, as has been fully elucidated in the General Preface by Guifeng.

The *Lanruo Chanzang* (Aranya Chan Treasury) consists of one hundred fascicles, including two fascicles of a general preface. Now, I ask: does this pertain to the "biting the bullet" (*niècù*) juncture of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) school?
It does not concern the two schools; what is taught by those two schools involves no such contradiction or obstruction. Regarding the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school:
according to what is taught by that school, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) delusive dharmas and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) pure dharmas have existed from time immemorial.
Each [delusion] has its own seed within the *ālaya-vijñāna*; when it encounters conditions and is perfumed, it arises from its respective seed.
This has nothing to do with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Who says that delusions arise from True Suchness?

That teaching holds that True Suchness is exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), quiescent, without arising and without ceasing; thus, one cannot challenge it by saying that delusions arise from the Real.

Question: As for the School of the Destruction of Characteristics (Poxiangzong), they maintain that all things—ordinary beings and sages, defilement and purity—are exclusively empty and fundamentally non-existent.

Even if one were to perceive a single dharma superior to nirvana, they would regard it as being like a dream or an illusion. Since they do not even establish the "true," how much less could they establish the "false"?
Therefore, one cannot raise the objection that "falsehood arises from the true. One can only harbor doubts regarding the School of the Dharma-nature (Faxingzong).
The School of Nature (Xingzong) uses the sutras and treatises of this school to argue that delusion arises based upon the Truth (zhen), as it is said: "The Dharma-body flows through the five paths;
the Tathāgatagarbha undergoes suffering and pleasure according to good and evil. Awakening to the fact that delusion is itself the Truth is as it is said:

"At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; knowing that delusion is fundamentally Truth, seeing the Buddha is itself the purity of a Bodhisattva."
The fusion of ordinary beings and sages is like the clouds; it is as if all sentient beings have from the beginning realized equal and perfect enlightenment.
Within the body of Vairocana’s parinirvāṇa, the sentient beings of the three realms and six paths are fully present.

Although there are many gates for realizing the mutual identity of the true and the false, this passage serves as an analogy for the immeasurable [teachings] stating that afflictions and bodhi are without beginning and without end.

Furthermore, it is taught that only when afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely exhausted is one called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is also termed "Initial Enlightenment" (*ādi-bodhi*).
However, the textual meanings and doctrinal principles of the sixth and seventh assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the beginning and end of the *Awakening of Faith* are mutually contradictory;

moreover, these are all teachings from definitive (*nītārtha*) One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) sūtras, and since one cannot selectively reject one while retaining another, they are already fully contained within this single sūtra.
It is said that one cannot select the former while rejecting the latter, nor select the latter while rejecting the former; yet when one attempts to synthesize them, they are difficult to reconcile.
If both are employed together, they contradict one another and can hardly be unified as a single truth. Therefore, I venture to ask the scholars of the world:

if there were one among them who had attained true realization of the Way, he would know that Fu Li was not lacking in understanding. This is a question posed for the purpose of testing, not for the sake of seeking out a person. Now...
The answers given by all those present were entirely confused regarding the intent of the question;

they all spoke in terms of dissolving appearances to return to principle, failing to understand at all the reason why delusion arises from the True from which the questioner was asking, nor the principle of cultivating and realizing the illusory within the Real.

Since the arising of delusion from the True has its causes and conditions, and the cessation of delusion to return to the True is not without its underlying reasons, and since they did not comprehend this, they ought to have remained silent.
Now, I shall merely describe my own view of the signless and the unconditioned; why then do you present these questions?

Furthermore, Master Fali, do you not know that both the true and the false are quiescent, and that both principle and phenomena are suchness? Within this quiescence of suchness, how can there be question and answer?

Nevertheless, there are two approaches through which the meaning and principle may be easily explained and understood, and which are free from contradiction or obstruction: first, one may exclusively speak of the existence of delusion that can be [eliminated].
The severance of existence and the true realization—these two are consistently taught as being neither true nor false, and neither noble nor ordinary;
these two gates are both conceivable and discussable. That which is difficult to explain and difficult to understand is that these two gates coexist without mutual contradiction or obstruction;
this is precisely what is inconceivable. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speaks of the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings as being "non-existent."
It is said that the defilement by afflictions—being undefiled yet defiled, and being defiled yet undefiled—is difficult to comprehend.
Fuli now asks: regarding this discussion, why do you answer only by speaking of "stainless defilement"?
Only the Master Huayan Shuzhu’s response—which posits that True Suchness is unchanging yet unimpeded in its conformity with conditions—is truly precise. Fuli thus explains his original question.
The intent behind the questions posed by the various worthies that Zongmi has set forth is for all people to reach a definitive resolution;
however, if one does not set a standard for oneself and instead merely cites examples from afar, how can one encourage others? Therefore, I shall attempt to answer as follows.
Fundamentally pure and fundamentally non-awakened, From this, deluded thoughts arise.
Knowing that truth and delusion are both empty, And knowing that emptiness and delusion are both still, The state of stillness is called "having an end. In delusion, it is termed "beginningless";
Yet causes and conditions are like illusions and dreams— What end can there be, and what beginning? This is the source of all successive births.

Regarding the statement that "the ultimate source of birth and death" is the mind, many students believe this truly means that the real gives rise to the false; thus, they doubt whether the false can ever be completely exhausted.
To resolve this principle, I shall provide another exposition as a response to the previous verse.
It is not that the real gives rise to the delusory; The delusory arises from being deluded regarding the real.

To know that the delusory is fundamentally real, And to know that with the real, delusion ceases— When delusion ceases, it seems like an end; But when awakening comes, it seems like a beginning. The nature of both delusion and awakening is empty;
In the emptiness of nature, there is neither end nor beginning. Birth and death arise because of delusion regarding this.
Having realized this, one transcends birth and death;
though human hearts differ between north and south, the Buddha-dharma remains the same from ancient times to the present. Thus, one does not destroy true illumination while engaging with the mundane.

Returning to form to discern emptiness, one probes the profound depths only to find the "imageless" (wangxiang). To lose the essential meaning is to be as ignorant as a child; when attachment exists, there is contention.

Through the delusions of false sentiment, one may naturally attain realization and experience the coolness of the Way. —A Verse on Realization by Qingliang (Zongmi) *Note: This verse is attributed to Zongmi (780–841), the founder of the Weishi (Consciousness-Only) school in China and a key figure in the Huayan tradition. It reflects his synthesis of Yogācāra and Tathāgatagarbha thought.*
To realize the nature of True Suchness, one must dispel the emotions of attachment and forgetfulness. Where there is a mind, there is the path of birth and death;
where there is no thought, there is the city of Nirvana. Who then presides over afflictions? Even Bodhi is but a provisional name.
When discriminative views do not exist, the Way of the Buddha is spontaneously accomplished.
Chan Master Huangbo’s Verse on the Great Dharma-Assembly Site of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s Dharmadhātu: Without moving a single hair, all is manifested at once;
though past and present differ, there is no coming or going. How could there ever be shortness or length in the extension and contraction [of time]?
The principal and its attendants interpenetrate like a net of Indra; The holy and the ordinary intersect like the light of a lamp.
Vairocana is fundamentally free from manifold appearances: If it is blue, it is simply blue; if it is yellow, it is simply yellow.
—A verse by Master Luohan.
The true realm of Avataṃsaka is vast as the sands of the Ganges; Each mote of dust and every hair-pore contains the entire Dharma-realm.
In the City of Enlightenment of the Five Stages, there is no longer any need for gathering or dwelling; Where could one seek further among these hundredfold layers?
Thoroughly clarifying the primary and secondary aspects within the perfect reality, One suddenly awakens to Vairocana and transcends all cultivation.
Do not say you have never been to the South; A single orb of bright moon seals the Mid-Autumn night.
Composed by Bai Juyi on the theme of Chan, based on "Ultimate Emptiness Beyond Characteristics":
One must know that all characteristics are non-characteristics; If one dwells in the state of no-remainder, there is yet a remainder.
To speak of "under the words" is to fear the words; to say "at once it is finished" is a dream within a dream—both are but double layers of empty space.
How could flowers in the sky ever seek out fruit? How can one further seek fish in a mirage?
To still the movement is Zen; Zen is movement. When there is neither Zen nor movement, that is suchness (*tathatā*).
On the Unimpeded Harmony of Principle and Phenomena (the following four verses), composed by the Śramaṇa Sicun.
When will the signless ever depart from the signful? Where can that which has a remainder obstruct that which is without remainder?
To say that forgetting words is "understanding" is not yet true understanding; To speak of dreams as empty is merely to cling to emptiness.
Though empty flowers may wither and empty fruits may form, how could this hinder illusory water producing illusory fish?
Non-meditation is motionless yet eternally meditative; when the movement of meditation is melted away, one accords with Suchness.
This reveals the Perfect Teaching, which is all-pervasive and universally inclusive.
The myriad virtues are perfectly integrated within a single thought-moment; this single thought encompasses the nine ages, past and present alike.
Form and emptiness differ yet are not two; essence and appearance interpenetrate without encroaching upon one another.
Mountains are not high, for kalpas are vast; rivers are not deep, for their paths are profound.
In my school, every phenomenon is fundamentally thus; if you wish to seek it, try seeking it briefly:
the primary and secondary realms rest upon the adamantine wheel, situated upon a great lotus flower; the Indra-net is originally my own home.
Why have you returned to within the triple world? You have turned your back on the ocean of lands and disobeyed the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The body of perfect retribution, endowed with all virtues in a state of complete interfusion—this very body is fundamentally of the same nature as my own.
For what reason does delusion and stagnation arise from this? One separately perceives the void as a cluster of dust.
A Verse on the Contemplation of True Emptiness Beyond All Characteristics (the following four verses are by the Śramaṇa Youcheng):
If you wish to know the principle of true emptiness, True emptiness is empty yet not empty; Though the paths of mountain streams differ, [they flow into the same sea].
Clouds and moon are fundamentally one;
this is the verse on the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena:
When principle is perfected, all marks vanish; The mind expands and the objects return to their source, Like the moon in every house last night.
Pure light blends with the great void, pervading everywhere and encompassing all hymns of contemplation.
Now present before us— Who comes after? Who comes first? Whether ordinary or sagely, there is no mind and no partiality.
The numinous light suddenly pours forth; daily life is luminously clear.
In a mere flash, if one lets it pass, one is sent from East to West—from China to India.
The Dharma is not in words; the Way is beyond speech. The ancestral style of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was never transmitted.
Strike the silence so that emptiness resounds; Forget the contrivances so that the lotus blooms from fire.
The wondrous purport of the Avataṃsaka accords with the Three Contemplations; The profound principle of the Vaipulya unites the Ten Mysteries.
Precious indeed is the partial realization that returns to the Sea-land; The One Vehicle brilliantly expounds the Great Conditions.
Sent off Guang Huayan to Xuedou by the Śramaṇa Renyue:
The Flower Treasury World—dust mote after dust mote reveals Samantabhadra; Seeking Xuedou from afar, what further cause could there be?
If anyone should ask you on the road, Do not say that you have left the sutras to study Chan.
Instruction to the Assembly (the following five verses), composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào.
Transcending Vairocana, surpassing Śākyamuni— All such things are like frogs competing for springtime.
Where in this eye could specks of dust ever be hidden? In emptiness, flowers have never taken root.
Studying the Way, how could one know it turns one’s back on the Great Way? Leaving home—who would believe one has not yet left the home?
How lamentable, dwelling deep in the forest clad in coarse wool; A bowl of cooked rice and two cups of tea.
Studying the teachings, practicing Chan, wandering in all four directions— Competing for fame and vying for profit, when will it ever cease?
The spirit merely chases the moon within the jar; who could know that this body and life are but bubbles upon the water?
Running through the dust and toil, one vainly sinks into anxiety; even hiding away in forests and fields is but a deluded scheme.
Only in recent years have I begun to recognize the true path home; I vow to bow my head in devotion to Amitābha.
Cultivating one's nature to harmonize with the multitude—how can such cultivation be called true cultivation? One must strictly avoid exhausting the spirit by seeking outward;
even at such a moment, one has already missed it. Even when there is a sudden resonance, one still lingers in hesitation.
Raising the mallet and brandishing the whisk still results in clumsiness; seeking commentaries and searching the sutras merely follows the current.
If you wish to recognize the ultimate meaning within the bamboo tube, you must directly ensure that the needle and the magnet meet in perfect alignment.
Fengyuan attained self-mastery through deep cultivation; one must emulate those of old and compete against the passing moments.
Fine rain falls in drifts, filling the ocean; motes of dust fly and gather, rising to high peaks.
Chasing empty profit on red thoroughfares leads only to death; with white hair and a mastery of the classics, one still cannot resolve the mind.
I delight in studying this principle with my peers; Only then do I realize there is neither past nor present.
In our shared vocation as students, we do not distance ourselves from our duties; We take up the classics to polish that single point of spiritual brilliance.
The curtains do not hinder the reception of the night moon; With an empty satchel, you must surely gather more autumn fireflies.
One should maintain the resolve of a Great Being while harboring the integrity of Cao Cao; Do not follow the common crowd by being the only one awake.
Diligent at the desk, forgetting both sleep and food— In years to come, who will surpass the green of the indigo?
Composed by the Chan Master Jingyuan of the Sanzhao Gate. An Inquiry Concerning the Xianshou School’s Doctrinal Judgments:

Question: The One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka* is precisely the source of the "One Mind" in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. Since this mind permeates all phenomena, it is already...
Because it establishes the four kinds of dharma-realms, Guifeng [Zongmi] considered it to be all-encompassing across all teachings and far superior to them;

he spoke of "perfection" (yuan) solely in terms of the one mind. Thus, while the *Awakening of Faith* takes the one mind as its fundamental source, Xianshou’s judgment was that this teaching pertains to the "mind at the end" and encompasses both the Sudden and the Gradual, yet does not include the Perfect. This stands in contrast to Guifeng’s own words.
How extraordinary! Now, for a long time, the hearts of these students have been filled with indignation and their mouths with the desire to speak; how could they remain silent?
There are discrepancies in the judgment of the teachings.
Question: Guifeng’s discourse on the origin of humanity begins with the human and celestial realms and concludes with the revelation of the nature, wherein the five teachings are contained.
Xianshou’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* first treats the Hīnayāna and subsequently the Perfect Teaching, wherein the five chapters are fully prepared.
Now, Xianshou is the patriarch of Guifeng, and Guifeng is the descendant of Xianshou; why is it that the traces of these descendants are identical?

Is there a difference in the efficacy of their doctrinal classifications? Nevertheless, since these two masters must have had a definitive basis for their teachings on the Way and its meaning, one should extract their excellent words to analyze both sides.
Regarding the Confucian and Buddhist explanations of "nature" (xing): [text continues]

Question: Those who specialize in the Three Piṭakas do not perceive the texts within the secular realm, and those who study the Six Classics exclusively do not understand the teachings beyond this world.
Thus, while the Duke of Zhou and Confucius rarely spoke of nature (*xing*) and destiny (*ming*), the instructions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are detailed.
Furthermore, Li Xizhi of the Great Tang followed Mencius, asserting that human nature is good; Du Ziwai took the school of Xunzi as his model, asserting that—

Regarding the nature of human beings as being evil, Huangfu Shi examined the views of Yang Xiong, who maintained that human nature is a mixture of good and evil. Furthermore, the Master of Han stated:
"Those at the highest level are good; those at the lowest level are evil; and those in the middle are mixed.

Among the scholar-officials (*shenshen*) of the Holy Song, such as Ouyang Yongshu, Zhang Biaomin, Wang Chen, and others, their theories were not uniform. They exhausted themselves in the study of principles and investigated the histories and records to the utmost.
Among the Six Classics and the works of various worthies, which ones accord with our teaching?
The National Teacher Xianshou, in a letter sent from the East Sea,
addressed the monk Fazang of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Capital of Tang.
The Great Avataṃsaka Dharma Master of Silla in海东 (East Sea), along with his attendant, have for over twenty years looked toward you with a sincerity that has never left their hearts or heads.
Furthermore, separated by ten thousand *li* of misty clouds and a thousand *li* of sea and land, this one lifetime prevents us from meeting again;
how can we express our grief and longing? This is surely due to shared causes from past lives. Now...
Born with shared karma, we have received this retribution together; we have all bathed in the Great Sūtra and been specially favored by our former teacher’s bestowal of this profound scripture.

We look up to the Venerable Master who, after returning to his native land, expounded the *Avataṃsaka*, proclaimed the Dharma-realm, and manifested the layered, interpenetrating net of Indra—a realm of Buddhas ever-new—bringing vast benefit and merit that deepens our joy. Thus we know that the Tathāgata...
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is only the Dharma Master who can cause the sun of the Buddha’s radiance to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more and ensure that the Dharma abides for a long time.

Although I, Fazang, have made no progress in my spiritual advancement and lack depth in my practice, I look up to this scripture with longing and feel both shame and gratitude toward my former teacher.
I shall uphold it according to my capacity and cannot bear to let it go; I hope to rely on this merit to form the causes for future lives. I do so simply...
The Master’s commentaries are rich in meaning yet concise in expression, making it difficult for later generations to enter their depths.

Therefore, I have recorded the Master’s subtle words and profound intent in full to compile this *Yiji* (Record of Meaning). I now respectfully entrust this work to the Venerable Shengquan to transcribe and carry back to his native land so that it may be transmitted there.
I pray that you, O Honored One, will examine its merits and flaws and graciously provide me with correction and instruction. I humbly beseech you to grant your favor.

In a future life, when casting off this body and receiving another, may I join the assembly of Vairocana to hear and receive such inexhaustible, wondrous Dharma, and practice such inexhaustible vows and conduct of Samantabhadra.

Should I, due to other evil karma, suddenly fall into ruin, I humbly hope that the Honored One will not forget our former connection and, while I am among the various realms of existence, show me the path of the True Person; thereafter, when I have gained faith, I shall come to visit you.
Fazang bows respectfully regarding matters of life and death (the twenty-eighth day of the first month).

The *Huayan tantuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka) in twenty fascicles—two of which are not yet complete; the *Yicheng jiaofen ji* (Record on the Classification of the One Vehicle Teachings) in three fascicles;

the *Xuanyi zhang deng zami* (Chapter on the Profound Meaning and Miscellaneous Meanings) in one fascicle; and the *Biefan huayan jing zhong fanyu* (Sanskrit Terms from the Separate Translation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) in one fascicle begin here.

The Stone Record of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Society.
There was a monk named Nancuo from Longxing Temple in Hangzhou who, during the second year of the Changqing era, requested the monk Daofeng of Lingyin Temple to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
When they reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" (*Huazang shijie pin*) and heard of its vast,
magnificent, and pure matters, Nancuo rejoiced and made a vow, wishing to exhort one hundred thousand people— both monastics and laypeople— to recite the *Avataṃsaka*.
There was one scripture in ten thousand fascicles, and he further exhorted a thousand people to recite one scroll of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Every year, during the four months of the seasons, this assembly gathered in a great conclave; they organized themselves into a society and observed fasts.
From the summer of the second year until the autumn of this year, there have been some ten or more such fasts. At each fast, they held incense, knelt on their right knees, and addressed the Buddha.

He said, "I vow that in a future life, I shall be born upon a precious lotus-golden wheel in the midst of the great fragrant ocean within the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpasaṃcayadhātu), before the presence of Vairocana Tathāgata, together with one hundred thousand people—this would suffice.

Furthermore, he recruited funds from among the assembly to purchase ten *qǐng* of fertile land, taking its annual yield to provide for the permanent support of vegetarian offerings. I heard this previously when I was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou.
Cao made this vow when he was serving as the Governor of Suzhou; now that he has achieved this merit, Cao personally came to me at Suzhou and requested it three times, saying:
"I am eighty-one years old; my life draws to a close day by day. I fear that after I am gone, those who come to the temple and the hall may not be able to continue my resolve.

Among the ancient collections of Tōdai-ji in Nanto, many volumes were damaged by woodworms; only this single copy remains, while the rest have been sought in vain.
It is a pity that this has not yet been obtained; I shed tears and leave it here.
One day, Qikong (契空), the Master of Pure Practices, came to my lodgings and discussed this matter at length.
We reached an agreement and he pledged to take charge of it with great reverence and joy beyond measure. He immediately commanded the Dharma Master Yingxian Ciyuan to have it transcribed.
Copied on the ninth day of the month of Yi-ze in the year Gengyin, the seventh year of the Bao Yong era,
by the Dharma Seal Jinxing of the Four-Saints Monastery.
